Question: A restaurant writes step-by-step instructions for opening each morning. What is this?
A: A lease agreement for the building
B: A financial report for investors
C: A standard operating procedure
D: A marketing plan for new customers
Why A: A lease agreement is a legal contract for renting the building and does not give steps for opening the restaurant.
Why B: A financial report for investors shows money results and does not describe steps for opening the restaurant each morning.
Why C: Step-by-step written instructions for a routine task are a standard operating procedure, which keeps work consistent from day to day.
Why D: A marketing plan outlines how to attract customers and does not give steps for opening the restaurant.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is quality?
A: How well a product or service meets customer needs
B: How many products a company sells in a given year
C: How large a product is when it is packaged for sale
D: How expensive a product is to produce in the factory
Why A: Quality is how well a product or service meets customer needs and expectations, including reliability, performance and satisfaction.
Why B: How many products a company sells is sales volume, which does not tell whether those products meet customer needs.
Why C: The packaged size of a product is a physical attribute, and size alone does not define quality.
Why D: Production cost describes expense to the firm, and it does not show how well a product meets customer needs.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is quality assurance?
A: Reducing the number of inspections to save money
B: Paying customers to ignore defects in what they buy
C: Checking finished products for defects only at the end
D: Planned activities that prevent defects from happening
Why A: Reducing inspections to save money may let defects through; quality assurance is planned prevention, not cutting checks to save cost.
Why B: Paying customers to ignore defects hides problems instead of fixing them, so it is not quality assurance.
Why C: Checking only finished products for defects is quality control, which detects problems after production rather than preventing them.
Why D: Quality assurance is planned activities that prevent defects from happening, such as training, standards and process design, built into production from the start.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is the best example of quality assurance rather than quality control?
A: Training workers on correct assembly steps before production begins
B: Inspecting finished items at the end and removing broken ones
C: Counting the number of items rejected last week by checkers
D: Testing a sample of items after they are packed for sale today
Why A: Training workers on correct assembly steps before production prevents defects in advance, which is quality assurance because it focuses on the process.
Why B: Inspecting finished items and removing broken ones detects defects after the work is done, which is quality control and not assurance.
Why C: Counting the items rejected last week measures results after the fact, which is a quality control measure and not prevention.
Why D: Testing a sample of items after packing finds defects after production, so it is quality control rather than quality assurance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a defect?
A: A package that is colorful and attractive to buyers
B: A price that is lower than rivals' prices for an item
C: A flaw that makes a product fail to meet standards
D: A feature that customers love and often ask for
Why A: A colorful package is an appearance feature and not a flaw that makes a product fail its standards.
Why B: A price lower than rivals is a pricing advantage and does not mean the product fails to meet quality standards.
Why C: A defect is a flaw that makes a product fail to meet standards or customer expectations, such as a crack or wrong size.
Why D: A feature customers love is a strength and not a flaw, so it cannot be a defect.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is total quality management (TQM)?
A: A method that focuses only on lowering prices of goods in the market
B: A company-wide approach to continuous improvement and customer satisfaction
C: A method that ignores customer feedback and all complaints from buyers
D: A method where only inspectors are responsible for the quality of goods
Why A: TQM is not only about lowering prices; it focuses on quality and customer satisfaction, not on price cutting alone.
Why B: Total quality management is a company-wide approach in which every employee works for continuous improvement and customer satisfaction.
Why C: TQM uses customer feedback and complaints as inputs for improvement, so ignoring them is the opposite of the method.
Why D: In TQM everyone shares responsibility for quality, so it is not left only to inspectors.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is continuous improvement?
A: Waiting for customers to complain before acting on it at all
B: Making ongoing small changes that raise quality and efficiency
C: Avoiding any change to existing methods or tools used in the plant
D: Making one large change and never changing it again afterward
Why A: Waiting for complaints is reactive; continuous improvement looks for ways to get better without waiting for customers to report problems.
Why B: Continuous improvement means making ongoing small changes that raise quality and efficiency over time, as in the Japanese practice of Kaizen.
Why C: Avoiding change to methods stops improvement, which is the opposite of the continuous effort to get better.
Why D: Making one large change and never changing again is a one-time fix, while continuous improvement is a steady, repeated effort.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A factory team meets weekly to find small ways to reduce waste. Which idea does this show?
A: Continuous improvement
B: Price fixing by rivals
C: Channel conflict in retail
D: Market skimming plans
Why A: Weekly meetings finding small ways to cut waste show continuous improvement, in which teams keep making small gains in quality and efficiency.
Why B: Price fixing by rivals is an illegal agreement on prices, and it has nothing to do with a team reducing waste.
Why C: Channel conflict arises when distribution partners compete, which has no relation to a factory team reducing waste.
Why D: Market skimming plans, or price skimming, set a high initial price on a new product, which is unrelated to cutting waste in production.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a quality standard?
A: A slogan that the company uses in its ads and signs
B: A discount offered to loyal customers of the firm
C: A measure or rule a product must meet to be acceptable
D: A schedule for delivering products to the customers
Why A: A slogan is a catchy advertising phrase used to promote a brand, not a measure of how good a product must be.
Why B: A loyalty discount is a pricing and promotion tool that rewards repeat buyers; it says nothing about the level of quality a product must reach.
Why C: A quality standard is a measure or rule a product must meet to be acceptable, such as size, strength or safety limits, so products are consistent and customers know what to expect.
Why D: A delivery schedule is a logistics and operations plan for when goods arrive; it does not define the level of quality a product must meet.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is ISO 9001?
A: A tax form for international sales, filed with customs
B: A law that sets minimum wages for workers in the state
C: A union agreement for workers about pay and work hours
D: An international standard for quality management systems
Why A: A customs form for international sales is a trade document; ISO 9001 is not a tax form and has nothing to do with filing duties.
Why B: Minimum wage rules come from government labor law such as the Fair Labor Standards Act; ISO 9001 is a voluntary standard, not a wage law.
Why C: Union agreements covering pay and hours are called collective bargaining contracts; ISO 9001 is not a labor agreement but a quality management standard.
Why D: ISO 9001 is an international standard from the International Organization for Standardization that sets requirements for quality management systems, helping firms show they consistently meet customer needs and improve their processes.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why might a supplier seek ISO 9001 certification?
A: To avoid inspecting its own products ever again after a sale
B: To raise the price of its goods above competitors' prices
C: To stop customers from comparing suppliers on price or quality
D: To show customers its processes meet recognized quality standards
Why A: Certification does not end inspections; ISO 9001 requires ongoing checks, records and audits, so a certified supplier still must verify its own products.
Why B: ISO 9001 does not set or raise prices; certification may help win business, but price depends on costs and competition rather than the standard itself.
Why C: Customers can always compare suppliers on price and quality; certification gives buyers more information about quality, it does not stop them from comparing.
Why D: Certification, checked by an outside auditor, shows customers a supplier's processes meet a recognized quality standard, which builds trust, helps win contracts and often is required by large buyers.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is Six Sigma?
A: A method that aims to reduce defects and variation in processes
B: A method of setting six different prices for one product
C: A method of printing six copies of reports for managers
D: A method of hiring six new managers for the firm's team
Why A: Six Sigma is a data-driven method that aims to cut defects and variation in processes, targeting about 3.4 defects per million opportunities, using steps like DMAIC to improve quality.
Why B: Six Sigma is about process quality, not pricing; setting several prices for one product would be price discrimination or tiered pricing, an unrelated idea.
Why C: Printing copies of reports is a clerical task; Six Sigma is a quality improvement method and has nothing to do with producing six report copies.
Why D: Six Sigma does not mean hiring six managers; the name comes from a statistical measure of variation, and the method focuses on defects, not staffing.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is benchmarking?
A: Ignoring rivals to focus on a firm's own internal data
B: Setting the lowest possible goals for a team to reach
C: Comparing a firm's performance with the best in the industry
D: Counting the benches in a company's front lobby each month
Why A: Benchmarking looks outward at other firms; ignoring rivals to use only internal data is the opposite of comparing against the best performers.
Why B: Benchmarking is used to find higher targets and improve; setting the lowest possible goals would prevent improvement rather than measure against the best.
Why C: Benchmarking compares a firm's performance, products or processes against the best in the industry to find gaps and learn practices that can raise its own quality and efficiency.
Why D: Benchmarking has nothing to do with literal benches; it is a management comparison technique, and counting lobby furniture measures no performance at all.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A delivery company compares its on-time rate with the industry leader's. What is this?
A: Market study
B: Benchmarking
C: Price fixing
D: Stock counting
Why A: A market study researches customers, demand and competitors to guide decisions; it does not compare on-time delivery performance against an industry leader.
Why B: Comparing the firm's on-time rate with the industry leader's is benchmarking, a quality technique that measures performance against the best so the company can see gaps and set improvement goals.
Why C: Price fixing is an illegal agreement among competitors to set prices; comparing delivery performance with a leader is unrelated to it.
Why D: Stock counting is an inventory task that tallies goods on hand; it does not measure delivery performance against a competitor.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a customer complaint?
A: A statement that a product or service did not meet expectations
B: A compliment about excellent service from a happy customer
C: An order for more products from a customer in the same town
D: A request to open a new account at a bank branch in the town
Why A: A customer complaint is a statement that a product or service did not meet expectations, which gives a firm direct feedback it can use to find and fix quality problems.
Why B: A compliment praises good service; a complaint is the opposite, since it reports that something fell short of what the customer expected.
Why C: An order for more products is a sale; it shows demand but does not report dissatisfaction, so it is not a complaint.
Why D: Asking to open an account is a banking service request; it expresses no dissatisfaction, so it is not a complaint.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the best way to treat customer complaints?
A: Blame the customer for every issue that comes up
B: Ignore them so staff stay positive and avoid bad news
C: Treat them as feedback that can reveal quality problems
D: Delete them from the record to keep the files neat
Why A: Blaming customers hides real problems and drives them away; effective firms listen to complaints instead of pointing fingers at buyers.
Why B: Ignoring complaints may feel comfortable but leaves problems unsolved, loses customers and invites bad word of mouth, which harms the business more than hearing the bad news.
Why C: Complaints are valuable feedback that can reveal quality problems, so firms should record, respond and use them to improve products and service, which also helps win back unhappy customers.
Why D: Deleting complaints erases the evidence needed to spot patterns and fix causes; tidy files are not worth losing information about quality.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a root cause?
A: The cost of fixing the problem once
B: The first person who noticed the problem
C: The most visible symptom of the problem
D: The underlying reason a problem happens
Why A: The cost of fixing a problem measures its impact after the fact; it does not tell you why the problem happens, which is the root cause.
Why B: Who first noticed a problem is just a reporting detail; the root cause is the underlying reason, not the person who spotted it.
Why C: The most visible symptom is the surface effect of a problem; fixing only symptoms lets the real cause keep producing the same trouble.
Why D: A root cause is the underlying reason a problem happens; fixing it prevents the problem from returning, while fixing only symptoms leaves the cause in place.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A store keeps getting damaged shipments. Replacing items each time does not stop it. What should it do?
A: Keep replacing items forever without checking why they break
B: Find and fix the cause, such as poor packing or rough handling
C: Blame customers for the damage done to the shipments they get
D: Stop selling any products that come in by shipment from them
Why A: Replacing items forever treats the symptom, costs money each time and never prevents damage; the shipments will keep breaking without a look at why.
Why B: Finding and fixing the root cause, such as poor packing or rough handling, stops the damage at its source, saves replacement costs and keeps customers satisfied.
Why C: Blaming customers does not explain damage that occurs in transit, and it hurts the store's reputation without stopping the damage itself.
Why D: Stopping sales of everything that ships is an extreme overreaction that loses revenue and still leaves the actual packing or handling problem unsolved.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a quality audit?
A: A review of employees' vacation days and time off requests
B: A review that checks whether quality procedures are followed
C: A review of competitors' prices and advertising spend this year
D: A review of how much tax a firm owes, done by the state
Why A: Reviewing vacation requests is an HR and payroll task; a quality audit looks at procedures and products, not employee time off.
Why B: A quality audit is a systematic review that checks whether quality procedures and standards are followed, finding gaps so the firm can correct them before customers are affected.
Why C: Reviewing competitors' prices and advertising is market analysis; a quality audit examines the firm's own procedures, not rivals' marketing.
Why D: Checking how much tax a firm owes is a tax audit by a tax agency; a quality audit reviews quality procedures instead.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a warranty claim a sign of?
A: A growing market for a new product line
B: A successful promotion campaign last month
C: A possible quality problem with a product
D: A fall in the product's price last month
Why A: A growing market shows up as rising sales and demand; warranty claims arise when products fail, so they signal problems instead of growth.
Why B: A successful promotion would raise sales or awareness; warranty claims come after purchase from product failures, not from advertising effectiveness.
Why C: Warranty claims are made when products fail or disappoint, so a rise in claims is a sign of a possible quality problem in design, materials or manufacturing.
Why D: A price drop affects what customers pay; warranty claims are tied to product performance after the sale, not to the price charged.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Warranty claims for one model jump 40 percent in a month. What should management do?
A: Investigate the cause and take corrective action
B: Remove all warranties from the product line
C: Ignore the rise because sales are up overall
D: Raise the price of the model immediately by half
Why A: A 40 percent jump in claims signals a likely defect, so management should investigate the cause and take corrective action to protect customers, costs and the brand.
Why B: Removing warranties would not fix the defect; it would anger customers, hurt trust and probably cut sales while the product still fails.
Why C: Rising sales do not excuse a sharp rise in claims; ignoring it lets a defect spread to more customers and increases repair costs.
Why D: Raising the price by half does not address why the model fails and would likely hurt sales while the quality problem continues.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a service quality gap?
A: The difference between a firm's sales and its yearly goals
B: The difference between a firm's cost and its final sale price
C: The difference between two competing products' prices in the market
D: The difference between what customers expect and what they receive
Why A: The difference between sales and yearly goals is a performance gap against targets; it is not about customers' expectations versus service received.
Why B: The difference between cost and sale price is the profit margin; it is a financial measure, not a service quality gap.
Why C: A difference between competitors' prices is a price gap in the market; it says nothing about how service compares to customer expectations.
Why D: A service quality gap is the difference between what customers expect and what they actually receive; closing it improves satisfaction and loyalty.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A hotel promises quiet rooms but guests report noisy hallways. What is this?
A: A pricing strategy
B: A channel decision
C: A successful promotion
D: A service quality gap
Why A: Pricing strategy is about setting what customers pay; a noisy hallway is a failure to deliver a promised service quality, not a price decision.
Why B: A channel decision is about distribution, how products reach customers; noisy hallways are a service experience problem instead.
Why C: A successful promotion would attract guests; here the hotel's promise did not match reality, which damages satisfaction rather than showing promotion success.
Why D: The hotel promised quiet rooms but guests experience noise, so what customers expect differs from what they get, which is a service quality gap that harms satisfaction and reviews.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does zero defects mean as a goal?
A: Producing nothing so no defects can ever occur
B: Striving to make every product right the first time
C: Hiding defects from customers who buy the product
D: Accepting any number of defects as quite normal
Why A: Zero defects does not mean producing nothing; it means making products correctly, so idle production would make no sense as a quality goal.
Why B: Zero defects is a goal of striving to do every task and product right the first time, preventing errors instead of fixing them later, which reduces waste and rework.
Why C: Hiding defects from customers is deceptive and unethical, and it may be illegal; zero defects aims to prevent defects, not conceal them.
Why D: Accepting any number of defects is the opposite of zero defects, which sets perfection as the goal even if it is hard to reach.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is just-in-time (JIT) production?
A: Making large amounts of goods far ahead of orders
B: Making goods only once each year in a single batch
C: Making goods only as they are needed to reduce waste
D: Making goods without any plan for what is needed
Why A: Making large amounts far ahead of orders is mass production for stock, which builds inventory; JIT does the opposite by matching output to demand.
Why B: Producing once a year in a single batch creates huge inventory and long waits; JIT produces frequently in small amounts as needed.
Why C: Just-in-time makes goods only as they are needed, with materials arriving as production requires, which cuts storage costs, waste and tied-up cash.
Why D: JIT depends on careful planning and close coordination with suppliers; producing without any plan would cause shortages or waste, not efficiency.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is a risk of just-in-time production?
A: A supply delay can halt production because there is little stock
B: Paying high storage costs for huge stockpiles of parts held
C: Having too much unsold inventory in storage for a whole year
D: Wasting materials through overproduction of goods nobody buys
Why A: Because JIT holds little stock, a supply delay can halt production, and that makes dependable suppliers critical to avoid costly shutdowns and late orders.
Why B: High storage costs for huge stockpiles are a problem of traditional stock-heavy methods; JIT reduces that cost instead of creating it.
Why C: Too much unsold inventory is what JIT is meant to avoid, since it produces only what is needed, so this is not its risk.
Why D: Overproduction of unwanted goods is the waste JIT targets by producing to order, so it is a benefit of JIT rather than a risk.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is customer satisfaction?
A: The number of products a company makes each day at its plants
B: The number of stores a company owns in the whole country
C: The price a customer pays for a product in a shop today
D: How well a product or service meets or exceeds expectations
Why A: Daily output counts production volume; it measures what a plant makes, not how customers feel about what they received.
Why B: The number of stores measures company size and reach, not whether customers are happy with products or service.
Why C: The price paid is a cost to the customer; satisfaction depends on how value and quality compare to expectations, not on price alone.
Why D: Customer satisfaction is how well a product or service meets or exceeds expectations, and satisfied customers tend to return, buy more and recommend the business.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which action best raises customer satisfaction?
A: Making returns more difficult for the customers
B: Reducing the training that service staff receive
C: Listening to feedback and fixing recurring problems
D: Ignoring feedback to save time and effort each day
Why A: Making returns harder frustrates buyers and lowers trust; easy returns usually raise satisfaction, so this choice would reduce it.
Why B: Cutting training leaves staff less able to help, which leads to more mistakes and unhappy customers, so satisfaction would fall.
Why C: Listening to feedback and fixing recurring problems shows customers they are valued and removes the causes of dissatisfaction, which raises satisfaction and loyalty over time.
Why D: Ignoring feedback saves little time and lets problems continue, so customers stay unhappy and may leave for competitors.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk?
A: A reward for taking a good decision at work
B: The chance that something will cause loss or harm
C: A certain outcome that cannot be avoided by anyone
D: A report on past results of the firm for the board
Why A: A reward is a positive result of a good decision; risk concerns the possibility of loss or harm, not a payoff.
Why B: Risk is the chance that something will cause loss or harm, such as theft, injury, fire or lawsuits, and managing it helps businesses protect people, assets and profits.
Why C: Risk involves uncertainty; a certain outcome that no one can avoid is not a risk but a known event.
Why D: A report on past results is a record of what already happened; risk looks ahead at the possibility of loss.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk management?
A: Identifying, assessing and reducing risks
B: Ignoring risks until a loss occurs at work
C: Taking as many risks as you possibly can
D: Avoiding all customers in the market
Why A: Risk management means identifying, assessing and reducing risks, using steps like avoiding, reducing, transferring or accepting them to protect people, property and profits.
Why B: Ignoring risks until a loss occurs is reactive and costly; risk management is planned and proactive, aiming to prevent losses before they happen.
Why C: Taking as many risks as possible would invite losses; risk management weighs risks and controls them, not seeks them out.
Why D: Avoiding all customers would end the business; risk management targets specific threats and does not mean giving up on sales.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What are the four basic ways to handle risk?
A: Ignore, hide, delay or deny the risk
B: Avoid, reduce, transfer or accept it
C: Buy, sell, trade or lend the risk
D: Print, store, mail or recycle it
Why A: Ignoring, hiding, delaying or denying risks are poor habits, not recognized strategies; none of them actually reduces the chance or impact of a loss.
Why B: The four basic ways to handle risk are to avoid, reduce, transfer or accept it, and a firm picks the one that fits how likely and costly the risk is.
Why C: Buying, selling, trading or lending are financial or commercial actions; they are not the standard strategies for handling a risk.
Why D: Printing, storing, mailing or recycling are paperwork or waste tasks, not risk management strategies recognized in business.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk avoidance?
A: Accepting the risk and planning to cover losses
B: Buying insurance to cover a loss that may occur
C: Taking steps to lower the chance of a loss or harm
D: Choosing not to do an activity that carries a risk
Why A: Accepting the risk and planning for losses is risk acceptance, where the firm chooses to bear the loss instead of avoiding it.
Why B: Buying insurance is risk transfer, because it shifts the financial burden of a possible loss to an insurer instead of avoiding the activity.
Why C: Taking steps to lower the chance of a loss is risk reduction, such as safety training, while avoidance removes the activity entirely.
Why D: Risk avoidance means choosing not to do an activity that carries a risk, such as declining to sell a dangerous product, which removes the chance of loss completely.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk transfer?
A: Lowering the chance of the loss with safety steps and training
B: Avoiding the activity altogether to remove the risk
C: Shifting the financial burden of a risk to another party
D: Accepting the loss as a normal cost of doing business
Why A: Lowering the chance of loss with safety steps and training is risk reduction, which keeps the risk but makes it smaller.
Why B: Avoiding the activity altogether is risk avoidance, which removes the risk rather than moving the financial burden to someone else.
Why C: Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a risk to another party, most often through insurance or contracts, so the firm is protected if a loss happens.
Why D: Accepting the loss as a normal cost is risk acceptance, where the firm keeps the risk instead of passing it to another party.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk reduction?
A: Taking steps to lower the chance or impact of a loss
B: Ignoring the possibility of loss or harm to the firm
C: Stopping the activity so the chance of loss is zero
D: Buying insurance for the loss that could occur
Why A: Risk reduction means taking steps, such as safety training, locks or maintenance, to lower the chance or impact of a loss while the business continues its activity.
Why B: Ignoring the possibility of loss does nothing to the risk; reduction requires active steps, not neglect of potential harm.
Why C: Stopping the activity entirely is risk avoidance, which removes the chance of loss instead of just lowering it.
Why D: Buying insurance is risk transfer, because it shifts the cost of a loss to an insurer instead of lowering its chance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A shop installs security cameras and alarms to prevent theft. Which strategy is this?
A: Risk avoidance
B: Risk acceptance
C: Risk reduction
D: Risk transfer
Why A: Avoidance would mean not operating the shop or not stocking items worth stealing; installing cameras keeps the activity going while lowering theft risk.
Why B: Acceptance would mean doing nothing and absorbing theft losses; the shop is spending money on cameras and alarms to prevent them.
Why C: Cameras and alarms lower the chance and impact of theft without stopping business, which makes this risk reduction, a safety and security step.
Why D: Transfer would shift the loss to another party, such as an insurer; cameras and alarms prevent theft instead of moving the cost.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A company buys fire insurance for its warehouse. Which strategy is this?
A: Risk avoidance
B: Risk transfer
C: Risk reduction
D: Risk acceptance
Why A: Avoidance would mean not storing goods in the warehouse at all; buying insurance keeps the activity and the risk in place.
Why B: Fire insurance shifts the financial burden of a possible warehouse fire to the insurer in exchange for premiums, which is risk transfer.
Why C: Reduction would involve sprinklers or alarms that lower the chance of fire; insurance does not make a fire less likely.
Why D: Acceptance would mean paying for fire losses out of pocket; buying insurance does the reverse by passing the cost to an insurer.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A company decides not to expand into a country with unstable politics. Which strategy is this?
A: Risk reduction
B: Risk transfer
C: Risk acceptance
D: Risk avoidance
Why A: Reduction would keep the expansion while adding safeguards; deciding not to enter the country removes the exposure altogether.
Why B: Transfer would shift the financial burden to another party like an insurer; the company is not passing the risk but skipping it.
Why C: Acceptance would mean expanding anyway and bearing any losses; this company chose to stay out of the unstable market.
Why D: Choosing not to expand into a politically unstable country avoids the risk entirely by not doing the risky activity, which is risk avoidance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is insurance?
A: A contract that pays for certain losses in exchange for premiums
B: A tax paid on risky activities carried out by large firms
C: A savings plan that earns interest for the account holder
D: A loan that must be repaid with interest over a set time
Why A: Insurance is a contract in which an insurer pays for certain covered losses in exchange for premiums, letting a business share the financial burden of unexpected events.
Why B: A tax is a government charge paid to the state; insurance is a private contract that pays covered losses and is not a tax.
Why C: A savings plan builds a balance that earns interest for the holder; insurance pays out only when a covered loss occurs.
Why D: A loan is borrowed money repaid with interest; insurance is not borrowed and does not require repayment when it pays a covered claim.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a premium?
A: The amount paid for an insurance policy
B: The amount the insurer pays after a loss
C: The profit that an insurer makes each year
D: The amount owed before coverage starts
Why A: A premium is the amount paid, often monthly or yearly, to buy an insurance policy, which is the price of transferring risk to the insurer.
Why B: The amount the insurer pays after a loss is the claim payment or benefit, not the premium the policyholder pays for coverage.
Why C: The insurer's profit is what remains after paying claims and costs; the premium is the price charged to the policyholder.
Why D: The amount owed before coverage starts describes a deductible, which the policyholder pays toward a loss before the insurer pays.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a deductible?
A: A refund given for no claims made during the year
B: The most the insurer will pay for a covered loss
C: The monthly cost of a policy paid by the policyholder
D: The amount the policyholder pays before insurance pays
Why A: A refund for no claims is a no-claims bonus or dividend; a deductible is paid by the policyholder when a covered loss happens.
Why B: The most the insurer will pay is the policy limit, which caps coverage; a deductible is the portion the insured pays first.
Why C: The regular cost of a policy is the premium; a deductible is paid only when a claim occurs and is separate from premiums.
Why D: A deductible is the amount the policyholder pays out of pocket before insurance pays, and a higher deductible usually means a lower premium.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A policy has a $1,000 deductible and a loss of $4,500 is covered. How much does the insurer pay?
Why A: $1,000 is only the deductible the policyholder pays; the insurer pays the rest of the covered loss after that amount, not the deductible itself.
Why B: The insurer pays the loss minus the deductible: $4,500 - $1,000 = $3,500, while the policyholder bears the first $1,000.
Why C: $5,500 would result from adding the deductible to the loss, but a deductible reduces what the insurer pays, so subtract it.
Why D: $4,500 ignores the deductible; the insurer pays only the part of the loss above it, which is $3,500, not the full amount.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is liability insurance?
A: Coverage for employees' retirement and pension plans
B: Coverage for a company's taxes owed to the state
C: Coverage for harm or damage a business causes to others
D: Coverage for a business's own property and buildings only
Why A: Retirement and pension plans are employee benefits; liability insurance covers harm a business causes to others instead of employee retirement.
Why B: Taxes owed to the state are an obligation that insurance does not cover; liability insurance protects against claims of harm to others.
Why C: Liability insurance covers harm or damage a business causes to others, such as a customer injury or property damage, and pays legal costs and settlements that could otherwise be ruinous.
Why D: Coverage for a business's own property and buildings is property insurance; liability insurance pays for harm caused to others, not own assets.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is property insurance?
A: Coverage for harm caused to customers who shop at the store
B: Coverage for a worker's illness or time off from work due to it
C: Coverage for loss or damage to a business's own buildings and goods
D: Coverage for a loan not repaid, paying the lender on default
Why A: Harm to customers is covered by liability insurance; property insurance pays for the business's own assets.
Why B: A worker's illness or time off is handled by health or workers' compensation coverage, not property insurance.
Why C: Property insurance covers loss or damage to a business's own buildings, equipment and inventory from events like fire, storms or theft, so the firm can repair or replace what it lost.
Why D: Coverage that pays a lender when a borrower defaults is credit or loan default insurance, not property insurance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is workers' compensation insurance?
A: Coverage for employees injured on the job
B: Coverage for a customer's complaints
C: Coverage for a supplier's late delivery
D: Coverage for a company's office building
Why A: Workers' compensation insurance covers employees injured on the job, paying medical bills and lost wages, and protects employers from most lawsuits over workplace injuries.
Why B: Customer complaints are handled through service and quality processes; they are not insured under workers' compensation, which relates to employee injuries.
Why C: A supplier's late delivery is a contract or supply issue; workers' compensation covers employees hurt at work, not delivery problems.
Why D: Coverage of a company's office building is property insurance; workers' compensation focuses on employees' work injuries or illness.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a hazard?
A: A plan for growth and new store sites
B: A rule that staff must follow always
C: A benefit that increases profits each year
D: A condition that may cause harm or loss
Why A: A plan for growth is a business strategy, not a hazard; hazards are conditions that can cause harm or loss.
Why B: A rule staff must follow is a policy or procedure; it helps manage risk but is not a hazard itself.
Why C: A benefit that raises profits is a positive result, while a hazard is a source of potential harm or loss.
Why D: A hazard is a condition that may cause harm or loss, such as a wet floor, faulty wiring or a dangerous chemical, and spotting hazards is the first step in controlling risk.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A wet floor with no sign is an example of a:
A: Benefit
B: Hazard
C: Policy
D: Warranty
Why A: A benefit is a positive outcome or perk; a wet floor with no sign can cause falls, so it is not a benefit.
Why B: A wet floor with no sign is a hazard, a condition that may cause harm, because someone could slip and be injured, so it should be marked or cleaned up.
Why C: A policy is a written rule; the wet floor is a physical condition that can cause harm, not a rule.
Why D: A warranty is a promise about a product's quality; a wet floor is a safety condition, not a product guarantee.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a risk assessment?
A: A forecast of next year's profits and sales made by the firm's finance team
B: A review that identifies risks and judges how likely and serious they are
C: A list of customers who might not pay, with the amounts that they owe
D: A report on employees' attendance and sick days taken in the year
Why A: Forecasting profits and sales is a financial planning task; a risk assessment looks at threats and how likely and serious they are.
Why B: A risk assessment identifies risks and judges how likely and how serious each is, so the business can rank them and decide which ones to control first.
Why C: A list of customers who might not pay is a credit review, which covers one financial risk but not the broad assessment of all risks.
Why D: A report on attendance and sick days is an HR record; a risk assessment evaluates possible losses and hazards to the business.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which risk should be addressed first?
A: One that is both likely and very costly
B: One that has already been fixed fully
C: One that no one has ever noticed yet
D: One that is unlikely and cheap to fix
Why A: A risk that is both likely and very costly deserves priority because it can do the most damage, so firms rank risks by likelihood and impact and tackle the worst first.
Why B: A risk already fixed fully needs no further attention, so it is not a priority for new action.
Why C: A risk no one has noticed cannot be ranked by likelihood or impact until it is identified; known high-impact risks come first.
Why D: An unlikely, cheap-to-fix risk has low priority, since it has low probability and small cost, so it can wait behind bigger risks.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a contingency plan?
A: A plan to hire more employees early next year
B: A plan to raise prices next year to cover costs
C: A plan for what to do if something goes wrong
D: A plan to open a new store in the city soon
Why A: Hiring more employees is a staffing decision for growth; a contingency plan prepares for problems and is not about future hiring.
Why B: Raising prices to cover costs is a pricing decision; a contingency plan covers what to do when something goes wrong.
Why C: A contingency plan sets out what to do if something goes wrong, such as a fire, outage or supply failure, so the business can respond quickly and keep operating.
Why D: Opening a new store is an expansion strategy; a contingency plan is a backup response to emergencies and unexpected events.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A restaurant keeps a backup generator in case of power loss. What is this?
A: A hiring process plan
B: A price discount plan
C: A marketing campaign
D: A contingency measure
Why A: A hiring process plan covers recruitment steps; a backup generator prepares for power loss, which is a different concern.
Why B: A price discount plan is a promotion tactic; a generator does not change prices but protects operations during an outage.
Why C: A marketing campaign promotes products to customers; a backup generator is not advertising, it keeps the kitchen running in an outage.
Why D: A backup generator is a contingency measure because it lets the restaurant keep operating if power fails, protecting food, sales and customers from the disruption.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why does a business keep emergency funds?
A: To cover unexpected costs without borrowing
B: To pay for yearly advertising costs only
C: To make employees spend more of their pay
D: To avoid ever earning profits from sales
Why A: Emergency funds cover unexpected costs, such as repairs or a revenue drop, without borrowing, which avoids interest and keeps the business stable.
Why B: Yearly advertising is a planned budget item; emergency funds are for unplanned costs, not routine marketing expenses.
Why C: Emergency funds protect the business; they are not designed to make employees spend more of their pay.
Why D: Businesses exist to earn profit; reserves are meant to protect the business from shocks and do not mean avoiding profits.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is fraud?
A: A late payment made to a supplier by the firm
B: An honest mistake in a calculation that is corrected
C: Intentional deception to gain something unfairly
D: A legal tax deduction taken by a business each year
Why A: A late payment to a supplier is a breach of terms or poor cash management, but it is not intentional deception, so it is not fraud.
Why B: An honest mistake that is corrected lacks intent to deceive, so it is an error, not fraud.
Why C: Fraud is intentional deception to gain something unfairly, such as falsifying records or stealing funds, and it is a crime that can bring fines and prison.
Why D: A legal tax deduction is allowed under tax law and is not deceptive, so it is not fraud.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which control best reduces the risk of employee theft of cash?
A: Keeping cash in an unlocked drawer that any staff member can open
B: Letting one person handle all of the cash with no second review
C: Skipping end-of-day cash counts and bank deposits for the week
D: Separating duties so no one person handles cash from start to finish
Why A: An unlocked drawer anyone can open invites theft and makes it hard to trace missing cash, so it increases risk instead of reducing it.
Why B: Letting one person handle all cash with no review removes checks and makes theft easy to hide, which raises the risk of loss.
Why C: Skipping cash counts and deposits leaves cash unprotected and unverified, so theft or errors could go unnoticed for days.
Why D: Separating duties means no one person handles cash from start to finish, so another employee checks the work and theft becomes harder to hide and easier to catch.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is cybersecurity risk?
A: The chance of prices falling in the market for all goods
B: The chance of loss from attacks on computer systems and data
C: The chance of a product being returned after being used
D: The chance of staff arriving late for work on any day
Why A: Prices falling in the market is market or economic risk; cybersecurity risk relates to computer systems and data.
Why B: Cybersecurity risk is the chance of loss from attacks on computer systems and data, such as hacking, malware or data breaches, which can cost money and trust.
Why C: Product returns after use are a quality or customer service issue, not a risk tied to computer systems or data.
Why D: Staff arriving late is an HR attendance matter; cybersecurity risk deals with threats to computers, networks and information.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which practice most reduces the risk of a phishing attack?
A: Sharing passwords by email with other staff members
B: Turning off all security updates on staff computers
C: Encouraging staff to click every link they receive
D: Training employees to spot and report suspicious emails
Why A: Sharing passwords by email exposes accounts to attackers and makes phishing more effective, so it raises the risk instead of reducing it.
Why B: Turning off security updates leaves known weaknesses open to attackers, which makes phishing and malware attacks more likely to succeed.
Why C: Clicking every link is exactly how phishing works, since attackers use fake links to steal passwords or install malware, so this raises risk.
Why D: Training employees to spot and report suspicious emails builds awareness, which is the best defense against phishing because attackers rely on someone being tricked into clicking.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is financial risk?
A: The chance that a store will be remodeled by its owners soon
B: The chance that a business will lose money or be unable to pay debts
C: The chance that products will be stolen from the main stockroom
D: The chance that employees will resign from their jobs this year
Why A: Remodeling a store is a property or planning decision, not a financial risk about losing money or paying debts.
Why B: Financial risk is the chance a business will lose money or be unable to pay its debts, often because of heavy borrowing, falling sales or unexpected costs.
Why C: Stolen products from a stockroom are a theft or security risk, though the loss has some financial effect, it is not defined as financial risk.
Why D: Employees resigning is a staffing or human resources risk, not a financial risk about losing money or paying debts.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A firm borrows heavily to expand and sales fall. What risk has increased?
A: Safety risk
B: Security risk
C: Financial risk
D: Legal risk
Why A: Safety risk concerns physical harm to people; borrowing and falling sales affect the firm's finances, not workplace safety.
Why B: Security risk concerns theft or attacks on assets and data; heavy debt and lower sales are not security problems.
Why C: Heavy borrowing with falling sales makes it harder to pay interest and repay loans, so financial risk, the chance of losing money or defaulting, rises.
Why D: Legal risk comes from lawsuits or breaking laws; debt and falling sales are money matters, not a legal exposure.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a safety data sheet (SDS)?
A: A document that explains hazards and safe handling of a chemical
B: A sheet that lists employees' pay and tax withholding each payday
C: A sheet that shows product prices for all the goods in the shop
D: A sheet that records sales made by the staff in the shop each day
Why A: A safety data sheet explains a chemical's hazards, safe handling, storage, first aid and emergency steps, and OSHA requires employers to make SDSs available to workers.
Why B: A list of pay and tax withholding is a payroll record; a safety data sheet covers chemical hazards and handling.
Why C: A sheet showing product prices is a price list; an SDS gives safety information about hazardous chemicals, not prices.
Why D: A record of daily sales is a sales report; an SDS describes chemical hazards and safe use.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: An employee must clean with a chemical they do not know. What should they do first?
A: Mix it with other cleaners to test how well it works
B: Read the safety data sheet and follow the instructions
C: Ask a customer in the store what to do about it next
D: Use it without looking at any instructions at all
Why A: Mixing cleaners can create toxic gases or violent reactions, so testing them together is dangerous and never the first step.
Why B: The SDS lists the chemical's hazards, protective equipment and safe handling, so reading it and following the instructions comes first before using an unfamiliar chemical.
Why C: A customer has no training or responsibility for workplace chemicals, so asking one is unreliable and could lead to injury.
Why D: Using an unknown chemical without instructions risks burns, fumes or fire, and it violates workplace safety rules.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does OSHA do?
A: Collects income taxes from employers for the state
B: Licenses all new businesses in a state or province
C: Sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards
D: Sets prices for goods sold in stores across the country
Why A: Collecting income taxes from employers is done by tax agencies like the IRS, not by OSHA, which handles workplace safety.
Why B: Business licensing is handled by state or local agencies, not OSHA, whose focus is safety and health at work.
Why C: OSHA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, inspects workplaces and can fine employers who fail to protect workers.
Why D: Prices of goods are set by businesses in the market; OSHA does not regulate prices but deals with workplace safety.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does compliance mean in business?
A: Advertising on as many online platforms as possible each year
B: Hiring as many employees as the budget will allow each year
C: Following the laws, rules and standards that apply to the business
D: Choosing the lowest prices to attract more customers each month
Why A: Advertising on many platforms is a marketing choice and does not mean a business is following laws or rules.
Why B: Hiring many employees is a staffing decision; compliance is about meeting legal and regulatory requirements, not headcount.
Why C: Compliance means following the laws, rules and standards that apply to the business, such as safety, labor, tax and privacy requirements, which avoids fines, lawsuits and lost trust.
Why D: Choosing low prices is a pricing strategy; compliance concerns obeying legal and regulatory requirements, not pricing choices.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a regulation?
A: A rule made by a government agency that businesses must follow
B: A discount offered to businesses that pay their taxes early
C: A suggestion that businesses may ignore if they prefer at any time
D: A contract between two private companies for the sale of goods
Why A: A regulation is a rule made by a government agency that businesses must follow, and it carries the force of law, with penalties such as fines for violations.
Why B: A discount for early taxpayers is a tax incentive, not a regulation, which is a binding rule rather than a reward.
Why C: Regulations are mandatory; a suggestion businesses may ignore would be a guideline or recommendation, not a binding rule.
Why D: A contract between two private companies is a private agreement, not a government rule, so it is not a regulation.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the purpose of a compliance officer?
A: To design advertisements for the company's new products
B: To make sure the company follows laws and internal policies
C: To repair equipment used in the company's main factory
D: To set the prices that customers pay for the products
Why A: Designing advertisements is a marketing role; a compliance officer checks that the company follows laws and policies.
Why B: A compliance officer makes sure the company follows laws, regulations and internal policies by monitoring, training staff and investigating issues, which reduces legal and financial risk.
Why C: Repairing equipment is a maintenance job; compliance officers focus on rules and legal requirements, not machinery.
Why D: Pricing is a management and marketing decision, while a compliance officer ensures legal and policy adherence.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a code of conduct?
A: A list of products offered by the company to its buyers
B: A secret list of passwords used by the managers to log in
C: A schedule of employee shifts for the whole month ahead
D: A written set of rules for ethical and professional behavior
Why A: A list of products offered is a catalog; a code of conduct describes expected behavior, not what the company sells.
Why B: Passwords are confidential security credentials; a code of conduct is a shared document of behavior standards, not a secret list.
Why C: A schedule of shifts is a staffing plan; a code of conduct sets behavior expectations, not working hours.
Why D: A code of conduct is a written set of rules for ethical and professional behavior, telling employees what is expected on honesty, conflicts of interest, respect and legal compliance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: An employee accepts an expensive gift from a supplier who wants a contract. What compliance issue does this raise?
A: A normal service practice accepted in most firms
B: A requirement of tax law for all employees of a firm
C: A possible conflict of interest or bribery concern
D: A way to lower company costs and raise yearly profits
Why A: Accepting costly gifts from someone seeking a contract is not normal practice; most firms have gift policies to prevent bias and bribery.
Why B: Tax law does not require employees to take supplier gifts; gifts are a conduct issue and may even need to be reported.
Why C: An expensive gift from a supplier seeking a contract may influence the employee's decision, creating a conflict of interest or looking like a bribe, which breaks most company policies and some laws.
Why D: A gift does not lower company costs, and it can lead to unfair contracts and legal trouble that hurt profits.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is whistleblowing?
A: Reporting illegal or unethical activity inside an organization
B: Quitting a job without notice to start work somewhere else
C: Asking a manager for a raise in pay after a very good year
D: Spreading false rumors about a coworker to damage their standing
Why A: Whistleblowing is reporting illegal or unethical activity inside an organization to those who can act, and many laws protect whistleblowers from retaliation.
Why B: Quitting without notice to take another job is just resigning abruptly; it is not reporting wrongdoing.
Why C: Asking for a raise is a pay negotiation, unrelated to reporting illegal or unethical conduct.
Why D: Spreading false rumors is harmful gossip or defamation, while whistleblowing reports real wrongdoing to the proper people.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)?
A: An agency that sets interest rates for the banks of a nation
B: An agency that sets and enforces workplace safety standards
C: An agency that collects federal income taxes each year
D: An agency that approves new drugs for sale to the public
Why A: Setting interest rates is done by a central bank, such as the Federal Reserve, not OSHA, which is a workplace safety agency.
Why B: OSHA is the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety and health standards, inspecting workplaces and fining employers that put workers at risk.
Why C: Collecting federal income taxes is the IRS's job, not OSHA's, which regulates safety in workplaces.
Why D: Approving new drugs is the job of the Food and Drug Administration, not OSHA, which focuses on workplace safety.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A warehouse worker is injured because required safety guards were removed. Which agency may investigate?
A: FCC
B: SEC
C: Fed
D: OSHA
Why A: The FCC regulates radio, television and communications, not workplace safety injuries, so it would not investigate a removed machine guard.
Why B: The SEC regulates securities markets and public company disclosures, not workplace safety, so it would not investigate this injury.
Why C: The Fed is the central bank that handles monetary policy and banking supervision, not workplace injuries.
Why D: OSHA enforces workplace safety standards, including machine guarding, so it may investigate an injury caused by removed safety guards and can issue citations and fines.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) enforce?
A: Laws that set the minimum prices of goods
B: Laws that regulate all stock trading
C: Laws against workplace discrimination
D: Laws that control imports and exports
Why A: Setting minimum prices of goods is not an EEOC role; prices are set by markets and, in some cases, other agencies.
Why B: Stock trading is regulated by the SEC, not the EEOC, which deals with employment discrimination.
Why C: The EEOC enforces federal laws against workplace discrimination based on race, sex, religion, age, disability and other protected traits, and it investigates complaints and can sue employers.
Why D: Imports and exports are controlled by customs and trade agencies, not by the EEOC.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A manager refuses to hire a qualified applicant because of the applicant's religion. What is this?
A: Illegal discrimination
B: A required hiring practice
C: A legal hiring preference
D: A tax compliance step
Why A: Refusing to hire a qualified applicant because of religion is illegal discrimination under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and the employer could face an EEOC complaint and lawsuits.
Why B: No law requires hiring decisions based on religion; employers must judge applicants on qualifications, not protected traits.
Why C: Religion is a protected characteristic, so preferring or rejecting applicants for it is not a legal hiring preference.
Why D: Hiring decisions are not tax compliance steps; this is a discrimination issue, not something tax rules require.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) mainly about?
A: Rules for food labeling on all packages
B: Rules for advertising claims in the news
C: Rules for stock market trading and broker reports
D: Minimum wage, overtime and child labor rules
Why A: Food labeling is regulated by the FDA and related agencies, not by the FLSA, which covers pay and labor rules.
Why B: Advertising claims are overseen by the FTC; the FLSA deals with wages, hours and child labor.
Why C: Stock market trading and broker reports fall under securities law enforced by the SEC, not the Fair Labor Standards Act.
Why D: The FLSA sets federal minimum wage, overtime pay rules and child labor limits, protecting workers by requiring pay for covered hours and limiting hazardous work by minors.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A non-exempt worker earns $14 an hour and works 44 hours. Overtime is 1.5 times pay after 40 hours. What is total pay?
Why A: $924 would come from paying all 44 hours at overtime rate (44 x $21); only the 4 hours beyond 40 earn overtime pay.
Why B: First 40 hours: 40 x $14 = $560. Overtime rate is $14 x 1.5 = $21, so 4 x $21 = $84. Total is $560 + $84 = $644.
Why C: $616 is 44 x $14 at straight time, which ignores the extra half-time premium owed for the 4 overtime hours.
Why D: $560 covers only the first 40 hours at $14, leaving out the 4 overtime hours that also earn pay at $21 each.

Question: What is the purpose of record keeping for compliance?
A: To increase the number of forms employees fill out
B: To raise product prices for customers each year
C: To prove that the company followed required rules
D: To hide mistakes from regulators and from the public
Why A: Record keeping aims to document compliance, not to create more paperwork for employees to fill out.
Why B: Records do not set prices; their purpose is to document actions, not to raise what customers pay.
Why C: Records prove the company followed required rules, such as tax, safety and employment laws, which helps pass audits, defend against claims and show good faith to regulators.
Why D: Hiding mistakes from regulators would be unethical and illegal; proper records are meant to be accurate and available for review.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: An audit finds missing safety training records. What is the best response?
A: Complete the training, fix the records and set up a tracking system
B: Ignore the finding until the next audit comes around once more
C: Blame the auditor for the finding and argue about the report
D: Destroy the audit report so no one sees it and carry on as before
Why A: The best response is to complete the training, fix the records and set up a tracking system, which corrects the gap and prevents it from happening again.
Why B: Ignoring a finding leaves the violation in place, risks fines and injuries, and will likely be flagged again at the next audit.
Why C: Blaming the auditor does not fix missing records and wastes time; audit findings are meant to help improve compliance.
Why D: Destroying an audit report is illegal obstruction and hides problems instead of solving them, which can lead to serious penalties.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a license?
A: A list of company rules that all staff members must follow
B: A discount for buying in bulk, given to customers who order lots
C: A report of annual profits that a firm shares with its owners
D: Official permission to operate a business or practice a profession
Why A: A list of company rules is a policy or code of conduct; a license is permission granted by an authority.
Why B: A bulk discount is a pricing incentive for large orders, not an official permission to operate.
Why C: A report of annual profits is a financial statement; a license is a government grant of permission.
Why D: A license is official permission from a government or authority to operate a business or practice a profession, such as a liquor license or a medical license, and operating without one can bring penalties.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A restaurant opens without a required health permit. What is the likely result?
A: Lower taxes for the whole year ahead
B: Fines or closure by the authorities
C: Faster deliveries from suppliers
D: A reward from the health department
Why A: Lower taxes are not a result of skipping a permit; opening without one is a violation that leads to penalties, not savings.

Why B: Forming the team and choosing goals happens in initiation, at the start. Closing happens at the very end, after the work has been completed and delivered.
Why C: Drafting the schedule is a planning task. Planning comes before execution, while closing is the last phase when the work is complete and results are handed over.
Why D: Doing most of the work while the plan is still changing describes the execution and monitoring phases. Closing starts only when the work is substantially complete.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a status report?
A: A promotion for the team that finishes early
B: An update on progress, issues and next steps
C: A list of staff birthdays for the whole year
D: A contract for new work from a new client
Why A: A promotion for a team that finishes early is a reward or incentive, not a report. A status report informs stakeholders on progress, not who gets rewarded.
Why B: A status report summarizes progress to date, current issues and risks, and next steps. It keeps sponsors and stakeholders informed so they can decide or help early.
Why C: A list of staff birthdays is an HR or social record. A status report is a project communication tool that covers work progress, not personal dates.
Why D: A contract for new work is a legal agreement setting terms and price. A status report does not commit anyone to new work, it only reports on current work.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why should project managers communicate regularly with stakeholders?
A: To avoid explaining problems to the sponsor later on
B: To keep stakeholders out of decisions and work alone
C: To make team meetings longer for no real reason at all
D: To keep expectations aligned and resolve problems early
Why A: Regular communication does the opposite of avoiding problems. It surfaces issues early so they can be explained and solved before they grow into bigger issues for the sponsor.
Why B: Keeping stakeholders out of decisions weakens support and risks missing needs. Good project managers involve stakeholders so they stay informed, engaged and committed.
Why C: Lengthening team meetings for no reason wastes time. Effective communication is planned, purposeful and sized to what stakeholders need to know.
Why D: Regular communication keeps expectations aligned, builds trust and lets problems be spotted and resolved early. It also helps secure approvals and support throughout the life of the project.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is resource allocation?
A: Deleting old project files to free up disk space for staff
B: Setting prices for the project's products and services
C: Assigning people, money and equipment to project tasks
D: Selling the project's results to customers at a profit
Why A: Deleting old project files is data management or housekeeping. Resource allocation is about assigning people, money and equipment to the tasks of a project.
Why B: Setting prices for products and services is a pricing decision made by marketing and management. Resource allocation decides who and what is used on project tasks.
Why C: Resource allocation means assigning people, money, equipment and materials to project tasks. Good allocation matches skills and capacity to the work and avoids overload or idle resources.
Why D: Selling project results at a profit is a sales or revenue activity. Resource allocation happens within the project to supply the inputs needed to do the work.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: One team member is overloaded while another has no tasks. What should the manager do?
A: Leave the workload unchanged for the team
B: Rebalance the workload among team members
C: Remove the overloaded member from the project
D: Give the idle member a large cash bonus
Why A: Leaving the workload unchanged lets one person burn out while another sits idle, which lowers productivity and morale. A manager should act on an imbalance, not ignore it.
Why B: Rebalancing means moving some tasks from the overloaded member to the one with spare capacity. This protects quality and morale and uses the team's full capacity to meet deadlines.
Why C: Removing the overloaded member loses skills and makes the problem worse, because the remaining people must absorb even more work. It also punishes the person doing the most.
Why D: A large cash bonus for an idle member rewards low output and does not fix the imbalance. Work should be redistributed so both people contribute fairly.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is agile project management?
A: An approach that delivers work in short cycles with frequent feedback
B: An approach that finishes all planning first and never changes it
C: An approach that ignores all customer input until the work is done
D: An approach that avoids teamwork and has each person work alone
Why A: Agile delivers work in short cycles, such as sprints, with frequent customer feedback. This lets teams adapt to changing needs and deliver usable results early and often.
Why B: Finishing all planning first and never changing it describes a rigid, plan-driven method like waterfall. Agile welcomes change and adjusts the plan as feedback arrives.
Why C: Agile relies heavily on customer input and collaboration throughout the project. Ignoring customers until the work is done is the opposite of the agile approach.
Why D: Agile emphasizes teamwork, daily communication and shared ownership in self-organizing teams. Having each person work alone goes against its principles.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a sprint in agile?
A: A race between two project teams to finish a task first each week
B: A meeting to assign blame for delays, held each month by managers
C: A final presentation to the client at the end of the project
D: A short, fixed period in which a team completes a set of work
Why A: A race between teams is not an agile practice. A sprint is a fixed work period for one team to complete agreed work, and teams collaborate rather than compete.
Why B: Assigning blame is not the purpose of any sprint event. Retrospectives look at how to improve the process, and a sprint is a work period, not a meeting.
Why C: A final client presentation at the end of the project is a closing activity. A sprint is a short repeating cycle, and each sprint ends with a review of finished work.
Why D: A sprint is a short, fixed period, often one to four weeks, in which a team completes a set of work. Each sprint produces a usable increment that can be reviewed with the client.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A team plans two-week cycles, reviews work with the client and adjusts the plan. Which method is this?
A: Lean
B: Pricing
C: Agile
D: Waterfall
Why A: Lean focuses on removing waste and improving flow, and does not by itself define fixed two-week cycles with client reviews. The described cycles, feedback and plan changes match agile.
Why B: Pricing is a marketing decision about what to charge, not a project management method. It has nothing to do with planning work in cycles.
Why C: Agile uses short cycles, such as two-week sprints, regular reviews with the client and plan adjustments. This lets the team respond to feedback and changing needs.
Why D: Waterfall completes each phase fully before the next begins, with no repeated cycles. Reviewing with the client and adjusting the plan every two weeks is not how waterfall works.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the waterfall method?
A: An approach that repeats short cycles of work with frequent customer feedback
B: An approach used only for water projects such as dams, pipes and pumps
C: An approach that has no planning and where each person just works alone
D: A step-by-step approach where each phase finishes before the next begins
Why A: Short cycles with frequent customer feedback describe agile, not waterfall. Waterfall moves in a fixed sequence of phases with little feedback until later stages.
Why B: Waterfall is a project management method used in many industries such as software, construction and manufacturing. Its name comes from work flowing downward through phases, not water.
Why C: Waterfall depends on detailed planning at the start and works as a team across clearly defined phases. It does not mean having no planning or working alone.
Why D: Waterfall is a sequential approach where each phase, such as requirements, design, build and test, finishes before the next one starts. It works best when requirements are clear and stable.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which project is best suited to the waterfall method?
A: Testing a market with unknown needs
B: Building an app with unclear features
C: Building a bridge from fixed plans
D: Testing a new idea with rapid changes
Why A: Testing a market with unknown needs calls for flexible, iterative learning, which suits agile. Waterfall needs requirements to be known up front, and here they are not.
Why B: An app with unclear features will probably change as it is built and tested. Waterfall is a poor fit because it resists changes once a phase is complete.
Why C: A bridge built from fixed plans has clear requirements, safety rules and a set sequence of steps. Waterfall fits because design must be complete before construction, and changes are costly.
Why D: Testing a new idea with rapid changes needs quick iteration and feedback. That is the strength of agile methods, while waterfall is too rigid for it.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a work breakdown structure (WBS)?
A: A rule that limits team size and the hours each person works
B: A way of dividing a project into smaller, manageable tasks
C: A list of reasons a project failed, written after it closed
D: A chart of the company's profits by month and by year
Why A: A rule limiting team size and hours is a staffing policy or constraint. A work breakdown structure divides the project's work into smaller tasks, not the people.
Why B: A WBS breaks the total project scope into smaller, manageable work packages. This makes tasks easier to assign, estimate, schedule and track toward the final deliverable.
Why C: A list of reasons a project failed is a post-project review or lessons learned report. A WBS is a planning tool used before and during the work.
Why D: A chart of profits by month is a financial report. A WBS shows how project work is divided and organized, not company earnings.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why break a large project into smaller tasks?
A: Smaller tasks are easier to assign, track and estimate
B: It hides the project from stakeholders and the sponsor
C: It makes the project take longer on purpose for the team
D: It removes the need for a schedule and a budget plan
Why A: Smaller tasks are easier to assign to people, track against the schedule and estimate for time and cost. This improves control and makes problems easier to spot early.
Why B: Breaking work down makes the project clearer to stakeholders, not hidden. It supports reporting by showing exactly what work must be completed.
