Why C: A claim total for the year is not a copay; a copay is a fixed payment made per service.
Why D: A fine for a missed appointment is a no-show fee, and a copay is paid for covered care you actually receive.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is coinsurance?
A: A percentage of costs you share after the deductible
B: A flat fee that you pay at every single doctor visit
C: A penalty for using out-of-network care at a hospital
D: The monthly premium that you pay to the insurer
Why A: After you meet your deductible, coinsurance splits remaining costs, such as the plan paying 80 percent and you paying 20 percent, until you reach the out-of-pocket maximum.
Why B: A flat fee per visit is a copay; coinsurance is a percentage of the cost rather than a fixed amount.
Why C: Out-of-network penalties or higher costs are a separate matter; coinsurance is the percentage split of covered costs after the deductible.
Why D: The monthly premium is a fixed charge to keep the policy; coinsurance is a share of covered costs that applies when you use care.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is life insurance?
A: Coverage that pays you money when you retire from work
B: Coverage that pays for car damage and repairs
C: Coverage that pays for medical costs and drugs
D: Coverage paying beneficiaries when the insured dies
Why A: Retirement income comes from pensions, annuities or savings; life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries when the insured dies.
Why B: Car damage and repairs are covered by auto insurance, not by life insurance, which pays out upon the insured person's death.
Why C: Medical costs and drugs are covered by health insurance, whereas life insurance pays a benefit after the insured dies.
Why D: Life insurance pays a death benefit to named beneficiaries when the insured person dies, replacing lost income and covering debts, funeral costs and other expenses. Term and whole life are two common types.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Who should consider buying life insurance?
A: Everyone with no dependents or debts to pay
B: Only people who never work at any job
C: People whose income dependents rely on
D: No one at all, ever, in any situation
Why A: People with no dependents or debts generally have little need for it, since there is no one financially relying on their income.
Why B: People who do not work may still have family responsibilities, and this option is clearly too narrow to be a real guideline.
Why C: Life insurance is most useful for people with dependents such as a spouse or children who would suffer financially if that income were lost.
Why D: Life insurance is useful for those with dependents or debts, so saying no one needs it ever is false.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is disability insurance?
A: Coverage that pays for damage to a car's body
B: Coverage replacing income if you cannot work
C: Coverage that pays for a vacation trip abroad
D: Coverage that pays the taxes you owe each year
Why A: Car body damage is covered by auto collision coverage, whereas disability insurance replaces income lost when injury or illness prevents work.
Why B: Disability insurance replaces a portion of your income, often 60 percent, if illness or injury keeps you from working. It protects your paycheck, which is usually your largest asset.
Why C: Vacations are not covered by disability insurance; travel insurance may cover trip problems, but disability pays income when you cannot work.
Why D: Taxes are not paid by disability insurance; it replaces lost wages when you cannot work.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is homeowners insurance?
A: Coverage for a home, belongings and liability
B: Coverage for car accidents and repairs only
C: Coverage that is meant for renters only today
D: Coverage that pays your mortgage if jobless
Why A: Homeowners insurance usually covers the dwelling, personal belongings, liability for injuries on your property, and additional living expenses after a covered loss.
Why B: Car accidents and repairs are covered by auto insurance, a separate policy; homeowners insurance protects your house and property.
Why C: Renters insurance is for tenants; homeowners insurance covers people who own their home, and mortgage lenders often require it.
Why D: Homeowners insurance does not pay your mortgage if you lose your job; that would require special payment protection, whereas homeowners covers property damage and liability.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk avoidance?
A: Taking safety steps to lower the chance of a loss
B: Saving money to cover a loss that may occur later on
C: Buying insurance for a loss that may occur later on
D: Choosing not to do something that could cause a loss
Why A: Safety steps that lower the chance of loss are risk reduction, which accepts the activity while making it safer, not avoidance.
Why B: Saving money to cover a possible loss is risk retention, because you plan to absorb the cost yourself rather than avoid it.
Why C: Buying insurance is risk transfer, shifting the cost of a possible loss to an insurer instead of avoiding the activity.
Why D: Risk avoidance means not doing the risky activity at all, such as not driving, which removes the chance of loss completely but also gives up the benefits.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk transfer?
A: Accepting a risk and paying for a loss yourself
B: Shifting the financial burden to an insurer
C: Avoiding a risk entirely by not taking part
D: Reducing the chance that a loss will happen
Why A: Accepting a risk and paying for losses yourself is risk retention, the opposite of transferring the risk to someone else.
Why B: Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a possible loss to another party, most commonly by buying insurance and paying premiums.
Why C: Avoiding a risk entirely by not taking part is risk avoidance, not transfer, because no one else takes on the loss.
Why D: Lowering the chance a loss happens is risk reduction, such as installing alarms; transfer moves the cost to someone else.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk retention?
A: Buying insurance to cover a possible loss of money or property
B: Installing safety devices to lower the chance of loss
C: Accepting a risk and planning to pay for a loss yourself
D: Avoiding the risky activity altogether and for good
Why A: Buying insurance to cover a possible loss is risk transfer, because the insurer takes on the cost rather than you.
Why B: Installing safety devices is risk reduction because it lowers the chance of loss, but you still bear any loss that occurs.
Why C: Risk retention means accepting the risk and paying for any loss yourself, often through savings or a high deductible, and works best for small, affordable losses.
Why D: Avoiding the risky activity altogether is risk avoidance, which eliminates the exposure rather than accepting and paying for it.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A family installs smoke detectors and keeps a fire extinguisher. Which risk strategy is this?
A: Risk reduction
B: Risk transfer
C: Risk retention
D: Risk avoidance
Why A: Smoke detectors and extinguishers lower the chance and size of a fire loss, which is risk reduction, also called loss control or prevention.
Why B: Risk transfer would be buying insurance or otherwise shifting the cost to another party; safety equipment does not do that.
Why C: Risk retention means accepting the possible loss and paying yourself, whereas installing safety equipment actively tries to prevent the loss.
Why D: Risk avoidance would mean not having the exposure at all, such as not owning a home; the family keeps the exposure but reduces it.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an insurance claim?
A: A type of savings that earns monthly interest
B: A fee that you pay for a policy each month
C: A refund of the premium you paid earlier
D: A request for payment after a covered loss
Why A: A savings type that earns interest is an account; an insurance claim is a request to the insurer for payment of a covered loss.
Why B: The regular fee you pay for a policy is the premium, whereas a claim is something you file after a loss.
Why C: A refund of premiums is not a claim; a claim asks the insurer to pay for a covered loss.
Why D: A claim is a formal request to your insurer for payment after a covered loss, such as an accident or theft. The insurer investigates and pays according to policy terms, minus your deductible.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an insurance exclusion?
A: A discount for very good driving habits
B: The monthly cost of the whole policy
C: Something the policy does not cover
D: The coverage limit in the policy
Why A: A discount for good driving is a credit that lowers cost; an exclusion limits what the policy pays.
Why B: The monthly cost of the policy is the premium; an exclusion is a specific loss or situation the policy does not cover.
Why C: An exclusion lists causes, property or situations the policy will not pay for, such as floods or earthquakes under standard homeowners policies. Reading exclusions helps you spot gaps in coverage.
Why D: The coverage limit is the most the insurer will pay; an exclusion is something not covered at all.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: After a flood damages a home, the owner learns the standard homeowners policy does not pay. What is the likely reason?
A: The owner is not allowed to file any claims at all
B: Floods are usually excluded; separate coverage is needed
C: The insurer simply made a mistake in the policy terms
D: Floods are always covered in standard policies at no extra cost
Why A: Owners are allowed to file claims on any policy; the issue is that flood damage is not a covered cause of loss in a standard policy.
Why B: Standard homeowners policies exclude flood damage, so owners must buy separate flood insurance, often through the National Flood Insurance Program. Check exclusions before disasters strike.
Why C: The insurer did not err; the policy terms exclude floods, and the written exclusion is the reason the claim is denied.
Why D: Floods are generally excluded from standard homeowners policies, and flood coverage costs extra, so this option states the opposite of the truth.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an emergency fund's role in managing risk?
A: It is meant only for paying for vacations
B: It replaces the need for all your insurance
C: It covers unexpected costs without borrowing
D: It increases the amount of risk a family faces
Why A: An emergency fund is meant for unexpected needs such as job loss or repairs, not planned expenses like vacations.
Why B: An emergency fund handles smaller shocks, but it cannot replace insurance, because large losses like a house fire or major illness can far exceed savings.
Why C: An emergency fund covers unexpected costs such as car repairs or lost income, so you avoid high-interest debt. Experts recommend three to six months of expenses.
Why D: An emergency fund reduces a family's exposure to financial risk by providing a cushion, so it does not increase risk.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why compare insurance quotes from several companies?
A: It removes the need for coverage
B: Prices and coverage can vary
C: It guarantees the lowest rate
D: All companies charge the same
Why A: Comparing quotes does not remove the need for coverage; it helps you choose among policies, not skip insurance.
Why B: Insurers set prices differently using their own formulas, so the same coverage can cost very different amounts, and shopping around can save significant money.
Why C: Comparing quotes can find a lower price, but it cannot guarantee that you get the lowest rate available anywhere, as rates change.
Why D: Companies price risk differently, which is exactly why comparing quotes is worth doing; rates are not identical across insurers.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is investing?
A: Borrowing money just to have fun
B: Hiding cash in a drawer at home daily
C: Spending money on daily needs each month
D: Putting money into assets to grow it
Why A: Borrowing for fun is spending financed by debt, not investing, which aims to build value over time through assets.
Why B: Hiding cash in a drawer earns nothing and loses value to inflation; investing puts money to work in assets.
Why C: Spending on daily needs is consumption, not investing, because it does not aim to grow your money.
Why D: Investing means buying assets such as stocks, bonds or real estate expecting them to grow in value or earn income over time, though returns are not guaranteed.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a stock?
A: A share of ownership in a company
B: A deposit held at a local bank
C: A type of insurance policy for cars
D: A loan made to a company and repaid
Why A: A stock represents a share of ownership in a corporation, so shareholders may gain from price growth and dividends and often can vote on company matters.
Why B: A deposit at a bank is a savings or checking account, not a stock; stocks represent ownership in a company.
Why C: Car insurance is a protection product; a stock is an ownership share in a company, so they are different things.
Why D: A loan to a company repaid with interest describes a bond; a stock gives ownership rather than lending.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a mutual fund?
A: A savings account at a local bank branch
B: A loan that a bank makes to a single borrower
C: A single stock owned by one person alone
D: A pool of money buying a mix of securities
Why A: A bank savings account is an insured deposit; a mutual fund pools many investors' money into securities and is not a bank deposit.
Why B: A bank loan to one borrower is lending; a mutual fund pools money from many investors rather than lending to a single borrower.
Why C: A mutual fund spreads money across many holdings, so it is not a single stock owned by one person alone.
Why D: A mutual fund pools money from many investors to buy a diversified mix of stocks, bonds or other securities, managed by professionals, giving small investors instant diversification.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an index fund?
A: A fund guaranteed to never lose any of your money ever
B: A fund that tries to beat the market through trading each year
C: A fund that aims to match the performance of a market index
D: A fund that holds only one stock at a time for its owners
Why A: No investment is guaranteed against loss; an index fund can lose value whenever the market it tracks declines.
Why B: Trying to beat the market describes an actively managed fund; an index fund simply tracks an index with low trading.
Why C: An index fund tracks a market index such as the S&P 500, so it holds the same stocks. It typically has low fees and broad diversification.
Why D: An index fund holds many securities in its index, which makes it diversified rather than a single stock holding.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is diversification?
A: Spreading money across different investments to reduce risk
B: Borrowing money in order to invest it in a business firm today
C: Putting all your money in one single stock that you like
D: Holding only cash and nothing else at all for many years
Why A: Diversification spreads money across different assets, industries or regions so a loss in one has less effect on the whole, lowering risk without necessarily lowering returns.
Why B: Borrowing to invest is leverage, which increases risk, whereas diversification reduces risk by spreading investments.
Why C: Putting everything in one stock is the opposite of diversifying and leaves you fully exposed to that company's performance.
Why D: Holding only cash is a single asset type and gives up growth; diversification means owning a range of different investments.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the relationship between risk and return?
A: Risk and return are unrelated, so one tells you nothing
B: Higher potential returns usually come with higher risk
C: Higher returns always come with no risk or cost to you
D: Low risk always guarantees high returns to everyone
Why A: Risk and return are linked, because investors demand higher potential returns for taking on greater uncertainty; saying they are unrelated is wrong.
Why B: Higher expected returns generally come with higher risk, as seen with stocks versus savings accounts. Investors need to be paid for accepting the chance of loss.
Why C: Higher returns do not come without risk; stocks may earn more over time but can fall sharply in the short term.
Why D: Low-risk investments such as savings accounts and Treasury bills usually pay low returns, so low risk never guarantees high returns.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which investment is generally expected to be riskiest?
A: A broad index fund of many stocks
B: A federally insured savings account
C: A U.S. Treasury bill held to the end
D: A single start-up company's stock
Why A: A broad index fund holds many stocks and is diversified, so it is far less risky than one company's shares.
Why B: Federally insured savings accounts are protected up to $250,000 by the FDIC, making them one of the safest options.
Why C: Treasury bills are backed by the U.S. government and, held to maturity, return the principal, making them very low risk.
Why D: A single start-up stock can lose all its value, and its price is volatile, so it carries high risk, though it also has potential for large gains.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a dividend?
A: A share of company profit paid to owners
B: A fee that is paid to a broker each time
C: Interest that is charged to each borrower
D: A tax that is charged on stock trades
Why A: A dividend is a payment to shareholders from company profits, often quarterly, which gives investors income in addition to any price growth.
Why B: Broker fees are commissions or charges for trades, not dividends, which are money received by owners.
Why C: Interest charged to borrowers is a cost of loans; a dividend is a payment to stock owners, not a charge.
Why D: Taxes on trades are a government charge, while a dividend is money that a company pays to its shareholders.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a capital gain?
A: Wages that are earned from a job each month of work
B: Profit from selling an investment for more than you paid
C: A gift of money from a relative in the family each year
D: Interest that is paid on a savings account balance daily
Why A: Wages earned from a job are ordinary income, not capital gains, which come from selling assets for more than their cost.
Why B: A capital gain is the profit when you sell an asset, such as a stock, for more than you paid. Assets held over a year get lower long-term tax rates.
Why C: Gifts from relatives are not capital gains; a gain arises only from the sale of an asset at a profit.
Why D: Interest on savings is interest income and is taxed as ordinary income, not capital gains, which arise from selling assets.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a 401(k)?
A: A car loan from a local bank for a new car
B: A type of health insurance plan for workers
C: An employer-sponsored retirement savings plan
D: A savings plan that is meant for college costs
Why A: A car loan is borrowing to buy a vehicle; a 401(k) is a retirement account, named after a section of the tax code.
Why B: Health insurance plans cover medical costs; a 401(k) is a retirement savings plan, so these are different products.
Why C: A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored plan where employees contribute from their paychecks, often pre-tax, and employers may match contributions. Investments grow tax-deferred until retirement.
Why D: Savings for college costs is described by a 529 plan, whereas a 401(k) is for retirement.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: An employer matches 100% of contributions up to 3% of pay. If you earn $30,000 and contribute 3%, how much does the employer add?
Why A: Employer matches 100 percent of contributions up to 3 percent of pay: 3% x $30,000 = $900 from you, so the employer adds an equal $900.
Why B: $90 comes from misplacing the decimal; 3 percent of $30,000 is $900, so the match equals $900 rather than $90.
Why C: $300 is only 1 percent of $30,000; the match is 100 percent of your 3 percent, which is $900.
Why D: $9,000 would be 30 percent of pay; 3 percent of $30,000 equals $900, so the match is $900.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an IRA?
A: A loan that is made to retired people only
B: A retirement account with tax advantages
C: An insurance policy for retirees only
D: A government tax form filed by retirees only
Why A: An IRA is an account, not a loan, and retirees are not its only users; people save in one while still working.
Why B: An IRA, or individual retirement arrangement, is a personal account for retirement savings that offers tax advantages, such as deductions or tax-free growth. Annual limits apply.
Why C: An IRA is an investment account and not an insurance policy; anyone with earned income can contribute, not just retirees.
Why D: An IRA is a retirement account, not a tax form for retirees; anyone with earned income can contribute.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the main feature of a Roth IRA?
A: It pays a guaranteed return of ten percent each year to you
B: Contributions are tax-deductible and withdrawals are taxed as income
C: Contributions are after-tax and qualified withdrawals are tax-free
D: Withdrawals are always free of any rules or limits at any age
Why A: No retirement account guarantees a return; Roth IRA investments rise and fall with the market, and no fixed ten percent is promised.
Why B: That describes a traditional IRA, where contributions may be deductible and withdrawals are taxed; a Roth works the opposite way.
Why C: Roth IRA contributions come from after-tax money, so qualified withdrawals in retirement, including earnings, are tax-free. This helps if you expect higher taxes later.
Why D: Roth withdrawals follow rules, such as the age 59 and a half and five-year requirements for tax-free earnings, so they are not rule-free.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why is it better to start investing early?
A: Fees are lower for all of the early investors
B: Taxes disappear for early investors in every year
C: Early investors never lose any money at all
D: Compounding has more time to grow your money
Why A: Fees are charged by funds and brokers regardless of how early you start, so starting early does not lower fees.
Why B: Taxes still apply to investors of any age, so starting early does not remove them; the benefit is growth over time.
Why C: Early investors can still lose money, as markets fluctuate; time horizon helps by allowing recovery, but nothing guarantees gains.
Why D: Compounding means earnings generate their own earnings, so more years lets small deposits grow substantially. Starting at 25 instead of 35 can mean much more by retirement.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is dollar-cost averaging?
A: Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule
B: Waiting for the lowest price to appear again
C: Selling when prices fall by a fair amount
D: Investing everything at once on a hunch about prices
Why A: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a set amount at regular intervals, such as $200 monthly, so you buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when high.
Why B: Waiting for the lowest price is market timing, which is very hard to do and not what dollar-cost averaging involves.
Why C: Selling after prices fall is a reaction to losses and not dollar-cost averaging, which involves steady, regular buying.
Why D: Investing everything at once on a hunch is lump-sum investing based on guessing, not the regular steady purchases of dollar-cost averaging.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a brokerage account?
A: An account that guarantees a set rate of return
B: An account to buy and sell stocks and funds
C: An account that is used only for borrowing
D: An account that is used for paying bills
Why A: No account guarantees a rate of return; a brokerage account holds investments whose value rises and falls.
Why B: A brokerage account lets you buy and sell investments such as stocks, bonds and funds through a brokerage firm. Unlike retirement accounts, it has no special tax benefits.
Why C: Borrowing is done through loans or credit lines; a brokerage account is for investing, though margin accounts can borrow.
Why D: Paying bills is the job of a checking account; a brokerage account is used to hold and trade investments.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the effect of fees on long-term returns?
A: Fees only affect investors who hold for the short term, not savers
B: Fees actually increase returns over time for long-term savers
C: Fees have no effect at all on returns over the long run
D: Higher fees reduce the amount that stays invested and compounds
Why A: Fees affect all long-term investors, and the effect grows with time, so they are not limited to short-term holders.
Why B: Fees subtract from your returns and never add to them, so claiming they increase returns is incorrect.
Why C: Fees compound against you over decades, so even small percentages matter, meaning they do have an effect on long-term returns.
Why D: Fees come out of your balance, so less money stays invested to compound. Even a 1 percent difference in annual fees can cost tens of thousands over decades.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a time horizon?
A: The time it takes to open an account
B: The date a company was first founded
C: How long you expect to stay invested
D: The time of day that a market opens
Why A: Opening an account is a quick setup task; a time horizon is the length of time you plan to invest before needing the money.
Why B: The founding date of a company is unrelated to your own investing plans; time horizon refers to how long you expect to stay invested.
Why C: A time horizon is how long you expect to keep money invested before you need it. Longer horizons can handle more stock risk, while short ones favor safer assets.
Why D: Market opening hours are a trading schedule, whereas a time horizon is the length of your investing plan.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which investment mix is most suitable for a goal 40 years away?
A: A diversified portfolio weighted toward stocks
B: A single speculative bet on one company only
C: Only a one-month Treasury bill held to maturity
D: Only cash kept hidden under a mattress at home
Why A: With 40 years, a portfolio weighted toward diversified stocks has time to ride out downturns and benefit from compounding, which historically offers higher long-term growth.
Why B: A single speculative bet is too risky for any goal, even a long one, because one company can fail completely.
Why C: A one-month Treasury bill would likely earn less than inflation over 40 years, so it is far too conservative for a long-term goal.
Why D: Cash under a mattress earns nothing and loses buying power to inflation over four decades, so it is a poor choice.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which investment mix is most suitable for a goal one year away?
A: All of the money in cryptocurrency coins of one type
B: All of the money in a single volatile tech stock
C: All of the money in a long-term growth fund each year
D: Safe, liquid options like a savings account or CD
Why A: Cryptocurrency can swing wildly in weeks, and a one-year goal cannot absorb a large drop, so it is too risky.
Why B: A single volatile tech stock could fall sharply, and with only a year, there is no time to recover.
Why C: Long-term growth funds hold stocks that can fall in the short run, which is risky when you need the money in a year.
Why D: For a one-year goal, protecting principal matters most, so savings accounts or CDs offer safety and easy access, even though returns are modest.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a Ponzi scheme?
A: A savings option that banks offer to savers
B: A bond program run by the government for savers
C: A fraud paying early investors with new money
D: A legal retirement plan for workers and firms
Why A: Savings options offered by banks are legitimate products; a Ponzi scheme is a fraud that pays returns using money from newer investors.
Why B: Government bond programs are legal and backed by the government; a Ponzi scheme is an illegal fraud.
Why C: A Ponzi scheme pays earlier investors with money from newer investors rather than real profits, and collapses when recruits run out. Bernie Madoff ran a famous one.
Why D: Legal retirement plans such as 401(k)s are regulated; a Ponzi scheme is an illegal fraud with no real investments.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is a red flag of investment fraud?
A: A registered adviser with a public record of past work
B: Promises of guaranteed high returns with no risk
C: Independent audited statements and records
D: Clear disclosures of risks and fees to investors
Why A: A registered adviser with a public record is a sign of legitimacy, since you can check their background through regulators.
Why B: Guaranteed high returns with no risk are impossible in real markets, so this is a hallmark of fraud. Higher returns always involve higher risk.
Why C: Independent audited statements indicate transparency and accountability, so they are a good sign, not a red flag.
Why D: Honest disclosure of risks and fees is expected from legitimate investments, so it is a good sign rather than a warning.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is inflation risk?
A: The risk that tax rates will rise again for you this year
B: The risk that a bank closes its doors for good this year
C: The risk that rising prices reduce the value of your money
D: The risk that a company fails and cannot repay its lenders
Why A: Higher tax rates are a different issue, called tax risk; inflation risk is about prices rising faster than your returns.
Why B: A bank closing is institutional risk, which FDIC insurance covers; inflation risk concerns loss of buying power.
Why C: Inflation risk is the chance that rising prices erode purchasing power, so money earning less than inflation buys less over time. Cash savings are especially exposed.
Why D: A company failing to repay lenders is credit or default risk, whereas inflation risk is about rising prices reducing what your money can buy.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the best reason to compare savings account interest rates?
A: Lower rates always earn you more money each year
B: Rates do not affect how much you earn at all
C: All accounts pay exactly the same rate to you
D: A higher rate earns more on the same deposit
Why A: Lower rates earn less, not more, so comparing rates is done to find the higher one.
Why B: Rates directly determine your interest earnings, so claiming they have no effect is wrong.
Why C: Banks set different rates, so accounts differ; online banks often pay more than traditional branches.
Why D: A higher interest rate, or APY, earns more interest on the same deposit, so comparing helps your savings grow faster.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a minimum balance requirement?
A: The most money you are allowed to keep in an account each month
B: The least amount you must keep in an account to avoid fees
C: The number of deposits that you must make each month
D: The interest that you must earn each month in total
Why A: The most you may keep is not a minimum; a minimum balance requirement sets the lowest amount you must maintain.
Why B: A minimum balance requirement is the lowest balance you must maintain, or you may be charged a monthly fee or lose interest. Compare accounts for low or no minimums.
Why C: The number of deposits is a transaction rule, whereas a minimum balance concerns the amount of money in the account.
Why D: Interest you earn is the bank's payment to you; a minimum balance is the least amount you must keep in the account.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a good first savings goal for most people?
A: An emergency fund
B: A luxury purchase
C: A fancy vacation fund
D: A risky investment
Why A: An emergency fund covers unexpected costs like car repairs or job loss, preventing debt. Most advisers suggest building a starter fund before other goals.
Why B: A luxury purchase is a want, not a priority; essential protections like an emergency fund should come first.
Why C: A vacation fund is a nice goal, but it comes after building basic financial security.
Why D: Risky investments should come only after you have a safety cushion, so they are not a good first goal.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why do employers withhold income tax from each paycheck?
A: To keep the money as a bonus for the firm
B: To lower the worker's total income by law
C: To collect tax gradually through the year
D: To pay the employee in advance for future work
Why A: Withholding is not a bonus for the employer; the money is sent to the government as an advance payment of your tax.
Why B: Withholding does not reduce your total income by law; it is just part of your pay sent toward taxes you owe.
Why C: Withholding spreads tax payments across the year, so you do not owe a lump sum on April 15. The amount depends on income and your W-4.
Why D: Withholding is a deduction from pay, not a payment to you; employees are paid after work is done.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A worker gets a large refund every spring. What does this suggest about withholding?
A: The worker did not earn any income last year at all
B: Too little tax was withheld from paychecks all year long
C: The employer paid the worker a surprise bonus in April
D: Too much tax was withheld from paychecks during the year
Why A: A refund requires income and tax already withheld; a worker with no income would have no tax withheld to refund.
Why B: Too little withholding results in owing money at tax time, not a refund, so this is the reverse situation.
Why C: A refund is not a bonus from the employer; it is the worker's own overpaid tax being returned.
Why D: A large refund means more tax was taken out than owed, so the worker gave the government an interest-free loan. Adjusting the W-4 raises take-home pay.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is self-employment tax?
A: A property tax that is charged on a home office space yearly
B: The Social Security and Medicare tax paid by the self-employed
C: A tax that applies to gifts given to employees by firms
D: A sales tax that is added to the price of products sold at a store
Why A: Property tax applies to real estate, whereas self-employment tax is a payroll-type tax on net earnings.
Why B: Self-employment tax is about 15.3 percent, covering Social Security and Medicare that employers normally split with employees. Self-employed people pay both halves.
Why C: Gift tax applies to large gifts; self-employment tax is for those who work for themselves.
Why D: Sales tax is collected on goods sold; self-employment tax is based on a person's net earnings from self-employment.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the main purpose of a resume?
A: To summarize your skills and experience
B: To list the prices of your services for all
C: To apply for a bank loan for a home
D: To report your income to the tax agency
Why A: A resume is a short document summarizing your education, skills and experience to persuade employers to interview you.
Why B: A list of service prices is a price sheet or quote, not a resume, which presents a person's qualifications.
Why C: A bank loan application is a different document that asks about income and assets, not employment qualifications.
Why D: Income reporting is done with tax forms like the W-2 and 1040, whereas a resume summarizes qualifications.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Two job offers pay $38,000. Job A includes health insurance worth $5,000 a year and Job B includes none. Which offer has the higher total value?
A: Neither, because the benefits have no value
B: Job B, because it pays the same salary with fewer rules
C: Job A, because benefits add to total compensation
D: They are exactly equal in total value to the worker
Why A: Benefits like health insurance have real financial value, since you would otherwise pay for them yourself.
Why B: Job B pays the same salary but lacks benefits, so its total value is lower, not higher.
Why C: Total compensation includes salary and benefits: Job A is $38,000 + $5,000 = $43,000, versus $38,000 for Job B, so Job A is worth more.
Why D: The offers are not equal because Job A adds $5,000 in health coverage, giving $43,000 against $38,000.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is job satisfaction mostly influenced by besides pay?
A: The number of coworkers who happen to share a birthday
B: The length of the daily commute and nothing else
C: The color of the walls in the office and nothing else
D: Work environment, growth and fit with your interests
Why A: Coworker birthdays are trivial, whereas satisfaction depends on meaningful factors like the environment and opportunities.
Why B: Commute matters but is not the only factor; satisfaction also depends on environment, growth and interests.
Why C: Wall color is minor; satisfaction comes mainly from the work environment, growth opportunities and interest fit.
Why D: Besides pay, people are more satisfied with supportive workplaces, chances to grow, and work that matches their interests and values.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why is it smart to keep receipts for major purchases?
A: They lower the price of the item at a later time, by half or more
B: They prove what you paid and help with returns, warranties and taxes
C: They let you spend the same money a second time if you like to
D: They are required by law for every purchase and must be filed with the state
Why A: Receipts do not change a price later; stores may offer price adjustments, but a receipt itself does not cut the price in half.
Why B: A receipt is proof of purchase for returns, exchanges, warranty claims, and tax deductions or business expenses. Keep receipts for big purchases.
Why C: Receipts cannot be used to spend money twice; they are records, not currency or credit.
Why D: Receipts are not legally required to be filed with the state; they are kept for your own protection and records.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a store credit card most likely to offer?
A: A discount on purchases at that store, often with a high interest rate
B: Lower interest rates than any other bank card ever offers to anyone
C: Free money that never has to be paid back by the cardholder at all
D: Complete protection from fraud and identity theft wherever it is ever used
Why A: Store cards often give an opening discount or rewards at that store but usually carry high APRs, and can only be used at that retailer or its brands.
Why B: Store cards typically have higher interest rates than bank cards, not lower, so the claim is the opposite of the truth.
Why C: Store credit is borrowed money that must be repaid, so there is no free money involved.
Why D: Store cards give limited fraud protection and no complete shield from theft; they do not prevent identity theft anywhere.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A store offers 'buy now, pay later' with no interest if you pay within 6 months. What risk should a shopper check?
A: Whether the item is also available in other colors
B: Whether deferred interest or fees apply if unpaid
C: Whether the logo of the store looks attractive
D: Whether the shopper has friends who also use the plan
Why A: Color options are a product feature, not a financial risk of the payment plan.
Why B: Deferred interest plans may charge all back interest from the purchase date if the balance is not fully paid by the end, so shoppers should check the terms.
Why C: The logo's appearance is irrelevant to the cost; the financial risk comes from the terms, fees and interest conditions.
Why D: Whether friends use the plan has nothing to do with its cost or risk; what matters are the plan's fees and conditions.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does it mean to live within your means?
A: Spending more than you make
B: Never spending money on anything
C: Borrowing money for every purchase
D: Spending no more than you earn
Why A: Spending more than you make is living beyond your means, which forces you to use debt or savings and is the opposite of the idea.
Why B: Never spending anything is unrealistic because everyone must pay for needs like food and housing; living within your means only requires spending to fit your income.
Why C: Borrowing for every purchase means spending beyond current income and piling up debt, which is the opposite of living within your means.
Why D: Living within your means means keeping spending at or below your income each month, so you avoid debt and can still build savings for the future.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is the best example of delayed gratification in spending?
A: Spending your whole paycheck on the same day
B: Buying the first item you see in a store on a whim
C: Saving for months to buy a quality item later
D: Charging a purchase you cannot repay to a card
Why A: Spending an entire paycheck right away is the opposite of delayed gratification, since it gives up any chance to save or plan for bigger goals.
Why B: Buying the first item you see on a whim is impulse buying, which is immediate gratification rather than waiting for something better or planned.
Why C: Delayed gratification means giving up an immediate purchase to get something better later, and saving for months toward a quality item is a classic example of it.
Why D: Charging a purchase you cannot repay is immediate gratification paid for with debt and interest, so it is the reverse of waiting and saving first.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A teen can spend $100 on concert tickets or save it toward a $400 laptop needed for school. What is the opportunity cost of buying the tickets?
A: Progress toward the laptop that the $100 would have funded
B: Nothing, because tickets are a want, so nothing is lost
C: The price of the laptop plus sales tax and any delivery fees
D: The cost of parking at the big concert venue for the night
Why A: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative you give up, so spending the $100 on tickets means losing $100 of progress toward the needed laptop.
Why B: Tickets being a want does not make them free; the $100 spent could have gone toward the laptop, so something valuable is still given up.
Why C: The laptop's price plus tax and delivery is the cost of buying the laptop, not what is given up by choosing the tickets instead.
Why D: Parking is an extra out-of-pocket expense of attending the concert, not the opportunity cost, which is the best alternative use of the $100.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why is a savings account safer than keeping large amounts of cash at home?
A: Cash kept at home earns higher interest than an account
B: FDIC insurance protects deposits from theft or fire
C: Savings accounts cannot be used when an emergency happens
D: Banks never charge any fees on a savings account
Why A: Cash kept at home earns no interest at all, while a savings account pays interest, so this claim reverses the real difference between them.
Why B: FDIC insurance protects deposits up to $250,000 per depositor per bank if the bank fails, whereas cash at home can be stolen or burned with no protection.
Why C: Savings accounts can be accessed in an emergency, usually by transfer or withdrawal, so this does not explain why they are safer than home cash.
Why D: Banks can charge fees on savings accounts, such as monthly maintenance or excess withdrawal fees, so the word never makes this statement false.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which statement about interest on savings is correct?
A: Interest is the amount you deposit every month into the bank
B: Interest is a fee you pay for opening an account at a bank
C: Interest is a tax you owe to the government on your balance each month
D: Interest is money the bank pays you for keeping funds on deposit
Why A: Money you put into the account is a deposit; interest is instead the amount the bank pays you for using your money, not what you contribute.
Why B: Interest is not an account opening fee; fees are charges you pay, while savings interest is a payment made to you by the bank.
Why C: Interest earned on savings is not a tax, although it may be taxable income; it is a payment from the bank, not an amount owed to government.
Why D: Interest is the money a bank pays you for letting it use your deposits, usually stated as an annual rate, and it grows your balance over time.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Priya deposits $2,000 at 3% compounded annually. About how much will she have after 2 years?
A: About $2,122
B: About $2,060
C: About $2,180
D: About $2,600
Why A: Compound interest: $2,000 x 1.03 x 1.03 = $2,121.80, which rounds to about $2,122 because interest in year two also earns interest.
Why B: This adds only simple interest for one year ($2,000 x 3% = $60) and ignores the second year, so it is far too low.
Why C: This option was reworded so it is clearly wrong; the correct total is $2,000 x 1.03 x 1.03 = $2,121.80, and $2,180 would need a higher rate.
Why D: About $2,600 would require roughly 30 percent growth, far above the 3% annual rate; $2,000 x 1.03^2 is only about $2,122.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a good way to avoid dipping into savings for small wants?
A: Carry large amounts of cash with you everywhere you go each day
B: Keep all of your money in one single account and never track it or set limits
C: Keep a separate account for goals and a small budget for fun spending
D: Cancel your savings account and spend what is in it right away
Why A: Carrying large amounts of cash makes spending easier and risks loss or theft, so it makes dipping into savings for wants more likely, not less.
Why B: Keeping everything in one account with no tracking or limits blurs savings and spending money, which makes it easy to spend savings on small wants.
Why C: Separating goal savings from a small fun budget keeps savings untouched and gives you guilt-free spending money, which helps you resist raiding savings for small wants.
Why D: Closing your savings account and spending the money is the exact opposite of protecting savings and would leave you with nothing for goals or emergencies.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does FDIC insurance cover?
A: Cash that is kept in a safe at home for emergency use only
B: Stocks that are bought through a bank or a broker up to the legal limit
C: Deposits in insured banks up to the legal limit if the bank fails
D: Losses that are caused by a drop in the stock market overall
Why A: FDIC insurance does not cover cash kept at home; it only protects money deposited in FDIC-insured banks, so home cash has no such protection.
Why B: Stocks bought through a bank or broker are investments, not deposits, so FDIC insurance does not cover them; SIPC covers broker failure, not losses.
Why C: FDIC insurance covers deposits in insured banks up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, and pays out if the bank fails.
Why D: FDIC insurance does not protect against market losses on investments; it only guarantees bank deposits if the bank itself fails, not falling stock prices.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why can closing an old credit card account sometimes lower a credit score?
A: It can shorten credit history and raise credit utilization
B: Old accounts are not counted in any credit score at all
C: Closed accounts are always deleted at once and never reopened
D: Banks punish customers for canceling their credit cards
Why A: Closing an old card shortens your average account age and removes available credit, which can raise your utilization ratio, and both effects may lower your score.
Why B: Old accounts do count in credit scores; length of credit history is a scoring factor, which is why closing them can matter at all.
Why C: Closed accounts in good standing often stay on your report for about ten years, so they are not deleted at once and the score drop has other causes.
Why D: Banks do not punish customers for closing cards; the score may fall because of changed history length and utilization, which are mathematical effects.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person with a 620 credit score and one with a 780 score both apply for a $15,000 car loan. Which is more likely to get a lower interest rate?
A: Neither of them can get a loan from any bank at all today
B: Both will receive exactly the same rate from the lender today
C: The person with the 620 score, because lenders need customers
D: The person with the 780 score, because lenders see less risk
Why A: Lenders do approve loans for fair or good credit scores, usually at higher rates for lower scores, so neither being denied outright is a safe assumption.
Why B: Lenders price loans based on risk, so different credit scores lead to different rates; the same rate for both borrowers is unlikely.
Why C: A 620 score signals higher default risk, so lenders charge more interest to offset that risk rather than offering a cheaper rate.
Why D: A 780 score signals reliable repayment, so lenders see less default risk and generally offer a lower interest rate on the $15,000 car loan.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a variable interest rate?
A: A rate that is chosen by the borrower at the start of the loan
B: A rate that can go up or down over time based on market conditions
C: A rate that is always set at zero for the whole of the loan term
D: A rate that never changes during the whole life of the loan itself
Why A: A borrower does not choose the rate; the lender sets it, and the term variable means the rate can change over time, not that it is picked by the borrower.
Why B: A variable rate is tied to a benchmark such as the prime rate, so it can rise or fall over time and change your payment amount.
Why C: A rate fixed at zero would be an interest-free loan, which is rare; a variable rate instead moves with market conditions above zero.
Why D: A rate that never changes during the loan is a fixed rate, which is the opposite of a variable rate that adjusts with the market.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a fixed interest rate?
A: A rate that stays the same for the full loan term
B: A rate that is repaid at the end of the loan only
C: A rate that is free of charge for the borrower
D: A rate that changes each month with the market
Why A: A fixed interest rate stays the same for the whole loan term, so the rate and usually the payment are predictable and do not change with the market.
Why B: Fixed refers to the rate staying constant, not to repaying everything at the end; most loans charge interest along the way, not only at maturity.
Why C: Interest is the price of borrowing and is not free; a fixed rate is still charged, it just does not change over the loan.
Why D: A rate that changes monthly with the market is a variable rate, which is the opposite of a fixed rate that stays constant.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Before taking out a loan, which comparison tells you the true yearly cost of borrowing from different lenders?
A: The color of the loan paperwork
B: The number of branches lenders have
C: The size of the lender's building
D: The annual percentage rate (APR)
Why A: The color of the paperwork says nothing about borrowing costs; the cost is shown in the interest rate and fees, which APR combines into one yearly percentage.
Why B: The number of branches tells you about convenience, not what the loan costs; it cannot be used to compare the yearly price of borrowing.
Why C: The lender's building size has no link to loan pricing; APR is the standardized measure that lets you compare real borrowing costs across lenders.
Why D: APR combines the interest rate and certain fees into one yearly percentage, so it is the best way to compare the true cost of loans from different lenders.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why should you review your insurance coverage after a major life change like buying a house?
A: Insurance is only needed once in a lifetime for any person
B: Insurance policies update themselves for free for everyone covered
C: Your needs and the value you need to protect may have changed
D: Reviewing a policy cancels it and ends your coverage for good
Why A: Insurance needs change with life events, so it is not a once-in-a-lifetime purchase; major changes like a home purchase require updating your coverage.
Why B: Policies do not update themselves automatically at no charge; you must contact the insurer to change coverage, and higher coverage usually raises the premium.
Why C: A major change like buying a house raises the value you need to protect and adds new risks, so reviewing coverage keeps you from being underinsured.
Why D: Reviewing a policy does not cancel it; you simply check whether limits and coverage still fit, and the policy remains in force during the review.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A driver causes an accident that injures another person and has only the state minimum liability coverage. What is the main risk?
A: The other driver must pay for everything that happened there too
B: Costs above the policy limits may have to be paid out of pocket
C: No costs will be owed because it was an accident, not on purpose
D: The insurer will pay unlimited amounts no matter the limits
Why A: The other driver is not responsible for your costs; as the at-fault driver you owe damages, and the issue is limits being too low to cover them.
Why B: State minimum limits are often low, so a serious injury claim can exceed them, and the at-fault driver may have to pay the excess out of pocket.
Why C: Causing an accident accidentally still creates liability, since negligence rather than intent determines responsibility, so costs can definitely be owed.
Why D: Liability policies pay only up to their stated limits, so the insurer will not pay unlimited amounts and the driver must cover anything above them.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which action reduces the risk of a home fire?
A: Leaving candles burning while you sleep at night in the home
B: Removing the batteries from all of the smoke detectors at home
C: Installing working smoke detectors and not overloading outlets
D: Storing flammable liquids close to a heater or a gas stove
Why A: Leaving candles burning unattended while you sleep is a common cause of house fires, so it raises fire risk rather than reducing it.
Why B: Removing smoke detector batteries disables the early warning that saves lives, so it increases the danger of a fire rather than reducing it.
Why C: Working smoke detectors give early warning and avoiding overloaded outlets prevents electrical fires, so together these actions lower the chance and damage of a home fire.
Why D: Storing flammable liquids near a heater or gas stove invites ignition and fire, so it raises the risk of a home fire.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is self-insurance?
A: Asking a friend to promise to pay for a loss that happens
B: Setting aside your own money to cover possible losses
C: Ignoring the possibility of loss and hoping for the best
D: Buying a policy from an insurance company every single year
Why A: A friend's promise to pay is an informal arrangement and not self-insurance, which means setting aside your own funds to absorb losses yourself.
Why B: Self-insurance means setting aside your own money to cover possible losses instead of buying a policy, and it works best for small, predictable risks.
Why C: Ignoring risk and hoping for the best is risk acceptance without any plan, not self-insurance, which involves actually saving funds to pay for losses.
Why D: Buying a yearly policy from an insurance company transfers risk to the insurer, so it is traditional insurance, the opposite of self-insuring.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which loss is best handled by buying insurance rather than saving for it?
A: A rare event that could cost far more than you could ever save
B: A regular expense that comes up every month, like rent or food
C: A cost that you choose to avoid completely in your life
D: A small cost that you can easily pay from your own savings
Why A: Insurance fits rare but very costly events like a house fire or major illness, which would wipe out savings, so spreading risk across many policyholders makes sense.
Why B: Regular predictable expenses such as rent or food are budgeted for, not insured, since insurance covers uncertain losses and not certain recurring bills.
Why C: Completely avoiding a cost is risk avoidance, a different strategy from insurance, which covers risks you are still exposed to.
Why D: A small cost you can easily afford is better handled by saving and self-insuring, since insurance premiums would likely cost more than the loss.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does it mean when an investment is liquid?
A: It never changes in value over time at all, ever
B: It cannot be sold for several years in a row
C: It is stored as water or some other fluid in a tank
D: It can be sold quickly for cash with little loss
Why A: A liquid investment is easy to convert to cash, which has nothing to do with value staying fixed; liquid assets can still rise and fall in price.
Why B: An asset that cannot be sold for years is illiquid, which is the opposite of liquid; liquidity is about how quickly you can turn it into cash.
Why C: Liquid here is a financial term, not a physical state of matter; the word describes how easily an asset converts to cash, not its form.
Why D: Liquid means you can sell the asset quickly for cash without losing much value, like savings or shares of large companies.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is usually the most liquid asset?
A: A house in a nice neighborhood
B: A rare painting from a gallery
C: Cash in a checking account
D: A piece of land in the country
Why A: A house takes weeks or months to sell and has closing costs, so it is illiquid compared with cash in a checking account.
Why B: A rare painting needs a specialized buyer and appraisal, which makes selling slow and uncertain, so it is far less liquid than cash.
Why C: Cash in checking is already money and can be used immediately, so it is the most liquid asset on the list.
Why D: Land can take a long time to sell and its value depends on location and buyers, so it is illiquid compared with cash.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: An investor puts all their money into one company's stock and the company fails. Which investing principle did they ignore?
A: Diversification
B: Tax deferral
C: Compounding
D: Inflation cover
Why A: Diversification means spreading money across many investments so one failure does not ruin you; putting everything into one company's stock ignores it.
Why B: Tax deferral delays taxes on investment growth; it has nothing to do with losing everything when a single company fails, which is concentration risk.
Why C: Compounding is earning returns on prior returns, which does not address the danger of holding only one company's stock that can fail.
Why D: Inflation cover is not a standard investing principle; the risk of loss from a single failed company is controlled by diversification instead.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a stock market index?
A: A single company's yearly profit report for its owners
B: A measure of the performance of a group of stocks
C: A government rule about taxes on stock trades
D: A list of the fees that brokers charge clients
Why A: A company's yearly profit report is an income statement, which describes one firm, while an index tracks the performance of many stocks together.
Why B: A stock market index, such as the S&P 500 or Dow, measures the performance of a chosen group of stocks and shows how the market is doing.
Why C: Tax rules on stock trades come from government law, such as capital gains tax, and are not what an index is, which only measures performance.
Why D: A list of broker fees is a fee schedule, not an index; an index tracks stock prices and gives a snapshot of market performance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is rebalancing a portfolio?
A: Selling everything and starting over from scratch each year
B: Buying only the single best performer in the portfolio
C: Ignoring the portfolio for years on end and hoping for gains
D: Adjusting investments back to your target mix of assets
Why A: Selling everything and starting over each year is expensive because of taxes and trading costs; rebalancing only adjusts holdings back to targets.
Why B: Buying only the best performer concentrates risk and abandons the target mix, which is the opposite of rebalancing a diversified portfolio.
Why C: Ignoring a portfolio lets asset weights drift away from your plan, so it is the opposite of rebalancing, which restores the intended mix.
Why D: Rebalancing means buying or selling to restore your target mix of assets, such as 60% stocks and 40% bonds, which keeps your risk level on plan.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A long-term investor sees the market drop 15% in a month. Which response is generally most sensible?
A: Borrow money so you can buy a single stock
B: Sell everything immediately because of fear
C: Stay with the plan and keep investing regularly
D: Stop looking at the plan and give up on your goal
Why A: Borrowing to buy a single stock adds debt and concentration risk during a downturn, which is a risky response rather than a sensible one.
Why B: Selling everything out of fear locks in losses and often misses the recovery, which makes it a poor response for a long-term investor.
Why C: Long-term investors generally do best staying with their plan and continuing regular investing, which buys more shares at lower prices during a dip.
Why D: Abandoning the plan and giving up on your goal turns a temporary decline into a permanent setback, which is not a sensible response.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does the saying 'don't put all your eggs in one basket' mean for investing?
A: Spend all of your money on eggs and baskets today
B: Buy only one single stock that you trust
C: Avoid investing in anything at all, ever again
D: Spread your money across different investments
Why A: This takes the saying literally; the proverb is about diversifying risk, and spending all your money on eggs and baskets has nothing to do with investing.
Why B: Buying one stock puts all your eggs in one basket, which is exactly what the saying warns against because one failure can wipe you out.
Why C: Avoiding investing altogether misses the lesson; the saying advises spreading money around, not refusing to invest, and cash can lose value to inflation.
Why D: The saying advises diversification, spreading money across different investments so that one loss does not destroy your whole portfolio.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the main benefit of an employer 401(k) match?
A: It adds extra money to your retirement savings for free
B: It guarantees investment gains every single year for you
C: It lets you withdraw money any time with no rules or taxes
D: It lowers your income tax to zero every single year for life
Why A: A 401(k) match is extra money your employer adds to your account based on what you contribute, which is a free boost to retirement savings.
Why B: A match adds money but guarantees no investment gains; the account's investments can still lose value, so returns are never guaranteed.
Why C: Withdrawals from a 401(k) before age 59 and a half usually bring taxes and a 10 percent penalty, so the match does not allow free access.
Why D: Traditional 401(k) contributions reduce taxable income but do not lower taxes to zero, and the match itself has no such effect.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Two investors each save $200 a month for 30 years. One earns 4% and the other 7%. Which result is most likely?
A: Neither investor earns any growth at all over time
B: The 7% investor ends far ahead through compounding
C: The 4% investor ends up with the larger balance overall
D: Both investors end up with the same final balance
Why A: Both investors earn growth because 4% and 7% are both positive returns; saying neither earns growth ignores the compounding that happens each year.
Why B: Over 30 years the higher 7% return compounds much more strongly than 4%, so that investor ends with far more money for the same deposits.
Why C: The 4% investor earns a lower return on identical deposits, so ends with a smaller balance, not a larger one.
Why D: Different returns over 30 years produce very different balances because compounding magnifies the gap, so the final amounts cannot be the same.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a bear market?
A: A period when prices rise steadily over a long period of time
B: A period when stock markets close for a holiday and no trading occurs
C: A market where people buy and sell wild animals for sport and food
D: A period when stock prices fall significantly, often 20% or more
Why A: Steadily rising prices describe a bull market, not a bear market, which is the opposite condition of falling prices.
Why B: Stock markets closing for a holiday is just a normal break in trading and has nothing to do with a bear market, which is about falling prices.
Why C: A bear market is a financial term about stock prices and has nothing to do with trading animals; the name refers to a bear swiping downward.
Why D: A bear market is a sustained decline in stock prices, commonly defined as a fall of 20 percent or more from a recent high.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a bull market?
A: A period when stock prices are rising or expected to rise
B: A period when prices fall sharply and investors grow afraid
C: A market where only livestock is traded each week in town
D: A period when prices never change at all for many years
Why A: A bull market is a period of rising or expected rising stock prices, with investor optimism, and the name comes from a bull thrusting its horns upward.
Why B: Sharp falling prices and investor fear describe a bear market, which is the opposite of a bull market.
Why C: A bull market refers to rising security prices, not a livestock market; the word is a financial term unrelated to trading cattle.
Why D: Prices never changing for many years would be a flat or stagnant market, not a bull market, which is defined by rising prices.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a stock split?
A: A company gives half its yearly profits to staff
B: More shares at a proportionally lower price each
C: A company merges with one of its rivals in a deal
D: A company cuts its workforce in half to save costs
Why A: Sharing half of profits with staff is profit sharing, not a stock split, which only changes the number of shares and not company earnings.
Why B: In a stock split, a company issues more shares and lowers the price per share proportionally, so each holder's total value stays the same.
Why C: Merging with a rival is a merger or acquisition, which combines companies; a stock split only divides existing shares into more pieces.
Why D: Cutting the workforce in half is a layoff or restructuring and is unrelated to a stock split, which changes only the number of shares.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which statement about past investment performance is accurate?
A: It guarantees the same results next year
B: It is the only factor that matters
C: It does not guarantee future results
D: It proves an investment cannot lose cash
Why A: Past performance cannot guarantee next year's results, since markets change, so saying it guarantees the same outcome is false.
Why B: Past performance is only one piece of information; costs, risk, goals and economic conditions matter too, so it is not the only factor.
Why C: Past performance does not guarantee future results, which is why investment ads carry this warning; markets change and previous gains may not repeat.
Why D: A good track record does not prove an investment cannot lose money; every investment carries risk, even one that has done well in the past.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which choice best protects the buying power of long-term savings from inflation?
A: A diversified mix that has outpaced inflation
B: Spending all of your savings right away today
C: Keeping all of your savings in cash for decades
D: Hiding cash in a drawer at home for decades
Why A: A diversified mix of investments that has outpaced inflation helps long-term savings keep or grow their purchasing power over decades.
Why B: Spending all your savings right away gives up future purchasing power altogether and does nothing to protect it from inflation.
Why C: Cash earning little interest loses buying power to inflation over decades, so holding all savings in cash does not protect them.
Why D: Cash in a drawer earns no interest, so inflation steadily reduces what it can buy, and it also risks loss or theft.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a good first step to take control of your spending?
A: Stop looking at your account balance for a month
B: Cancel your bank account altogether and use cash
C: Borrow money so you can cover your purchases this month
D: Track a month of spending to see where money goes
Why A: Not checking your balance hides spending problems and may cause overdrafts, so it does not help you gain control over your spending.
Why B: Cancelling your bank account and using only cash removes safety and records and does not itself show where your money goes.
Why C: Borrowing to cover purchases adds debt and interest, which makes spending harder to control rather than easier.
Why D: Tracking a month of spending shows exactly where money goes, which reveals patterns and gives a base for budgeting and cutting waste.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the best way to avoid paying credit card interest?
A: Use the card only for cash advances at the bank ATM each month
B: Pay the full statement balance by the due date every month
C: Pay the bill a few days after the due date has already passed
D: Pay only the minimum amount each month on the card balance
Why A: Cash advances usually carry fees and start accruing interest immediately with no grace period, so they increase interest costs rather than avoid them.
Why B: Paying the full statement balance by the due date keeps the grace period, so purchases are not charged interest at all.
Why C: Paying after the due date usually triggers a late fee and may lose the grace period, so interest and penalties apply.
Why D: Paying only the minimum leaves a balance that accrues interest, which can make the debt costly and slow to pay off.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a cash advance on a credit card?
A: Earning cash back on the purchases you make with the card
B: Paying a bill early using your own money from savings
C: Borrowing cash on your card, with fees and interest
D: Depositing cash into your own bank account at a branch
Why A: Earning cash back is a rewards benefit for purchases, not a cash advance, which is borrowing actual cash against your credit line.
Why B: Paying a bill early from savings uses your own money and involves no card borrowing, so it is not a cash advance.
Why C: A cash advance is borrowing cash against your card, usually at a higher rate, with an upfront fee and interest from day one.
Why D: Depositing cash into your own account is a normal bank deposit, not a card transaction, so it has nothing to do with cash advances.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the difference between earned income and unearned income?
A: Earned income comes from gifts; unearned from jobs and pay
B: Earned income is never taxed, unearned always is taxed
C: Earned income comes from work; unearned from interest
D: There is no real difference between the two kinds of income
Why A: This reverses the definitions; earned income comes from working at jobs and pay, while gifts are not earned income.
Why B: Earned income is taxed, including income tax and payroll taxes, and unearned income such as interest is also generally taxable, so the claim is wrong.
Why C: Earned income comes from work such as wages and salary, while unearned income comes from sources like interest, dividends and rent without working.
Why D: There is a real difference: earned income comes from working, unearned income comes from assets, and they are taxed differently in many cases.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the purpose of an emergency fund in relation to spending?
A: It covers unplanned costs without using credit
B: It is meant for planned vacations and trips abroad
C: It is meant to grow quickly through risky bets
D: It replaces the need for insurance of all kinds
Why A: An emergency fund covers unplanned costs like medical bills or car repairs so you do not need credit cards or loans that would add interest.
Why B: Planned vacations belong in a separate savings goal, since an emergency fund should be reserved for unexpected, urgent expenses.
Why C: An emergency fund should be safe and easy to access, not exposed to risky bets that could lose value when you need it.
Why D: An emergency fund cannot replace insurance because one major accident or illness can cost far more than the fund holds.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is income?
A: Money a person spends on needs and wants each single month
B: Money received from work, investments or other sources
C: Money borrowed from a bank for a large purchase like a car
D: Money set aside for use in an emergency fund account
Why A: Money spent on needs and wants is expenses, which is the opposite of income, the money coming in.
Why B: Income is money received from work, investments, or other sources such as interest, gifts or benefits, and it funds spending and saving.
Why C: Money borrowed from a bank is a loan that must be repaid, not income, which does not create an obligation to repay.
Why D: Money set aside for emergencies is savings, which is held from income already received rather than being the income itself.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the difference between wages and salary?
A: There is no difference between the two terms of pay at all
B: Wages are fixed yearly pay; a salary is paid by the hour worked
C: Wages are tips; a salary is a bonus paid out at year end
D: Wages are paid by the hour; a salary is a fixed yearly amount
