Why C: Lower costs are the result of staying in-network, where negotiated rates apply, so out-of-network care does the reverse.
Why D: Costs usually differ sharply: in-network care has discounted rates and lower cost sharing, while out-of-network care is billed at higher patient cost.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is term life insurance?
A: Coverage for the whole life with cash
B: Coverage for car repairs and damage
C: Coverage for health care costs only
D: Coverage for a set number of years
Why A: Lifelong coverage with cash value describes whole life insurance; term life lasts only a set period and has no cash value.
Why B: Car repair coverage is auto collision insurance; term life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries, not repair bills.
Why C: Health care costs are covered by health insurance; term life pays a death benefit rather than medical expenses.
Why D: Term life insurance pays a death benefit only if the insured dies within a set term such as 10, 20 or 30 years, and it is usually cheaper than whole life.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is whole life insurance?
A: Coverage for a set number of years only, which then ends
B: Coverage for a home and all the belongings in it
C: Coverage for your entire life that builds cash value
D: Coverage for medical bills of your family members
Why A: Coverage for a set number of years that then ends describes term life insurance; whole life stays in force for the insured's entire life.
Why B: Coverage for a home and its contents is homeowners insurance, which has nothing to do with life insurance on a person.
Why C: Whole life lasts the insured's lifetime if premiums are paid, pays a death benefit and builds cash value the owner can borrow against, at higher cost than term.
Why D: Medical bill coverage is health insurance; whole life pays a death benefit to beneficiaries rather than paying a family's medical expenses.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A young single person with no dependents is least likely to need:
A: A large life insurance policy
B: Renters insurance for the flat
C: Auto insurance if they drive
D: Health insurance for a young man
Why A: Life insurance replaces income for dependents, so a young single person with no dependents has little need for a large policy.
Why B: Renters insurance protects belongings and liability in a rental unit, which a young single person with possessions still may need.
Why C: Auto insurance is legally required in nearly all states for anyone who drives, so a young driver still needs it.
Why D: Health insurance is needed for everyone, since a single serious illness can cost tens of thousands of dollars even for a young person.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is renters insurance?
A: Coverage for a renter's belongings and liability
B: Coverage for the landlord's income if a fire hits
C: Coverage for the building that the landlord owns
D: Coverage for rent payments that you owe each month
Why A: Renters insurance covers your belongings against fire and theft and gives liability protection, usually for a low cost of around $15 to $30 a month.
Why B: A landlord's income loss is covered by landlord insurance, not a renter's policy, which protects the tenant's own property and liability.
Why C: The landlord's building is covered by the landlord's property policy, not a renter's policy, which only covers the tenant's items.
Why D: Renters insurance does not pay your monthly rent; it covers property loss and liability, though some policies cover temporary housing after a loss.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A fire destroys a renter's belongings. Which policy covers them?
A: Health insurance
B: Renters insurance
C: Auto insurance
D: The landlord's policy
Why A: Health insurance pays medical expenses, not property losses, so it will not replace belongings destroyed by fire.
Why B: Renters insurance covers personal property damaged by fire, and many policies also pay for temporary living expenses while the home is repaired.
Why C: Auto insurance covers vehicles and driving liability, not household belongings destroyed in an apartment fire.
Why D: The landlord's policy covers the building structure, not tenants' personal belongings, so renters need their own policy.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: After a flood damages a home, the owner learns the standard policy does not pay. Why?
A: Floods are always covered by a standard home policy
B: The insurer made a mistake in handling the claim
C: The owner cannot file claims, as insurers exclude water damage
D: Floods are usually excluded and need separate insurance
Why A: Standard homeowners policies typically exclude flood damage, so saying floods are always covered is false.
Why B: The refusal is not an insurer error; flood is a standard, written exclusion in homeowners policies, so the claim is properly denied.
Why C: Owners can file claims for many covered losses, but water damage from floods is a standard exclusion, not a ban on filing claims.
Why D: Standard homeowners policies exclude flooding, so owners in risk areas need separate flood insurance, often through the National Flood Insurance Program.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an umbrella policy?
A: Coverage for cars only, and for nothing else at all
B: Coverage for rain damage only, when a storm harms the roof
C: Extra liability coverage beyond other policies' limits
D: Coverage for jewelry only, and not for other goods
Why A: An umbrella policy applies to liability from many incidents, not only cars; it extends liability limits on auto, home and other policies.
Why B: Rain damage to a roof falls under homeowners property coverage; an umbrella policy provides extra liability coverage, not weather damage coverage.
Why C: An umbrella policy adds extra liability coverage, often $1 million or more, once the limits of your auto or home policy are exhausted.
Why D: Jewelry is insured by a scheduled personal property rider; an umbrella policy covers liability for lawsuits, not specific items.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person decides not to ride a motorcycle because it is dangerous. Which strategy is this?
A: Risk retention
B: Risk transfer
C: Risk reduction
D: Risk avoidance
Why A: Risk retention means accepting the risk and paying for losses yourself, but this person avoids the activity entirely.
Why B: Risk transfer shifts the risk to another party such as an insurer; the person here simply chose not to ride at all.
Why C: Risk reduction lowers the chance or severity of loss, for example by wearing a helmet, but the person still engages in the activity.
Why D: Risk avoidance eliminates the risk by not taking part in the dangerous activity at all, so no motorcycle loss can occur.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which loss is best handled by retention rather than insurance?
A: A huge medical bill too large to pay from savings
B: A house fire that destroys the whole home
C: A small cost you can easily pay from savings
D: A major lawsuit for a large amount of money
Why A: A huge medical bill beyond your savings is a severe loss that insurance is designed to cover, so retention would be unaffordable.
Why B: A house fire can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, a catastrophic loss that needs insurance rather than retention.
Why C: Small, affordable losses are best retained, since you save premiums and a minor cost, paid from savings, will not create hardship.
Why D: A major lawsuit could cost far more than anyone has in savings, so liability insurance is better than retention for this risk.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does comparing insurance quotes help you do?
A: Lower your deductible to zero
B: Find better prices and coverage
C: Avoid ever filing a claim again
D: Make all companies charge the same
Why A: Comparing quotes does not change deductibles; deductible choices are made when selecting a policy, and zero is not a result of comparison.
Why B: Quotes from several insurers show different prices and coverage terms for the same needs, so you can pick the best value.
Why C: No quote comparison prevents future claims; you may still file claims whenever a covered loss happens, and comparing only affects what you buy.
Why D: Companies set their own rates using their own risk models, so comparing quotes cannot make them charge the same price.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why might a person with a good driving record pay less for auto insurance?
A: They are viewed as lower risk
B: They have a much longer last name
C: Insurers like their car color
D: They live near a big bank branch
Why A: Insurers use driving history to estimate claims, and a clean record signals lower risk of accidents, which earns lower premiums.
Why B: Last name length has no bearing on risk or rates; insurers price based on driving record, age, vehicle and location instead.
Why C: Car color does not affect rates; insurers consider the vehicle's make, model, safety and repair costs, not paint color.
Why D: Living near a bank branch is irrelevant to risk; insurers consider the garaging ZIP code for theft and accidents, not nearby businesses.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the main purpose of an emergency fund in managing risk?
A: To increase risk for the whole family unit
B: To replace all insurance, as a fund pays all
C: To fund vacations and trips abroad each year
D: To cover unexpected costs without borrowing
Why A: An emergency fund reduces the financial harm of surprises, so it lowers rather than increases risk for a household.
Why B: An emergency fund does not replace insurance; a few thousand dollars cannot pay a major hospital, lawsuit or house-fire loss.
Why C: Vacation spending is a discretionary goal; an emergency fund is set aside for unexpected needs like job loss or urgent repairs.
Why D: An emergency fund of three to six months of expenses pays for surprises such as car repairs or medical bills so you avoid credit card debt.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is the best first step if your wallet is stolen?
A: Cancel cards and report the theft
B: Wait to see if anything happens
C: Post about it online with details
D: Share your PIN with a close friend
Why A: Cancel cards quickly to stop charges and report the theft to police and the card issuers; consider a fraud alert or freeze for added protection.
Why B: Waiting lets a thief run up charges or open accounts in your name, so delay increases your losses and recovery time.
Why C: Posting details online can expose more of your personal data and help thieves, rather than protecting you from further harm.
Why D: Sharing your PIN, even with a friend, exposes your accounts to misuse; PINs should stay private and be changed after a theft.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is identity theft insurance or monitoring meant to do?
A: Raise your credit score by a set amount
B: Help detect and recover from identity theft
C: Erase your debts from your credit file
D: Prevent all theft forever, so you never check
Why A: These services cannot raise your credit score by a set amount; scores depend on your payment history, credit use and other real behavior.
Why B: Monitoring alerts you to suspicious activity and many plans help pay recovery costs and give restoration support after identity theft.
Why C: They cannot erase valid debts from your file; only accurate corrections or disputes of fraudulent items can change your credit report.
Why D: No service can prevent all theft; you still need to check statements and reports, and these products only detect problems and aid recovery.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does it mean to own a share of stock?
A: You hold an insurance policy from it
B: You have a savings account there
C: You own a small part of a company
D: You lent money to a firm to be repaid
Why A: An insurance policy gives you protection against a loss, not ownership; owning stock makes you a part-owner of the company.
Why B: A savings account is a deposit with a bank; stock is ownership in a company, with value that can rise or fall.
Why C: A share of stock is a unit of ownership, called equity, which may entitle you to dividends and voting rights in the company.
Why D: Lending money to a firm to be repaid describes buying its bonds; stockholders are owners, not creditors.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: How can a stockholder earn money?
A: Only by working at the company, which pays shareholders wages
B: Through dividends and by selling shares at a higher price
C: Only by borrowing money from the company's own bank
D: Only by paying a monthly fee to the stock exchange
Why A: Wages come from working for the company as an employee; shareholders earn from dividends and price gains, not from working there.
Why B: Stockholders can receive dividend payments out of profits and can profit by selling shares for more than they paid (a capital gain).
Why C: Stockholders do not earn by borrowing from the company's bank; returns come from dividends and share price growth, not from borrowing.
Why D: Investors do not earn from paying a monthly fee to an exchange; fees are costs of trading, while returns come from dividends and price changes.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: You buy 10 shares at $40 and sell them at $55. Ignoring fees, what is your gain?
Why A: Gain = (sale price - purchase price) x shares = ($55 - $40) x 10 = $15 x 10 = $150, before any fees or taxes.
Why B: $400 is the original cost (10 x $40), not the gain; the gain is only what the shares earned above that cost.
Why C: $550 is the total sale proceeds (10 x $55), not the gain; subtract the $400 cost to find the $150 profit.
Why D: $15 is the gain per share ($55 - $40), but you hold 10 shares, so the total gain is 10 x $15 = $150.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a bond's maturity date?
A: The date interest rates change for the bond
B: The date the bond is first sold to the public
C: The date the issuer repays the principal
D: The date the buyer pays taxes on the bond
Why A: Interest rate changes are not what maturity means; a bond's coupon is usually fixed, and maturity is when principal is returned.
Why B: The date a bond is first sold is its issue date, which differs from the maturity date when the issuer repays what it borrowed.
Why C: At maturity the issuer repays the bond's face value (principal) to the holder, and interest payments end on that date.
Why D: Taxes on bond interest are paid when interest is earned each year; maturity is not a tax date but the date principal is repaid.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A $1,000 bond pays 5% interest each year. How much interest does it pay annually?
Why A: $1,050 is principal plus one year of interest ($1,000 + $50), the value after a year, not the annual interest itself.
Why B: $500 would be a 50% rate; 5% is 0.05, so the interest on $1,000 is far smaller than $500.
Why C: $5 would be 0.5% of $1,000; a 5% rate is ten times larger, giving $50, so the decimal is misplaced.
Why D: Interest = principal x rate = $1,000 x 0.05 = $50 per year, which is the bond's annual coupon payment.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a Treasury bond?
A: A bond issued by a small company
B: A bond issued by the U.S. government
C: A bond issued by a city's government
D: A stock issued by the government
Why A: Bonds from small companies are corporate bonds; Treasury bonds are issued by the federal government and are backed by its full faith and credit.
Why B: Treasury bonds are long-term debt (10 to 30 years) issued by the US government, considered very low in default risk.
Why C: Bonds from a city's government are municipal bonds, which often have tax advantages but are not Treasury bonds.
Why D: A Treasury security is a debt instrument, not a stock; stocks represent ownership in a company and governments do not issue stock.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a corporate bond?
A: A type of insurance that covers company assets
B: A government savings plan for company workers
C: A loan investors make to a company for interest
D: A share of ownership in a company with voting rights
Why A: Insurance covering company assets is a business property policy; a corporate bond is a debt security that investors buy.
Why B: A government savings plan is a different product; a corporate bond is issued by a company and not by any government.
Why C: A corporate bond is a loan made to a company; the company pays periodic interest and returns the principal at maturity.
Why D: Ownership with voting rights describes common stock; a bondholder is a lender with no ownership or voting power.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is generally riskier: a corporate bond from a struggling firm or a Treasury bond?
A: Neither of them has any risk at all
B: They carry exactly the same risk
C: The Treasury bond from the government
D: The struggling firm's corporate bond
Why A: Every investment carries some risk; even Treasury securities have inflation and interest-rate risk, so none is risk-free.
Why B: The two bonds do not carry the same risk; a struggling firm is far more likely to default than the US government.
Why C: Treasury bonds are backed by the US government and have very low default risk, so they are safer, not riskier, than a weak corporation's bond.
Why D: A struggling firm may fail to pay interest or principal, so default risk is higher, and it must offer higher yields to attract investors.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why might many beginners prefer a broad index fund to picking individual stocks?
A: It spreads risk across many companies at low cost
B: It avoids all market ups and downs for the beginner
C: It guarantees the highest return in every year
D: It requires no money at all to buy shares in it
Why A: An index fund holds hundreds of companies (like the S&P 500), so one failure matters little, and expense ratios are often below 0.1%.
Why B: Index funds still rise and fall with the market; diversification reduces single-company risk but cannot avoid overall market swings.
Why C: No fund guarantees top returns; an index fund matches the market return and can lose value in down years.
Why D: Buying fund shares requires money; some brokers allow fractional shares or low minimums, but nobody can buy without paying anything.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an ETF?
A: A basket of securities that trades like a stock
B: A type of insurance for the owner of a stock
C: A loan to a company that must be repaid in time
D: A bank savings account that pays fixed interest
Why A: An exchange-traded fund holds many stocks or bonds and trades on an exchange throughout the day, so it offers diversification with a single purchase.
Why B: Insurance for stock owners is not an ETF; an ETF is an investment product that holds assets, not a protection policy.
Why C: A loan to a company that must be repaid describes a bond; an ETF is a pooled fund and not a debt contract.
Why D: A bank savings account pays a fixed interest rate and is FDIC insured, whereas an ETF's value changes with its holdings.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an expense ratio?
A: The interest rate on a loan, charged to the borrower yearly
B: The tax rate on dividends that you receive each year
C: The ratio of debt to income for a family each year
D: The yearly cost of owning a fund as a percent of assets
Why A: The yearly interest on a loan is an APR; an expense ratio measures fund costs and not borrowing costs.
Why B: The tax rate on dividends is set by tax law; the expense ratio is a fee charged by the fund and not a tax.
Why C: The ratio of debt to income is a lending measure; an expense ratio is a fund cost compared with its assets.
Why D: The expense ratio is the annual fund fee as a percent of assets; 0.5% on $10,000 costs $50 a year, taken out of the fund's returns.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Fund A charges 0.05% yearly and Fund B charges 1.0%. Other things equal, which likely leaves you with more over 30 years?
A: Neither
B: Both equal
C: Fund A
D: Fund B
Why A: One of the funds likely leaves you with more, since the fee gap is large and compounds over three decades; the result is not neutral.
Why B: The funds differ by 0.95 percentage points yearly, so outcomes are not equal; the lower fee fund keeps more of the same gross return.
Why C: With the same gross return, Fund A's 0.05% fee versus Fund B's 1.0% leaves more compounding in your account, potentially tens of thousands of dollars after 30 years.
Why D: Fund B charges twenty times the fee of Fund A, and that drag compounds yearly, so it likely leaves you with less.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a Roth IRA?
A: A savings account insured by the FDIC up to the legal limit set for each saver
B: A retirement account funded with after-tax money with tax-free qualified withdrawals
C: A retirement account funded with pre-tax money, with fully taxed withdrawals later in life
D: A loan for retirees that is repaid from their yearly pension and their savings
Why A: A savings account insured up to a legal limit by the FDIC is a bank deposit, not a Roth IRA, which is a retirement investment account.
Why B: Roth IRA contributions use after-tax dollars, and qualified withdrawals in retirement (after age 59 and a half with a five-year rule) are tax-free.
Why C: Pre-tax contributions with fully taxed withdrawals describe a traditional IRA, which is the opposite tax treatment from a Roth IRA.
Why D: A loan for retirees repaid from pensions is not a Roth IRA, which is an account you fund yourself and later withdraw from.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Who might benefit most from a Roth IRA?
A: Someone who needs the money next month for a new car purchase
B: Someone who wants a guaranteed return of ten percent
C: Someone who expects to be in a higher tax bracket later
D: Someone with no income now or in the near future
Why A: Someone needing money next month should not use a retirement account, because early withdrawals of earnings face taxes and penalties.
Why B: No IRA guarantees a return of ten percent; investments inside the account can gain or lose value depending on the markets.
Why C: A Roth locks in today's tax rate on contributions, so it benefits people who expect a higher tax bracket in retirement or later in their careers.
Why D: A Roth IRA requires earned income to contribute, so someone with no income now or soon cannot fund it.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a traditional IRA?
A: A retirement account with tax-free withdrawals, funded with after-tax money by its owner
B: An insurance policy that pays out when a person retires from work and stops working
C: A bank loan that a retiree takes out against the house to pay for their expenses
D: A retirement account where contributions may be tax-deductible and withdrawals are taxed
Why A: Tax-free withdrawals from after-tax contributions describe a Roth IRA; a traditional IRA instead offers deductible contributions and taxable withdrawals.
Why B: An insurance policy paying out at retirement describes an annuity or pension; a traditional IRA is an account you invest in yourself.
Why C: A bank loan against a house is a reverse mortgage or home equity loan, which is unrelated to an individual retirement account.
Why D: Traditional IRA contributions may be tax-deductible and grow tax-deferred, but withdrawals in retirement are taxed as ordinary income.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What penalty usually applies to early withdrawals from retirement accounts before age 59 and a half?
A: A 10% bonus paid by the IRS for any early use
B: A 10% additional tax plus ordinary income tax
C: No penalty applies if you take the money out early
D: A free refund of tax paid by the state on money
Why A: The IRS does not pay bonuses for early withdrawals; instead it charges a penalty on taxable amounts taken before 59 and a half.
Why B: Early withdrawals typically face a 10% additional tax on top of regular income tax, with exceptions such as certain first-home or medical uses.
Why C: A penalty usually does apply, so saying nothing applies is wrong; the 10% additional tax exists to discourage early use of retirement money.
Why D: The IRS and states do not refund tax on early withdrawals; taking money early generally adds a tax cost rather than a refund.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a pension?
A: A retirement plan that pays a regular benefit
B: A loan for retirees paid back from their pensions
C: A one-time bonus for new hires who stay one year
D: A payment for unused vacation days at the firm
Why A: A pension is an employer-sponsored plan that pays retirees a regular income, often based on salary and years of service.
Why B: A pension is not a loan; retirees receive benefits from it rather than borrowing money and paying it back from their own pensions.
Why C: A one-time bonus for new hires is a signing or retention bonus, whereas a pension pays ongoing income after retirement.
Why D: Payment for unused vacation days is a payout of accrued leave, which is separate from a pension that pays retirement income.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is Social Security?
A: A stock market fund that pays benefits to every adult citizen of the state
B: A loan program for homes run by the government to help buyers with low pay
C: A government program that provides retirement, disability and survivor benefits
D: A private savings account owned by each worker and paid out when they retire from work
Why A: Social Security is not a stock market fund; it is a government insurance program funded by payroll taxes and paid to eligible workers, not every adult.
Why B: A government home loan program for buyers with low pay is a housing program like FHA or VA lending, not Social Security.
Why C: Social Security, funded by payroll taxes under FICA, pays retirement, disability and survivor benefits to eligible workers and their families.
Why D: Social Security is a federal program funded by payroll taxes and not a private savings account owned by each worker.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why should most people not rely only on Social Security for retirement?
A: It never changes over time and always covers all living costs
B: It is a private account that grows fast, so benefits cover costs
C: It pays more than most people ever earned while working
D: Benefits typically replace only part of pre-retirement income
Why A: Social Security benefits are adjusted for inflation and do not always cover living costs; saying it never changes and covers everything is wrong.
Why B: Social Security is not a private account that grows quickly; it is a government program funded by payroll taxes, and benefits are limited.
Why C: Benefits generally replace less than half of average pre-retirement earnings, so it does not pay more than most people earned.
Why D: Social Security replaces roughly 40% of average pre-retirement income, so savings, 401(k)s and IRAs are needed to maintain your standard of living.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is generally taxed at a lower rate: a long-term or a short-term capital gain?
A: A long-term capital gain
B: A short-term capital gain
C: Neither one gets taxed
D: They are taxed the same
Why A: Assets held more than a year are taxed at long-term rates of 0%, 15% or 20%, which is lower than the ordinary income rates on short-term gains.
Why B: Short-term gains, from assets held a year or less, are taxed at ordinary income rates, which are higher, not lower.
Why C: Capital gains are taxable income when you sell an asset at a profit, so saying neither is taxed is incorrect.
Why D: The two are taxed differently: long-term gains get special lower rates, and short-term gains are taxed as ordinary income.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: You invest $100 monthly. Prices are $10, $20 and $10. What happens to your average cost versus the average price?
A: It cannot be calculated
B: Your average cost is lower
C: It equals the highest price
D: Your average cost is higher
Why A: The average cost can be calculated by dividing total dollars invested by shares bought; dollar-cost averaging makes this simple.
Why B: $300 buys 10 + 5 + 10 = 25 shares, so average cost = $300 / 25 = $12, below the average price of ($10 + $20 + $10) / 3 = $13.33.
Why C: Your average cost is not the highest price of $20; you buy more shares when prices are low, so your average cost stays below that.
Why D: Your average cost is lower, not higher, since the fixed $100 buys more shares at $10 than at $20; the average price is $13.33 and your cost is $12.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is rebalancing?
A: Buying only the winners and selling the losers each week
B: Ignoring your portfolio and letting it drift over the years
C: Adjusting your portfolio back to your target mix of assets
D: Selling everything and then buying a new set from scratch
Why A: Buying only winners and selling losers weekly is chasing momentum, not rebalancing, which restores target percentages.
Why B: Ignoring your portfolio and letting it drift is the opposite of rebalancing, which means actively bringing allocations back to target.
Why C: Rebalancing sells assets that have grown beyond their target share and buys those that fell short, keeping risk in line with your plan.
Why D: Selling everything and starting over is a full liquidation that creates taxes; rebalancing makes smaller adjustments to restore the target mix.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Your target is 60% stocks and 40% bonds, but stocks have grown to 75%. What does rebalancing involve?
A: Buying more stocks to restore the target
B: Selling all bonds and holding all stocks
C: Doing nothing at all to the portfolio
D: Selling some stocks and buying bonds
Why A: Buying more stocks would push the stock share even higher above 60%, moving away from the target instead of restoring it.
Why B: Selling all bonds and holding only stocks would abandon the 40% bond target and make the portfolio far riskier.
Why C: Doing nothing leaves stocks at 75%, which is 15 points over target and carries more risk than you planned.
Why D: Stocks grew to 75%, so you sell some stocks and buy bonds to return to 60/40, which locks in gains and restores your planned risk level.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is risk tolerance?
A: How much a stock paid last year in dividends to holders
B: How much loss in value you can accept without panic
C: How much you earn from your job each year in total
D: How many accounts you hold at different banks
Why A: Last year's dividends measure an investment's income, while risk tolerance describes your willingness and ability to endure losses.
Why B: Risk tolerance is how much decline in value you can accept without panic selling, and it helps decide the right mix of stocks and bonds.
Why C: Your job earnings are your income, which can affect risk capacity but are not the definition of risk tolerance.
Why D: The number of accounts you hold has no bearing on your comfort with loss, so it does not define risk tolerance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which investor most likely holds a higher share of stocks?
A: A 25-year-old saving for retirement in 40 years
B: A person saving for a car to buy next year
C: A person with no time to wait for any growth
D: A retiree needing the money next month for bills
Why A: With 40 years until retirement, a young investor can ride out downturns, so holding a larger share of stocks, which grow more over long periods, makes sense.
Why B: Someone saving for a car next year needs safe, liquid assets, because stocks could fall right before the money is needed.
Why C: A person with no time to wait should avoid volatile stocks, since there is no chance to recover from a drop.
Why D: A retiree needing money next month needs stable cash, because a market dip could force selling at a loss.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is inflation risk for investors?
A: The risk that rising prices erode the value of returns
B: The risk that a company fails and its shares are worthless
C: The risk that taxes rise on your investment gains
D: The risk that a bank closes its doors for good and fails
Why A: Inflation risk is the chance that rising prices reduce purchasing power, so returns that do not outpace inflation lose real value.
Why B: A company failing and shares becoming worthless is business or credit risk, not inflation risk, which concerns price levels across the economy.
Why C: Rising taxes on gains is tax risk, a separate risk from inflation reducing the real value of your returns.
Why D: A bank failing is institutional risk, and FDIC insurance covers deposits up to $250,000, so it differs from inflation risk.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is liquidity risk?
A: The risk of rising taxes on income that you earn from investments
B: The risk that prices fall for all assets at the same time in the market
C: The risk of default by a borrower who cannot repay what they owe
D: The risk that you cannot sell an asset quickly without losing value
Why A: Rising taxes on income describe tax risk, which differs from liquidity risk, the difficulty of selling quickly at a fair price.
Why B: Prices falling for all assets together is market or systematic risk, while liquidity risk is about the ability to sell without a loss.
Why C: A borrower failing to repay is default or credit risk, a different risk from not being able to sell an asset quickly.
Why D: Liquidity risk is the chance you cannot turn an asset into cash fast without taking a price cut, as with real estate or thinly traded stocks.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which asset is typically the least liquid?
A: A bank deposit
B: Blue chip stock
C: Real estate
D: Cash in hand
Why A: A bank deposit can be withdrawn at once, so it is highly liquid, not the least liquid.
Why B: Blue chip stocks trade daily on exchanges with high volume and settle in days, so they are liquid.
Why C: Selling real estate takes weeks or months and has high transaction costs, making it one of the least liquid common assets.
Why D: Cash in hand is the most liquid asset since it can be spent immediately without conversion.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which portfolio is best diversified?
A: Five stocks from one industry that the investor follows daily
B: Stocks, bonds and cash across many companies and industries
C: One company's stock held by a single investor in a brokerage
D: Ten bonds from one issuer, all with the same maturity date
Why A: Five stocks in one industry are exposed to the same sector risks, so a downturn in that industry would hit all of them.
Why B: Mixing stocks, bonds and cash across many companies and industries spreads risk, so no single event harms the whole portfolio.
Why C: One company's stock puts all your money in one place, the opposite of diversification, so a single failure could wipe out your savings.
Why D: Ten bonds from one issuer share the same default risk and maturity, so they are not diversified despite the number of bonds.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: During a bear market a long-term investor with a steady plan should generally:
A: Borrow to buy the single stock that has fallen most
B: Stop looking at the plan and hope for the best
C: Sell everything immediately and keep only the cash
D: Stay with the plan and keep investing regularly
Why A: Borrowing to buy a fallen stock adds debt and concentrates risk, which can magnify losses and is not a sound long-term approach.
Why B: Ignoring the plan and hoping is not a strategy; a long-term investor should follow the plan and review it periodically.
Why C: Selling everything in a downturn locks in losses and misses the recovery, which often hurts long-term results.
Why D: Staying invested and continuing regular contributions buys shares at lower prices, helping long-term returns when markets recover.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a market order?
A: An order to buy only at a set price, and wait for it to appear
B: An order that triggers at a set loss, selling if price falls
C: An order to buy or sell immediately at the best available price
D: An order that cancels itself at the end of each trading day by rule
Why A: Buying only at a set price and waiting describes a limit order, while a market order executes right away at the current price.
Why B: An order that triggers at a set loss is a stop order, which differs from a market order that trades immediately.
Why C: A market order executes immediately at the best available price, which gives speed but no guarantee of the exact price.
Why D: An order that expires at the end of the trading day is a day order, a duration setting rather than a market order.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: You want to buy a stock only if the price falls to $20. Which order fits?
A: A market order
B: A limit order
C: A day trade
D: A margin call
Why A: A market order buys immediately at the current price, so it would not wait for the price to fall to $20.
Why B: A limit order sets the maximum price you will pay, so it buys only if the stock falls to $20 or less.
Why C: A day trade is buying and selling a security on the same day, not an order type that waits for a target price.
Why D: A margin call is a broker demand for more funds when a margin account falls in value, not an order to buy a stock.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is margin investing?
A: Borrowing money from a broker to buy securities
B: Investing only with cash that you have saved up
C: Investing in small amounts each week or month
D: Investing on market edges where prices rarely move
Why A: Buying on margin means using a loan from your broker to purchase securities, which magnifies both gains and losses.
Why B: Investing only with saved cash is a cash account, which is the opposite of using borrowed funds.
Why C: Investing small amounts regularly is dollar-cost averaging, which does not involve borrowing from a broker.
Why D: Margin refers to borrowing, not market edges; there is no strategy of investing where prices rarely move that is called margin.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why is margin investing considered risky for beginners?
A: Losses can exceed your own money
B: It removes all risk for investors
C: It guarantees profit to investors
D: It is illegal for everyone to use it
Why A: With borrowed money, a falling price can wipe out your own funds and leave you owing the broker more than you invested.
Why B: Margin increases risk rather than removing it, because losses are magnified and margin calls can force sales at bad prices.
Why C: Nothing guarantees a profit in investing; margin can amplify gains, but it equally amplifies losses.
Why D: Margin accounts are legal for qualified investors, with limits set by regulators; the danger is leverage, not illegality.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an initial public offering (IPO)?
A: A company paying a dividend to its owners
B: A company buying back its own shares from investors
C: A company's first sale of shares to the public
D: A company going bankrupt and closing its doors
Why A: Paying a dividend to owners is a distribution of profit, while an IPO is when a company first sells shares to the public.
Why B: A company buying back its own shares is a stock buyback, which differs from an IPO that issues new shares to the public.
Why C: An IPO is a company's first sale of stock to the public, usually to raise capital, after which its shares trade on an exchange.
Why D: A company closing after bankruptcy is liquidation, which has nothing to do with first offering shares to the public.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio compare?
A: A fund's fees compared with its yearly returns to date
B: A stock's price with the company's earnings per share
C: A bond's price with its rate of interest, shown yearly
D: A company's debt compared with its total yearly assets
Why A: A fund's fees compared with returns is a cost measure, whereas P/E compares a stock's price to its earnings.
Why B: P/E = share price / earnings per share; it shows how many dollars investors pay for each dollar of annual earnings.
Why C: A bond's price compared with its interest is a yield measure, not the price-to-earnings ratio used for stocks.
Why D: Debt compared with assets is a leverage ratio, while P/E compares a stock's price with its earnings per share.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A stock trades at $60 and earns $4 per share. What is its P/E ratio?
Why A: 56 comes from subtracting earnings from price ($60 - $4); P/E is found by dividing price by earnings per share, not by subtracting.
Why B: 0.067 is earnings divided by price ($4 / $60), the earnings yield, which is the inverse of P/E.
Why C: 240 results from multiplying price by earnings ($60 x $4); P/E divides them instead.
Why D: P/E = price / EPS = $60 / $4 = 15, meaning investors pay $15 for each $1 of yearly earnings.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is dividend yield?
A: Price divided by earnings per share, which compares costs
B: Annual dividends per share divided by the share price
C: Profit divided by sales for the whole year of trading
D: Debt divided by equity held at the end of the year
Why A: Price divided by earnings per share is the P/E ratio, not dividend yield, which compares dividends with price.
Why B: Dividend yield = annual dividends per share / share price; a $2 dividend on a $50 stock yields 4%.
Why C: Profit divided by sales is the profit margin, a measure of operating efficiency rather than dividend yield.
Why D: Debt divided by equity is the debt-to-equity ratio, a measure of leverage, not dividend yield.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A stock priced at $50 pays $2 a year in dividends. What is the dividend yield?
Why A: Yield = annual dividend / price = $2 / $50 = 0.04, or 4%, which shows income as a percent of the share price.
Why B: 52% would come from adding $2 to $50; yield is found by dividing the dividend by the price, not by adding.
Why C: 2% would be the result if you divided the dividend by $100, but the stock is priced at $50, so the yield is $2 / $50 = 4%.
Why D: 25% comes from dividing the price by the dividend ($50 / $2 = 25), which is the reverse of the yield calculation.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is a red flag of an investment scam?
A: Clear disclosure of fees and risks to clients
B: Independent audited statements and reviews
C: Promises of guaranteed high returns with no risk
D: A registered adviser with a public record of past work
Why A: Clear disclosure of fees and risks is a sign of an honest firm, not a red flag, since scams hide or downplay those details.
Why B: Independently audited statements show transparency and outside checks, which legitimate firms provide, and scammers avoid.
Why C: No legitimate investment can promise guaranteed high returns with no risk, since higher return always comes with higher risk, a classic sign of fraud.
Why D: A registered adviser with a public record is a sign of legitimacy, as it allows clients to verify credentials and history.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: How can you check whether a financial adviser is registered?
A: Count their social media followers and their likes
B: Look at their car and their office furniture
C: Ask them whether they are honest and trustworthy
D: Use FINRA BrokerCheck or the SEC adviser search
Why A: Social media followers and likes say nothing about licensing or regulatory history, and they can be bought or faked.
Why B: A person's car and furniture show nothing about credentials and may be used to impress victims, as scammers often do.
Why C: Asking someone whether they are honest proves nothing, because anyone including a fraudster will claim to be trustworthy.
Why D: FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure site show licenses, employment history and any disciplinary actions.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a fiduciary?
A: A professional legally required to act in your best interest
B: A person who maximizes their own profit at a client's own cost
C: A person paid only by commissions on the products sold
D: A person who sells without disclosure of fees or risks
Why A: A fiduciary has a legal duty to put the client's interests ahead of their own and must avoid or disclose conflicts of interest.
Why B: Maximizing profit at a client's expense is the opposite of a fiduciary duty, which requires loyalty and care toward the client.
Why C: Being paid only by commissions describes a compensation method, and a commission-based seller is not necessarily a fiduciary.
Why D: Selling without disclosing fees or risks violates fiduciary standards, which require full disclosure to the client.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: An adviser recommends a fund mainly because it pays a higher commission. What is this?
A: Good practice overall
B: A conflict of interest
C: A required procedure here
D: An unavoidable event
Why A: Recommending a fund for the adviser's own commission is not good practice because it puts the adviser's pay ahead of the client's interest.
Why B: When an adviser's pay influences the advice instead of the client's needs, it is a conflict of interest that should be disclosed or avoided.
Why C: Rules require advice to be suitable and in the client's interest, so choosing a fund for commission is not a required procedure.
Why D: The conflict is a choice by the adviser and can be avoided with disclosure or fee-only pay, so it is not an unavoidable event.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which investment mix suits a goal one year away?
A: All in a volatile stock that may fall sharply in the year
B: All in cryptocurrency that may swing wildly during the year
C: All in a long-term growth fund that may fall in value in the year
D: Safe, liquid options such as a savings account or short-term CD
Why A: A volatile stock can fall sharply within a year, and you would have little time to recover before you need the money.
Why B: Cryptocurrency can swing wildly in a year, so it is far too risky for a goal that is just one year away.
Why C: A long-term growth fund can lose value in a single year, so it is not suited to a short-horizon goal that needs the money soon.
Why D: With a one-year goal, you need stability and easy access, so a savings account or short-term CD protects principal and offers modest interest.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the Rule of 72 used for in investing?
A: Estimating taxes owed on your yearly investment income
B: Setting a retirement age, so savers know when to draw
C: Estimating how long an investment takes to double
D: Finding loan payments on a new car or a house
Why A: Estimating taxes owed uses tax tables and brackets, not the Rule of 72, which concerns the growth of invested money.
Why B: The Rule of 72 does not set a retirement age; retirement timing depends on savings, income needs and Social Security rules.
Why C: Divide 72 by the annual return to estimate years to double; at 6% it takes about 12 years, since 72 / 6 = 12.
Why D: Loan payments are found with an amortization formula, not the Rule of 72, which estimates doubling time for investments.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: At an 8% average return, about how long does it take an investment to double?
A: 16 years
B: 8 years
C: 9 years
D: 72 years
Why A: 16 years would be right at about a 4.5% return; at 8% the doubling time is shorter, about 9 years.
Why B: 8 years confuses the rate with the answer; the Rule of 72 divides 72 by the rate, which gives 9 years at 8%.
Why C: Using the Rule of 72, 72 / 8 = 9 years, so a $10,000 investment growing 8% a year would be about $20,000 after nine years.
Why D: 72 years is the number used in the rule, not the answer; you must divide 72 by the 8% return to get 9 years.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a 'load' on a mutual fund?
A: Its interest rate on the savings account offered
B: A sales charge paid when buying or selling shares
C: The weight of its holdings, counted in tons or lots
D: Its yearly dividend paid to all of the investors
Why A: A fund's load is a sales charge and not an interest rate on a savings account, which is a bank product.
Why B: A load is a sales commission, either front-end when buying or back-end when selling, which reduces the money actually invested.
Why C: A load has nothing to do with physical weight or lots; it is a fee and not a measure of how much the holdings weigh.
Why D: The yearly dividend paid to investors is a distribution, whereas a load is a sales charge on buying or selling shares.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a target-date fund?
A: A fund that pays out all assets on one date to investors who hold it
B: A fund that holds one stock and never buys or sells any shares
C: A fund that never changes its holdings for the whole of its life
D: A fund that shifts toward safer assets as a retirement date nears
Why A: A target-date fund does not pay out all assets on one date; it stays invested, shifting its holdings as that date approaches.
Why B: A target-date fund holds many funds and rebalances automatically, rather than holding one stock and never trading.
Why C: A target-date fund changes its holdings over time, which is its defining feature, so a fund that never changes is not one.
Why D: A target-date fund starts with more stocks and gradually moves toward bonds and cash as the target retirement year nears, reducing risk.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is compound growth in investing?
A: Earnings that generate their own earnings over time
B: Fees added each year to the price of the fund
C: Losses that cancel gains made in the same year
D: Earnings that are spent at once, leaving nothing to grow
Why A: Compounding means reinvested earnings generate their own earnings, so growth accelerates; $1,000 at 7% becomes about $7,612 in 30 years.
Why B: Fees added each year are costs that reduce returns, which is the opposite of compounding, where earnings add to growth.
Why C: Losses that cancel gains describe a flat or negative result, whereas compounding is earnings building on earlier earnings.
Why D: Spending earnings immediately leaves nothing to build on, so there is no compounding when returns are not reinvested.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Two people each invest $200 monthly for 30 years. One earns 4% and the other 7%. Which is likely larger?
A: The 7% investor's balance
B: Neither one grows at all
C: The 4% investor's balance
D: They are exactly equal here
Why A: A higher return compounds faster, and over 30 years at 7% the balance is about $244,000 versus about $139,000 at 4%, on $72,000 contributed.
Why B: Both accounts grow since each receives $200 each month and earns a positive return, so neither stays flat.
Why C: The 4% investor makes the same contributions but earns a lower return, so the balance after 30 years is smaller, not larger.
Why D: The balances are not equal because the rates differ by 3 points, and compounding for 30 years widens that gap to over $100,000.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is a reason to start investing early?
A: Early investors never lose any money
B: More time for compounding to work
C: Taxes vanish for early investors
D: Fees are lower for early investors
Why A: Investing always carries some risk of loss, and starting early does not remove it; it only gives more years to recover from market downturns.
Why B: The earlier you start, the longer your returns earn their own returns, so even small regular deposits can grow into a much larger balance over decades.
Why C: Taxes do not disappear for anyone; early investors still owe taxes on gains, though accounts like a Roth IRA or 401(k) can defer or reduce them.
Why D: Fund fees depend on the product chosen, such as expense ratios, not on when you begin; starting early does not make fees any lower for you.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a real estate investment trust (REIT)?
A: A property tax paid by owners of real estate each year
B: A mortgage for a home that a family buys with a bank loan
C: A company that owns or finances income-producing real estate
D: A homeowners policy that covers fire damage to a house and goods
Why A: Property tax is a levy local governments charge real estate owners each year; a REIT is an investment company, not a tax owed on property.
Why B: A mortgage is a loan used to buy a home, repaid to a lender; a REIT is a company that investors buy shares in, not a loan.
Why C: A REIT is a company that owns or finances income-producing property such as offices or apartments, and it must pay most of its income to shareholders as dividends.
Why D: Homeowners insurance is a policy covering fire and theft damage to a house and its contents; a REIT is an investment company, not a form of insurance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why might an investor add a REIT to a portfolio?
A: To avoid all risk in the whole portfolio
B: To guarantee profit every year, as real estate
C: To avoid all taxes on the income it pays you
D: To diversify into real estate and earn income
Why A: No investment removes all risk, and REIT shares can fall in price with real estate markets and interest rates, so this would not eliminate portfolio risk.
Why B: REITs offer no guaranteed profit; rents, property values and share prices can all fall, and returns vary from year to year like other stocks.
Why C: REIT dividends are generally taxable income to the shareholder, often taxed at ordinary rates, so a REIT does not let you avoid taxes on what it pays.
Why D: REITs let investors own real estate without buying buildings directly, spreading portfolio risk across asset types while paying regular dividend income that must be distributed from rents and property profits.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a penny stock?
A: A stock issued only to children who cannot buy any shares
B: A low-priced stock often traded in small, risky markets
C: A government bond that pays a fixed rate of interest
D: A stock worth one cent forever and never more or less
Why A: Penny stocks are not a children's product; anyone with a brokerage account can buy them, and the name refers to their very low share price instead.
Why B: Penny stocks generally trade for under five dollars, often on small over-the-counter markets, with little public information and thin trading, which makes them prone to sharp swings and manipulation.
Why C: A government bond is a debt security paying fixed interest, such as a Treasury; a penny stock is an equity share in a small company.
Why D: Penny stock prices move up and down like any stock; the name only describes a low price, and the price is never fixed at one cent.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A social media post urges you to buy a penny stock before it soars. What is a wise response?
A: Send your password to claim your free shares
B: Share it with all friends right away
C: Invest everything immediately on the tip
D: Be cautious and research before investing
Why A: Sending your password to a stranger is a classic scam; no legitimate offer requires your login, and doing so gives criminals access to your accounts.
Why B: Passing along an unverified tip can spread a pump-and-dump scheme, where promoters inflate a price and sell, leaving others holding losses; it also may expose you legally.
Why C: Investing everything on one social media tip ignores diversification and due diligence, and penny stocks are often manipulated, so you could lose your entire stake quickly.
Why D: Urgent hype about a cheap stock is a warning sign of a pump-and-dump scheme, so verify the company with SEC filings and independent research before putting any money in.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why does the IRS require some self-employed people to pay estimated taxes each quarter?
A: No employer withholds tax from their income during the year
B: Estimated taxes are optional for everyone with income
C: Self-employed people are exempt from paying income tax in the year
D: Estimated taxes replace the need to file a return each year
Why A: Employees have tax withheld from each paycheck, but self-employed people have no employer doing this, so they pay estimated tax quarterly to the IRS to cover income and self-employment taxes.
Why B: Estimated taxes are required for those expected to owe about $1,000 or more after withholding and credits; skipping them can bring underpayment penalties.
Why C: Self-employed people are not exempt; they owe income tax plus self-employment tax for Social Security and Medicare on their net earnings every year.
Why D: Estimated payments are only advance payments toward the bill; the self-employed still must file an annual return, typically with Schedule C, to report income and reconcile.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A tutor earns $800 in a month from private students and receives no pay stub. What should the tutor do about taxes?
A: Hide the income so that no one ever knows
B: Nothing, because tutoring is never taxed at all
C: Track income and set money aside for taxes
D: Wait for the students to pay the tax for you
Why A: Hiding income is tax evasion, which is illegal and can bring penalties and interest; all income must be reported whether or not a pay stub exists.
Why B: Tutoring income is taxable as self-employment income, and net earnings of $400 or more in a year require reporting and self-employment tax, so doing nothing is wrong.
Why C: With no employer withholding, the tutor should keep records of income and expenses and set aside part of each payment, since taxes will be due and estimated payments may be required.
Why D: Students who pay for tutoring are not responsible for the tutor's income tax; the tutor, as the earner, must report the income and pay the tax.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a probationary period at a new job?
A: An early period when performance is reviewed closely
B: A period when the employee is not paid for work
C: A paid vacation for new hires in their first week
D: A period when the employee cannot be reviewed by the boss
Why A: A probationary period, often 30 to 90 days, lets an employer evaluate a new hire's performance and fit, and it may be easier to end employment during this time.
Why B: Probationary employees are paid for their work under wage laws; the period is about evaluation, not unpaid service, and unpaid work would break minimum wage rules.
Why C: A paid first week of vacation is not what probation means; new hires usually earn vacation later, and the period is about evaluating performance instead.
Why D: Employees on probation are typically reviewed more closely, not less, so a boss being unable to review them is the opposite of what the period involves.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is job security?
A: A guard who protects an office and checks badges
B: A password for work computers and email accounts
C: The likelihood that a person will keep their job
D: A list of job openings at a firm or a company
Why A: A security guard protects a building and checks badges, which is physical security for property; job security is about a worker's employment, not about the workplace.
Why B: A password protects work accounts and is called information security; job security is about whether your employment continues and has nothing to do with login credentials.
Why C: Job security is how likely someone is to stay employed; it is higher in stable industries and roles, with steady demand and contracts, than in seasonal or declining ones.
Why D: A list of openings is a job board or posting; job security concerns whether you are likely to keep your current job, not what positions exist.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is more likely to provide steady income: a salaried office job or seasonal freelance work?
A: They are identical
B: A salaried office job
C: Seasonal freelance work
D: Neither earns income
Why A: The two are not identical; a salaried job pays a fixed amount each pay period, while seasonal freelance work varies with demand and may stop for months.
Why B: A salary pays a set amount on a regular schedule, which makes budgeting easier, while seasonal freelance income swings with demand and can disappear for part of the year.
Why C: Seasonal freelance work pays only during busy periods and can leave gaps with no income, so it is less steady than a salaried office job.
Why D: Both kinds of work earn income; the question is which is steadier, and a salaried position is more predictable than seasonal freelance gigs.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a paycheck stub used for?
A: Filing your taxes for you each year
B: Requesting a raise from your boss now
C: Applying for a loan automatically
D: Checking how gross pay became net pay
Why A: A pay stub does not file taxes; it shows earnings and deductions, and you use that information, along with your W-2, when you prepare a return yourself.
Why B: A pay stub is a record of your pay, not a request form; asking for a raise is done by talking with your employer or manager.
Why C: Pay stubs cannot apply for loans; they can serve as proof of income when you apply, but you must submit the application to a lender yourself.
Why D: A pay stub lists gross pay and each deduction, such as taxes and insurance, so you can see how it becomes the net pay deposited into your account.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A pay stub shows gross pay of $900, taxes of $135 and insurance of $45. What is net pay?
Why A: $1,080 is wrong because it subtracts nothing close to the deductions; $900 minus $180 would give $720, so adding $180 to gross is a mistake.
Why B: Net pay is gross pay minus deductions, so $900 - $135 taxes - $45 insurance = $720, which is the amount actually received in your paycheck.
Why C: $180 is the total of deductions, $135 + $45; it is the amount taken out, not the take-home pay left after subtracting it from gross pay.
Why D: $765 results from subtracting only the $135 in taxes ($900 - $135) and forgetting the $45 insurance deduction, so the net pay is overstated.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a good reason to wait before buying an expensive item?
A: Time can reveal whether you really need it
B: You will forget about your real needs later
C: Prices never change at any time of the year
D: Waiting always makes the item cheaper to buy
Why A: Waiting a few days or weeks helps you tell a lasting need from an impulse, and it gives time to compare prices and save, which prevents regret.
Why B: Waiting does not make you forget what you really need; if the item matters, you will still want it later, and the pause only filters out impulse buys.
Why C: Prices change often because of sales, seasons and new models, so claiming they never change is false, and waiting can even let you catch a discount.
Why D: Waiting does not always lower the price; items can rise in cost or sell out, though it may let you find a sale or a better alternative.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A phone costs $600 new or $420 refurbished with a warranty. Which is the better value if both meet your needs?
A: The most expensive one
B: Neither, they are equal
C: The refurbished phone
D: The newest phone model
Why A: The most expensive option is not automatically the best value; if both phones meet your needs, paying $180 more for the same use gives no extra benefit.
Why B: The two are not equal, since one costs $600 and the other $420; the refurbished phone saves $180 while its warranty protects against defects.
Why C: When both meet your needs, the refurbished phone at $420 saves $180 ($600 - $420) and the warranty covers repairs, so it gives more value per dollar spent.
Why D: The newest model is the $600 one here, and its higher price buys features you do not need, so it is the poorer value for the same use.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a rebate?
A: A coupon used before you buy at the till
B: A fee charged at checkout by the store
C: A tax on a purchase made at a retail store
D: A partial refund after you buy a product
Why A: A coupon is redeemed at purchase to cut the price immediately, whereas a rebate gives money back after you buy and send in proof of purchase.
Why B: A fee charged at checkout adds to your cost, while a rebate returns money to you; the two work in opposite directions.
Why C: A sales tax is a government charge added to purchases; a rebate is a refund of part of the price offered by a maker or store.
Why D: A rebate is a partial refund of the purchase price, usually claimed after the sale by mail or online with a receipt, and some buyers forget to claim it.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A $200 item has a $30 mail-in rebate. What is your final cost if you claim it?
Why A: $30 is only the rebate amount, not the final cost; you must subtract it from the $200 price to find what you actually paid.
Why B: $230 adds the rebate to the price instead of subtracting it; a rebate returns money to you, so it lowers the cost rather than raising it.
Why C: The rebate returns part of the price, so $200 - $30 = $170, assuming you send in the claim on time and in the right form.
Why D: $200 is the price before the rebate; if you claim the $30 mail-in rebate, your final cost drops by that amount, to $170.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why read reviews before a major purchase?
A: They guarantee your full satisfaction
B: They give experiences of real buyers
C: They remove the need to compare options
D: They set the price of the item you buy
Why A: No review guarantees satisfaction; reviews are other people's opinions, and a product can still disappoint you, though they reduce the chance of a bad buy.
Why B: Reviews reveal how real buyers found quality, durability and problems, which helps you spot weaknesses before spending, especially when many detailed reviews agree on the same points.
Why C: Reviews are one input to comparing options, not a replacement; you still compare features, prices and warranties across several products before deciding.
Why D: Sellers and markets set prices, not reviewers; reviews describe quality and experience, though a well-reviewed product may help justify a price you see.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which review is most useful?
A: A detailed review explaining what worked and what did not
B: A review that says Worst ever, with no reasons given at all
C: A review that says Great!!! and nothing else at all
D: A review with no text at all, only a star rating given
Why A: A detailed review gives specifics about quality, performance and flaws, so you can judge whether the product fits your needs and spot patterns across many reviews.
Why B: A bare complaint with no reasons gives you no facts to evaluate; it could reflect shipping trouble or a personal gripe unrelated to product quality.
Why C: An enthusiastic review with no details tells you nothing about what the buyer liked, and such posts can be fake or paid, so it is little help.
Why D: A star rating alone shows overall satisfaction but not why, so you cannot tell whether low scores came from the product or from other issues.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a refund?
A: Extra pay for overtime, added to a paycheck when hours exceed forty
B: A discount before a sale starts, offered only to members
C: A tax paid at checkout on the items that you buy in a store
D: Money returned to a buyer for a returned or cancelled purchase
Why A: Overtime pay is extra wages for hours beyond forty in a week under federal law, paid to workers; a refund is money returned to a buyer.
Why B: A pre-sale member discount lowers the price you pay up front; a refund returns money after a purchase has already been paid for.
Why C: Sales tax is a government charge added at checkout, which you pay on top of the price; a refund returns money instead of collecting it.
Why D: A refund returns money to a buyer when a purchase is returned or cancelled, and stores' return policies set time limits and conditions for getting one.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a savings account's APY?
A: The minimum balance required by the bank
B: The yearly fee for owning the account itself
C: The monthly deposit amount you must make
D: The yearly return including compounding
Why A: A minimum balance is a required amount the account must hold to avoid fees; APY measures the interest you earn, not a balance requirement.
Why B: A yearly fee is an annual maintenance charge that reduces your money; APY is the interest you earn, expressed as a yearly percentage.
Why C: A required monthly deposit is a bank rule for certain accounts; APY describes the interest return, not any deposit that you must make.
Why D: APY, or annual percentage yield, is the real yearly return including compounding, so it lets you compare accounts fairly even if they compound at different frequencies.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Account A pays 3.0% APY and Account B pays 2.2% APY. If you deposit $1,000 for a year, how much more does A earn than B?
Why A: $1,000 x 3.0% = $30 and $1,000 x 2.2% = $22, so Account A earns $30 - $22 = $8 more over the year.
Why B: $0.80 is off by a factor of ten; the rate gap is 0.8 percentage points, and 0.8% of $1,000 is $8, not $0.80.
Why C: $52 adds the two earnings, $30 + $22, instead of subtracting them; the question asks how much more A earns than B, which is the difference.
Why D: $80 mistakes the 0.8 percentage point gap for 8%; the correct figure is $1,000 x 0.008 = $8, not $80.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a money market account?
A: A loan for a car that is repaid in fixed monthly payments over several years
B: A deposit account that often pays more than regular savings but limits transactions
C: A retirement plan that employers offer and fund with tax savings for all staff
D: A stock account for buying shares in public companies, with high risk and no trade limits
Why A: That describes an auto loan, which is debt repaid monthly with interest; a money market account is a deposit account where you earn interest, not borrow.
Why B: A money market account is an insured deposit account that often pays higher interest than regular savings, but it may limit withdrawals or transactions and require a higher balance.
Why C: That describes an employer retirement plan such as a 401(k); a money market account is a bank deposit account that you open yourself for savings.
Why D: That describes a brokerage account for buying shares; money market accounts hold insured deposits at banks and carry low risk instead of the high risk of stocks.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Your account requires a $500 minimum balance or charges $10 a month. Your balance is often $300. What is the yearly fee?
Why A: $30 is only three months of the $10 fee; the question asks for the full year, which covers twelve months of charges.
Why B: $10 is the monthly charge, not the yearly total; multiplying by the 12 months of the year gives the amount the question asks for.
Why C: With the balance often under $500, the $10 fee applies each month, so $10 x 12 months = $120 per year in fees.
Why D: $500 is the minimum balance required to avoid the fee, not the fee itself; the fee is $10 a month, which is $120 over a year.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an overdraft?
A: Spending more than the balance in a checking account
B: Closing an account at the bank for good this year
C: Earning interest on a balance, which the bank adds monthly
D: Depositing more than needed into a savings account
Why A: An overdraft happens when you spend more than your checking balance; the bank may cover it but often charges a fee, or may decline the payment.
Why B: Closing an account is a decision made by the customer or bank; an overdraft is a negative balance caused by spending more than is available.
Why C: Earning interest on a balance is a gain, not a shortfall; an overdraft is the opposite, where the account goes below zero and costs you money.
Why D: Depositing extra funds into savings is a smart habit that adds money; an overdraft happens when too much is taken out of checking.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which habit best helps avoid overdraft fees?
A: Spending first and checking your balance later
B: Ignoring your balance and all of your account alerts
C: Using several cards without tracking any of the balances
D: Tracking your balance and setting low-balance alerts
Why A: Spending first and checking later is how overdrafts happen, since a purchase can exceed your balance before you notice, which triggers a fee.
Why B: Ignoring alerts removes your early warning; alerts tell you when the balance is low, so skipping them makes an overdraft more likely.
Why C: Using several cards without tracking balances makes it easy to lose sight of spending and money available, so overdrafts and debts become more likely.
Why D: Knowing your balance and setting low-balance alerts warns you before an account runs short, and linking savings for overdraft protection can also help avoid fees.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is direct deposit?
A: Handing out cash to staff every week
B: Mailing a paper check to be deposited later
C: Paying wages straight into a bank account
D: Paying wages in goods rather than in money
Why A: Handing out cash is a manual payment method, not direct deposit; direct deposit moves pay electronically into a bank account without cash or paper.
Why B: Mailing a paper check requires depositing it yourself later; direct deposit sends the pay electronically so no paper check is involved or delayed.
Why C: Direct deposit electronically sends your pay from the employer straight into your bank account, which is fast, safe from loss and often available on payday.
Why D: Paying in goods is bartering, not direct deposit; direct deposit is a way of paying wages in money through the banking system.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a credit inquiry?
A: A bill for credit sent to you by a store
B: A lender's request to view your credit report
C: A payment reminder sent by the lender's office
D: A request to cancel a card, made by a cardholder
Why A: A bill for credit is a statement of what you owe; an inquiry is when someone checks your credit file, not a bill sent to you.
Why B: A credit inquiry occurs when a lender or other party requests your credit report; hard inquiries come from applications and can slightly lower your score.
