Question: What does a lender look at when deciding whether to approve a loan?
A: Shoe size and hair color too
B: Social media followers and likes
C: Credit history, income and debts
D: Favorite color of the applicant
Why A: Physical traits like shoe size and hair color have no bearing on whether a borrower can repay, and lenders may not use them to decide.
Why B: Social media popularity says nothing about repayment ability, so lenders do not weigh followers or likes in a loan decision.
Why C: Lenders review credit history, income, and existing debts to judge how likely a borrower is to repay the loan on time.
Why D: A favorite color has no connection to the ability to repay, so it plays no role in a lender's decision.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A loan has a 6% APR and a 4% APR offer is available from another lender for the same terms. Which is cheaper?
A: Neither costs
B: The 6% APR loan
C: They cost the same
D: The 4% APR loan
Why A: Loans always cost something, since interest is the price of borrowing; 'neither costs' ignores that both loans charge interest.
Why B: A 6% APR charges more interest per year than 4% on identical terms, so the 6% loan is the more expensive choice.
Why C: The rates differ by two percentage points, so the costs differ; the 6% loan charges noticeably more interest over the same term.
Why D: With identical terms, a lower APR means less total interest paid, so the 4% APR loan is the cheaper option.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person with no credit history wants a first card. Which option is often easier to qualify for?
A: A big home mortgage loan
B: A secured credit card
C: A small business loan
D: A large unsecured limit
Why A: A mortgage needs good credit and a large down payment, so someone with no credit history is unlikely to qualify for one first.
Why B: A secured card is backed by a cash deposit, which lowers the lender's risk and makes approval easier for people building credit for the first time.
Why C: Business loans typically require financial records, collateral, or a track record, which a person with no credit history lacks.
Why D: Large unsecured limits go to borrowers with proven credit; with no history, lenders will not offer a big limit without collateral.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does a hard inquiry mean?
A: You closed an account and the bank checked all your records
B: You paid a bill early and the lender thanked you for doing so today
C: You checked your own score and no lender looked at your file
D: A lender checked your credit report because you applied for credit
Why A: Closing an account does not create an inquiry; a hard inquiry occurs when a lender pulls your report in response to an application.
Why B: Paying a bill early may help your record, but it does not trigger a hard inquiry; those come from credit applications.
Why C: Checking your own score is a soft inquiry that does not affect your score, which is the opposite of a hard inquiry.
Why D: A hard inquiry happens when a lender reviews your credit report because you applied for credit, and it can lower your score slightly for a while.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the grace period on a credit card?
A: Time to pay the balance without being charged interest on new purchases
B: A permanent waiver of fees on every purchase you make with the card
C: A reward for late payment that the issuer gives to loyal cardholders
D: The time to ignore the bill without any penalty or interest being added
Why A: A grace period lets you avoid interest on new purchases if you pay the statement balance in full by the due date, usually about 21 days.
Why B: A grace period does not waive fees permanently; fees such as annual or late fees still apply when they are charged.
Why C: Late payments are penalized, not rewarded; a grace period only applies when the full balance is paid by the due date.
Why D: The grace period does not allow ignoring the bill; unpaid balances start accruing interest, and late payments bring fees and credit damage.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person pays only the minimum on a $3,000 balance at 20% APR. What is the main effect?
A: Interest stops being charged and the whole debt is wiped out
B: The credit limit is cut to zero, so the card cannot be used again
C: Much of the payment goes to interest and the debt lasts longer
D: The debt is erased quickly and the card is closed by the bank
Why A: Interest keeps accruing on the unpaid balance, so paying only the minimum never wipes out the debt or stops charges.
Why B: Issuers do not cut a limit to zero for paying the minimum; the real problem is that interest keeps compounding on the remaining balance.
Why C: At 20% APR on $3,000 (about $600 a year), minimum payments mostly cover interest, so the balance shrinks slowly and the debt lasts for years.
Why D: Minimum payments pay down debt slowly, not quickly, and the bank does not close an account simply because minimums are made.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why check your credit report for errors?
A: Credit reports are private and cannot be corrected
B: Errors can lower your score and cost you money
C: Reports never contain errors of any kind at all
D: Errors only help you and never cost you money
Why A: Credit reports can be corrected; under the Fair Credit Reporting Act you can dispute errors with the bureaus and the lender.
Why B: Errors such as wrong balances or accounts that are not yours can lower your score and lead to higher rates or denied credit.
Why C: Reports do contain mistakes, and studies have found errors on many of them, which is why free annual checks are recommended.
Why D: Errors usually hurt, not help; wrong late payments or accounts can raise your borrowing costs, so checking is worthwhile.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A teen is offered a credit card with a 29% APR. What is the best advice?
A: Carry a balance to build credit, as lenders like it
B: Compare lower-rate options and pay in full each month
C: Ignore the APR and sign up for the card straight away
D: Take every offer that arrives in the mail this year
Why A: Carrying a balance does not build credit; it only racks up interest at 29%, and paying on time and in full is what lenders reward.
Why B: A 29% APR is very high, so comparing lower-rate options and paying the full balance monthly avoids costly interest charges.
Why C: Ignoring the APR is risky because the rate determines the cost of carrying a balance, and 29% is much higher than typical cards.
Why D: Accepting every mailed offer can create many accounts and hard inquiries and tempt overspending, which can hurt a young person's finances.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A $300 payday loan charges a $45 fee for two weeks. What is the approximate APR?
A: About 15.0%
B: About 45%
C: About 390%
D: About 0%
Why A: About 15% is the fee as a share of the loan for one two-week period ($45 / $300), not the annualized rate.
Why B: 45% mistakes the $45 fee for a percentage; the fee is 15% of $300 and must be annualized to get the APR.
Why C: $45 / $300 = 15% per two weeks; with 26 two-week periods in a year, 15% x 26 = 390% APR, which is why payday loans are so costly.
Why D: The loan charges a $45 fee, so the APR cannot be zero; the fee on $300 works out to a very high annual rate.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does it mean to default on a loan?
A: To fail to make required payments
B: To refinance the loan at a lower rate
C: To pay the loan off early in full
D: To ask a question about your loan
Why A: Default means failing to make required payments, which can bring late fees, collections, credit damage, and possibly loss of collateral.
Why B: Refinancing replaces a loan with a new one at better terms; it is a deliberate action, not a failure to pay.
Why C: Paying off a loan early in full is a good outcome that closes the debt; it is the opposite of defaulting.
Why D: Asking a question about a loan is normal customer service and has no effect on the loan or your payment record.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is refinancing?
A: Paying a loan with a credit card, moving debt between lenders
B: Ignoring a loan and not paying it back to the lender
C: Canceling insurance that you pay for every month to protect you
D: Replacing a loan with a new one, often to get better terms
Why A: Paying a loan with a credit card just moves the debt to a different lender and is not what refinancing means; refinancing replaces the loan itself.
Why B: Ignoring a loan is a default, which damages credit and can lead to collections; refinancing is a planned change of terms.
Why C: Canceling insurance is unrelated to loans; refinancing deals with replacing existing debt, not coverage payments.
Why D: Refinancing replaces an existing loan with a new loan, often to get a lower rate, lower payment, or different term.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the best way to build a good credit score over time?
A: Pay bills on time and keep balances low
B: Max out your cards each month for fun
C: Close all accounts that you have opened
D: Apply for many cards at once to get credit
Why A: Payment history and utilization are the biggest score factors, so paying bills on time and keeping balances low builds good credit over time.
Why B: Maxing out cards drives utilization up, which hurts your score and creates large debts that cost interest.
Why C: Closing accounts shortens your credit history and cuts available credit, which can raise utilization and lower your score.
Why D: Applying for many cards at once creates multiple hard inquiries and signals risk, which can lower your score.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the difference between a credit card and a debit card?
A: They are identical in every way and in every use of them
B: Debit cards charge interest monthly on the balance, like credit
C: Credit cards use only your cash and never any loan from a bank
D: Credit cards borrow money and debit cards use your own funds
Why A: Credit and debit cards work differently: credit borrows from the issuer, while debit takes money directly from your checking account.
Why B: Debit cards use your own funds and do not charge interest, so describing them as charging interest monthly is wrong.
Why C: Credit cards lend you money up to a limit, so saying they use only your cash and no loan describes debit cards instead.
Why D: A credit card is a loan you repay later, often with interest, while a debit card pulls money straight from your own account.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A customer is offered 0% APR for 12 months followed by 22% on any balance. What should she do?
A: Spend as much as possible in the promotion, since the rate is low
B: Plan to pay the balance before the promotional period ends
C: Ignore the end date of the offer and keep on spending
D: Make no payments until the offer ends in twelve months
Why A: After 12 months the rate jumps to 22%, so heavy spending without a payoff plan could leave a large balance charged that high rate.
Why B: Planning to pay off the balance before the 0% period ends avoids the 22% rate, so she gets the benefit of the offer without the cost.
Why C: Ignoring the end date risks owing a big balance at 22% APR, which can erase any benefit of the promotion.
Why D: Not paying anything for a year wastes the 0% window, and late payments or missing minimums can cancel the promotional rate.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a credit utilization ratio?
A: The fee for a card that you pay each year
B: The number of cards you own on the credit report
C: The share of available credit you are using
D: The interest on a card that is charged monthly
Why A: An annual fee is a yearly charge for holding the card, while utilization compares your balance to your credit limit.
Why B: The number of cards you own is a different credit factor; utilization measures how much of your available limit you are using.
Why C: Utilization = balances divided by total credit limits, and keeping it low, ideally below 30%, helps your credit score.
Why D: Monthly interest is a cost of carrying a balance; the utilization ratio is a percentage of credit used, not a charge.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person with a $1,000 deductible has a $4,000 covered car repair. How much does the insurer pay?
Why A: $5,000 adds the deductible to the repair cost; insurance pays the covered cost minus the deductible, so it cannot exceed the bill.
Why B: The insurer does not pay the full $4,000 because the policyholder pays the first $1,000 deductible out of pocket.
Why C: $1,000 is the deductible, which the driver pays, not the amount the insurer pays.
Why D: Insurer pays covered cost minus the deductible: $4,000 - $1,000 = $3,000, while the driver pays the $1,000 deductible.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which insurance protects against losses from damage to your own car in an accident?
A: Life insurance
B: Collision coverage
C: Health insurance
D: Renters insurance plan
Why A: Life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries and has nothing to do with repairing your car after an accident.
Why B: Collision coverage pays to repair or replace your own car after a crash with another vehicle or object, regardless of who was at fault.
Why C: Health insurance covers medical expenses for illness or injury, not damage to a vehicle.
Why D: Renters insurance covers belongings and liability in a rented home, not damage to your car in an accident.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A renter owns $15,000 of belongings. Which policy best protects them from theft or fire?
A: Renters insurance
B: Disability insurance
C: Auto insurance
D: Term life insurance
Why A: Renters insurance covers a tenant's personal property against theft, fire, and other covered events, and often includes liability coverage as well.
Why B: Disability insurance replaces income if you cannot work due to injury or illness; it does not cover stolen or burned possessions.
Why C: Auto insurance protects a vehicle and driver liability, and a renter's household belongings inside the apartment are not covered by it.
Why D: Term life insurance pays a death benefit to beneficiaries, not the replacement cost of belongings lost to theft or fire.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does term life insurance provide?
A: Coverage for car damage and its repairs
B: Income during retirement paid out each month
C: A death benefit for a set number of years
D: Lifetime investment growth with a cash value
Why A: Coverage for car damage and repairs is provided by auto insurance, not by a life insurance policy of any kind.
Why B: Retirement income comes from annuities, pensions, or Social Security; term life insurance pays only when the insured person dies.
Why C: Term life pays a death benefit to beneficiaries if the insured dies during a set term, such as 10, 20, or 30 years.
Why D: Cash value and lifetime coverage belong to permanent policies such as whole life; term insurance has no cash value.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is health insurance used for?
A: Paying property taxes owed
B: Paying for groceries each week
C: Paying part of medical costs
D: Paying all costs, no deductible
Why A: Property taxes are paid to local government and are not covered by health insurance, which handles medical expenses.
Why B: Groceries are everyday living costs; health insurance only helps pay medical bills such as doctor visits and hospital stays.
Why C: Health insurance pays part of medical costs, with the insured sharing costs through premiums, deductibles, and copays.
Why D: Health insurance rarely pays everything; deductibles, copays, and coinsurance mean the insured still pays a share of costs.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which choice usually lowers an insurance premium?
A: A higher deductible
B: More coverage added
C: A lower deductible
D: More claims filed
Why A: A higher deductible means you carry more of each loss, so the insurer charges a lower premium in return.
Why B: Adding coverage increases what the insurer might pay out, so it normally raises the premium rather than lowering it.
Why C: A lower deductible shifts more cost to the insurer, which typically raises the premium rather than lowering it.
Why D: Filing more claims marks a driver as higher risk, which tends to raise premiums at renewal rather than lower them.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a good way to protect against identity theft?
A: Ignore bank statements when they arrive in the mail
B: Share your passwords with friends and with family
C: Use one simple password everywhere, so it is never lost
D: Use strong, unique passwords and monitor accounts
Why A: Ignoring bank statements lets fraud go unnoticed; reviewing statements is how you catch unauthorized charges early.
Why B: Sharing passwords gives others access to your accounts and raises the chance of theft or misuse, even with trusted people.
Why C: One simple password reused everywhere means a single breach exposes every account, so reuse is a major security weakness.
Why D: Strong, unique passwords plus regular monitoring of accounts and credit reports help prevent and quickly catch identity theft.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A text says your account is locked and asks you to click a link and enter your password. What should you do?
A: Reply with your card number and your PIN code at once
B: Contact the company using a trusted number or app
C: Forward it to friends and ask what they think of it
D: Click the link and enter your password before it locks
Why A: Sending a card number and PIN to someone who texted you hands criminals what they need to commit fraud.
Why B: Contact the company through a number or app you already trust; unexpected texts like this are typical phishing attempts.
Why C: Forwarding a phishing message may spread it to others and does nothing to verify whether your account is really locked.
Why D: Clicking the link and entering a password sends your login to scammers, who built the urgency to rush you into acting.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is liability insurance?
A: Coverage for harm or damage you cause to others
B: Coverage for your own injuries only, none for others
C: A warranty on a product that you have recently bought
D: A savings account for lawsuits that a firm may face
Why A: Liability insurance pays for injury or property damage you cause to others, and covers legal defense costs if you are sued.
Why B: Covering only your own injuries describes other policies; liability insurance protects others harmed by your actions.
Why C: A warranty covers repair or replacement of a defective product, while liability insurance covers harm you cause to others.
Why D: Insurance is a risk-sharing contract with an insurer, not a savings account that a firm sets aside for lawsuits.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is an example of self-insuring?
A: Ignoring risk completely and hoping nothing goes wrong
B: Borrowing at high interest to pay for every loss that occurs
C: Saving an emergency fund to cover small losses yourself
D: Buying a full policy for every risk, however small
Why A: Ignoring a risk hoping nothing goes wrong is not self-insuring because there is no plan or funds set aside for a loss.
Why B: Borrowing at high interest after each loss is costly and unplanned, unlike self-insuring, which relies on money saved beforehand.
Why C: Self-insuring means setting aside your own money, such as an emergency fund, to pay for small, predictable losses instead of buying insurance.
Why D: Buying a policy for every small risk transfers risk to an insurer, which is the opposite of self-insuring.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does it mean to avoid a risk?
A: Accept it and plan to pay for any loss yourself
B: Choose not to do the activity that creates it
C: Reduce its effects with safety steps and training
D: Buy a policy for it, so an insurer pays the loss
Why A: Accepting a risk and planning to pay for any loss yourself is risk retention, not risk avoidance.
Why B: Avoiding a risk means not doing the activity that creates it, such as not riding a motorcycle to avoid the chance of a crash.
Why C: Using safety steps and training is risk reduction, which lowers the chance or size of a loss instead of eliminating the activity.
Why D: Buying insurance transfers the financial risk to an insurer, which is risk transfer rather than avoidance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A driver causes an accident injuring another person. Which coverage most directly pays that person's medical bills?
A: Roadside assistance plan
B: Comprehensive insurance
C: Collision coverage plan
D: Bodily injury liability
Why A: Roadside assistance covers towing, jump-starts, and similar services for your own car, not medical bills of an injured person.
Why B: Comprehensive insurance covers non-collision damage to your own car, such as theft, fire, hail, or hitting an animal.
Why C: Collision coverage pays for damage to your own vehicle, and it does not pay medical bills for another person you injured.
Why D: Bodily injury liability pays medical costs and related claims for people you injure when you are at fault in an accident.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A student can earn $15 per hour at a café or $12 per hour with a $1.50 per hour tip average at a bookstore. Which pays more per hour on average?
A: The bookstore at $13.50, because tips are always higher
B: They pay exactly the same per hour of work they do
C: The bookstore at $12 plus extra benefits only, each hour
D: The café at $15, because $12 plus $1.50 is only $13.50
Why A: The bookstore pays $12 + $1.50 = $13.50 per hour, but that is less than the café's $15, and tips are not always higher.
Why B: The totals differ: the café pays $15 per hour while the bookstore averages $13.50, so the two jobs do not pay the same.
Why C: Even if benefits were counted, the question asks about pay per hour, and the bookstore's $13.50 is already below the café's $15.
Why D: Bookstore total is $12 + $1.50 = $13.50 per hour, which is less than the café's $15, so the café pays $1.50 more per hour.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which document shows a worker's earnings and taxes for the whole year?
A: A W-2 form
B: A W-4 form
C: A pay stub
D: A bank record
Why A: A W-2 is issued by an employer after year end and shows total wages and taxes withheld for the full year.
Why B: A W-4 is filled out by the employee to tell the employer how much tax to withhold; it does not report annual earnings.
Why C: A pay stub shows earnings and deductions for a single pay period, not the totals for the entire year.
Why D: A bank record lists deposits and withdrawals, but it does not show gross earnings and taxes withheld the way a W-2 does.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why do employers withhold income taxes from paychecks?
A: To pay the company's profits out to the owners each year
B: To lower the employee's wage rate, so the firm pays less
C: To pay part of the employee's tax bill during the year
D: To fund the employee's vacation and sick days at the firm
Why A: Withholding is taken from employee wages and sent to the government, not used to pay company profits to the owners.
Why B: Withholding does not change the wage rate; it simply sends part of the employee's earned pay to the tax authorities.
Why C: Employers withhold income tax so employees pay part of their tax bill gradually during the year instead of in one lump sum.
Why D: Vacation and sick days are employer benefits; withheld income tax goes to the government and not to those benefits.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A worker is paid $52,000 a year, biweekly. What is her gross pay per paycheck?
Why A: $1,000 is the weekly amount ($52,000 / 52), but biweekly pay comes every two weeks, so each check is double that.
Why B: Biweekly means 26 pay periods a year, so gross pay per check is $52,000 / 26 = $2,000 before taxes and deductions.
Why C: $4,333 is the monthly figure ($52,000 / 12), which does not match a biweekly pay schedule.
Why D: $26,000 is half a year's pay ($52,000 / 2), as if paid twice a year, not every two weeks.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a signing bonus?
A: A fee for starting work, paid by the new hire
B: A yearly tax refund from the state or city
C: A one-time payment offered to a new hire
D: A monthly loan paid back to the employer
Why A: A signing bonus is paid by the employer to the new hire, not a fee the new hire pays to start working.
Why B: A tax refund comes from the government after filing a return, whereas a signing bonus is paid by an employer.
Why C: A signing bonus is a one-time payment an employer offers to attract a new hire, often with conditions such as staying a certain time.
Why D: A signing bonus is a payment to the worker, not a loan to be repaid monthly to the employer.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which action best helps a worker earn a promotion?
A: Doing the minimum amount of work that is asked of you
B: Arguing with supervisors about every decision they make
C: Avoiding responsibility for any of the tasks you are given
D: Consistently performing well and building new skills
Why A: Doing only the minimum rarely shows initiative, and managers usually promote employees who go beyond basic expectations.
Why B: Arguing with supervisors about every decision damages working relationships and makes promotion less likely.
Why C: Avoiding responsibility shows a lack of reliability, so employers are unlikely to trust such a worker with a higher position.
Why D: Employers promote workers who consistently perform well and keep building new skills, since those workers show reliability and growth potential.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Two job offers pay $45,000. Offer A has a 6% employer retirement match; Offer B has none. About how much extra does A provide per year if the worker contributes 6%?
Why A: The match is 6% x $45,000 = $2,700 per year of extra compensation that Offer B does not provide to the worker.
Why B: $27,000 is ten times the correct amount; 6% of $45,000 is $2,700, not 60%.
Why C: Offer A provides a match and Offer B does not, so the difference cannot be zero when she contributes 6%.
Why D: $270 would be 0.6% of salary, a decimal slip; 6% of $45,000 is $2,700.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a union?
A: A government tax office that collects income tax from workers
B: An organization of workers that bargains with employers
C: A company's marketing team that plans ads for its brands
D: A type of bank that lends only to members of the public
Why A: The tax office is a government agency, while a union is an organization formed by workers themselves.
Why B: A union is an organization of workers that bargains collectively with employers over pay, benefits, and working conditions.
Why C: A marketing team is a department inside a company that plans advertising, which is unrelated to workers' collective bargaining.
Why D: A credit union lends to members, but a labor union is not a bank; it represents workers in negotiations with employers.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does an employer's matching contribution to a 401(k) mean?
A: The employer deletes the account when pay is too low to match it
B: The employer adds money based on what the employee contributes
C: The employer pays the employee's taxes for the whole year
D: The employer takes money from savings to pay its own bills
Why A: The employer does not delete the account; a match is extra money added when the employee contributes, not a penalty for low pay.
Why B: Employer matching means the company adds money to the employee's 401(k) based on the employee's contribution, often up to a stated percentage of pay.
Why C: Employer matching contributions go into the retirement account; they do not mean the employer pays the employee's yearly taxes.
Why D: The match is added to the employee's retirement account by the employer, not taken from savings to cover the employer's bills.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A worker's hourly wage rises from $14 to $16. What is the percent increase?
A: About 2.0%
B: About 20.0%
C: About 12.5%
D: About 14.3%
Why A: A 2% answer mistakes the $2 dollar raise for a percentage; the percent increase must be measured against the old wage.
Why B: 20% would need a raise of $2.80 on $14, which is more than the actual $2 raise.
Why C: 12.5% divides the $2 raise by the new wage of $16, but percent change must use the original wage as the base.
Why D: Percent increase = ($16 - $14) / $14 = $2 / $14 = about 14.3%, using the original wage as the base.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a part-time job?
A: A job with no pay for the worker at all
B: A job with exactly 60 hours each week of work
C: A job with fewer hours than a full-time job
D: A job for only one day a year, like a holiday
Why A: A job with no pay is volunteering; part-time work is paid but involves fewer hours than a full-time job.
Why B: Sixty hours a week is more than a typical full-time schedule, so it is not part-time work.
Why C: A part-time job has fewer hours than full-time work, often under 30 to 35 hours a week, and may offer fewer benefits.
Why D: One day a year would be an occasional job, not part-time work, which involves regular weekly hours.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does 'net income' mean for a self-employed person?
A: Business income left after business expenses
B: Taxes paid on the business income that you earn
C: All sales before costs, the total money taken in
D: Money borrowed from a bank to run the business
Why A: Net income is business revenue minus business expenses; it is the profit left for the owner before personal considerations.
Why B: Taxes on business income are a cost the owner pays and do not define net income.
Why C: All sales before costs describes gross revenue, which is higher than net income.
Why D: Borrowed money is a loan to be repaid, not income, and borrowing does not measure what the business earned.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A freelancer earns $60,000 in sales and has $18,000 in business expenses. What is the net business income?
Why A: $18,000 is the expense total, not what remains after expenses are subtracted from sales.
Why B: $60,000 is gross sales before expenses; net income subtracts the $18,000 of costs.
Why C: Net income = sales - expenses = $60,000 - $18,000 = $42,000 of business income before personal taxes.
Why D: $78,000 adds expenses to sales, but expenses must be subtracted to find net income.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does an employer look for in a reference?
A: A person who can speak honestly about your work
B: A friend who does not know you well but is nice
C: A stranger who has never met you or seen your work
D: A relative who will lie to make you look good
Why A: A good reference is someone who knows your work and can speak honestly about your skills, reliability, and character to an employer.
Why B: A friend who barely knows you cannot give meaningful details about your work, so employers gain little from their opinion.
Why C: A stranger has no knowledge of your work or character, so cannot serve as a reference to an employer.
Why D: A relative who lies would hurt your credibility; employers want honest, informed references, usually from supervisors or teachers.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is job satisfaction?
A: The number of coworkers on the staff team
B: The size of the office you work in each day
C: The distance to work from your home each day
D: How content a worker feels with their job
Why A: The number of coworkers is a team-size fact and not a measure of how content a worker feels in the job.
Why B: Office size describes the workplace, while job satisfaction measures how fulfilled a worker feels, regardless of space.
Why C: Commute distance is a logistics factor that may influence satisfaction, but it is not what the term itself means.
Why D: Job satisfaction is how content and fulfilled a worker feels about the job, influenced by pay, duties, coworkers, and growth.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A family spends $450 on groceries each month. They cut it by 10%. How much do they save per year?
Why A: $54 is 12% of $450, which does not match the 10% cut or the yearly total.
Why B: A 10% cut saves $45 a month ($450 x 0.10), and $45 x 12 months = $540 per year.
Why C: $450 is the entire monthly grocery bill, not the yearly savings from a 10% cut.
Why D: $45 is only the monthly savings; the question asks for the yearly figure, which is 12 times that.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a 'needs versus wants' decision about a cell phone plan?
A: Plans have no cost, so the choice is never a trade-off for anyone
B: Every plan is a want, so none of them can ever count as a need
C: A basic plan may be a need while a premium unlimited plan may be a want
D: Every plan is a need at any price, since phones are essential to all of us
Why A: Phone plans cost money, so choosing one always involves trade-offs between price and features.
Why B: Calling every plan a want ignores that basic phone service may be essential for work, school, or safety.
Why C: A basic plan may be a need for communication, while a premium unlimited plan with extras goes beyond what is necessary and is a want.
Why D: Not every plan is a need; a premium unlimited plan with extras goes beyond what is essential, so some plan features are wants.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is a variable expense?
A: Entertainment spending
B: Monthly rent payment
C: A fixed car loan payment
D: Insurance premium bill
Why A: Entertainment spending changes from month to month depending on choices, which makes it a variable expense.
Why B: Monthly rent is usually the same amount each month, which makes it a fixed expense.
Why C: A fixed car loan payment is the same amount each month, so it is a fixed expense rather than variable.
Why D: Insurance premiums are typically set amounts due on a schedule, so they are fixed rather than variable expenses.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person's rent is $900, car payment $250, and insurance $100 monthly. Take-home pay is $2,400. What share of pay goes to these fixed costs?
A: About 25%
B: About 100%
C: About 12%
D: About 52%
Why A: 25% would be about $600; fixed costs total $900 + $250 + $100 = $1,250, which is more than that.
Why B: 100% would mean fixed costs equal all take-home pay, but they total $1,250 out of $2,400.
Why C: 12% would be about $288, far below the $1,250 total of fixed monthly costs.
Why D: Fixed costs are $900 + $250 + $100 = $1,250, and $1,250 / $2,400 = about 52% of take-home pay.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a bargain hunter's best approach?
A: Buy the most expensive item that you can find in the whole shop
B: Compare unit prices and quality, not just the sticker price
C: Buy without checking the price or the quality of the item
D: Buy the cheapest item always, whatever its quality or use
Why A: The most expensive item is not necessarily the best; a smart shopper looks for value rather than the highest price.
Why B: Comparing unit prices and quality lets a shopper find the best value, not just the lowest sticker price.
Why C: Buying without checking prices or quality risks overpaying and getting poor items, which is the opposite of bargain hunting.
Why D: Always buying the cheapest item can backfire if it breaks or doesn't do the job, so quality and use matter too.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the cost of 'convenience' purchases?
A: Always better value than anything else
B: Always lower than all other options
C: Free of any fees or extra charges at all
D: Often a higher price for saving time
Why A: Convenience items often cost more than comparable ones, so they are not always better value than other options.
Why B: Convenience items such as pre-cut food or delivery frequently cost more than alternatives, so they are not always cheaper.
Why C: Convenience purchases often carry delivery or service fees and higher markups, so they are not free of extra charges.
Why D: Convenience purchases, such as ready-made meals or delivery, often charge a premium for saving the buyer's time or effort.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A shopper pays $4.50 daily for coffee on 250 workdays. How much does she spend in a year?
Why A: $450 equals only 100 days of $4.50 coffee, far fewer than the 250 workdays in the problem.
Why B: Yearly cost = $4.50 x 250 workdays = $1,125, which shows how small daily purchases add up over time.
Why C: $11,250 is ten times the correct total; $4.50 x 250 equals $1,125.
Why D: $112 corresponds to about 25 days of coffee, not 250 workdays, so it is far too low.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a shopping 'trade-off'?
A: Giving up one item to be able to buy another
B: Returning all items that you bought last month
C: Buying everything at once on one shopping trip
D: Trading with friends only, swapping goods
Why A: A trade-off means giving up one thing to get another, such as skipping a new game to afford shoes, because resources are limited.
Why B: Returning items bought last month is a refund choice, not a trade-off, which is about choosing between alternatives.
Why C: Buying everything at once ignores limited money; a trade-off arises exactly because you cannot afford every item.
Why D: A trade-off is not limited to swapping goods with friends; it is any choice that gives up one option for another.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the best way to avoid overdraft fees?
A: Ignore your balance and spend all that you please
B: Close your bank account and keep cash at home
C: Track your balance and set low-balance alerts
D: Write checks without checking your balance first
Why A: Ignoring your balance and spending freely is the quickest way to trigger overdraft fees when payments exceed your funds.
Why B: Closing your account and holding cash gives up banking services and safety, and does not teach balance management.
Why C: Tracking your balance and setting low-balance alerts helps you avoid spending more than you have, preventing overdraft fees.
Why D: Writing checks without checking the balance risks overdrafts and fees, since checks can bounce when funds are short.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person has $250 left in a monthly budget for fun. She spends $80 on a concert, $60 on a game and $70 on dining. How much remains?
Why A: $210 is the total spent ($80 + $60 + $70), not the amount left over from the $250 budget.
Why B: Zero would mean all $250 was spent, but she spent only $210 of the budget.
Why C: $140 would be left only if she had spent $110; her three purchases total $210.
Why D: Spending is $80 + $60 + $70 = $210, so the budget remaining is $250 - $210 = $40.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a store loyalty program?
A: A return penalty charged by the store
B: A fee to enter a store and look around
C: A program that rewards repeat shoppers
D: A tax on frequent buyers added at the till
Why A: A return penalty is a store policy fee, whereas a loyalty program gives rewards to repeat customers.
Why B: Stores don't charge people to enter; loyalty programs offer perks to encourage customers to come back.
Why C: A loyalty program rewards repeat shoppers with points, discounts, or special offers to keep them buying from the store.
Why D: Loyalty programs reward frequent buyers; they do not tax them at the register.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why compare insurance quotes before buying?
A: Prices for similar coverage can differ
B: All quotes are always identical in price
C: Quotes are illegal in most of the states
D: Quotes eliminate all risk for the buyer
Why A: Prices for similar coverage vary by insurer, so comparing quotes can help you find the same protection for less money.
Why B: Quotes are not identical, because insurers weigh risk differently, which is the very reason comparing them is worthwhile.
Why C: Insurance quotes are legal and free to request, and shopping around is a standard consumer practice.
Why D: A quote is just a price estimate; it cannot eliminate risk, which is why insurance is bought separately.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A coupon takes $10 off a purchase of $50 or more. A shopper has $46 in items and adds a $4 item to reach $50. Is this smart?
A: Yes always, because coupons are free money for the shopper too
B: Yes, if she wants the item, since she pays $40 instead of $46
C: Yes, because she saves $50 on the whole purchase total
D: No, because coupons never work in any store she visits
Why A: Coupons are not free money; spending on an item you do not need can cancel the savings from the discount.
Why B: If she wants the item, buying it brings her total to $50, and after the $10 coupon she pays $40 instead of $46.
Why C: The coupon saves $10, not $50; $50 is the minimum purchase needed to qualify, not the savings.
Why D: Coupons do work when their conditions are met, including at stores she visits, so saying they never work is false.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does it mean to shop with a budget?
A: Avoid looking at prices while you shop in a store
B: Spend all your money on the first things you see there
C: Buy whatever looks nice to you at the time in the shop
D: Set a spending limit before shopping and stick to it
Why A: Avoiding prices makes it hard to stay within a budget, because you cannot compare costs to the limit you set.
Why B: Spending all your money on the first things you see ignores budgeting and leaves nothing for other needs.
Why C: Buying whatever looks nice is impulse shopping, which tends to lead to overspending.
Why D: Shopping with a budget means setting a spending limit beforehand and sticking to it so you spend on priorities, not impulses.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an installment plan?
A: Receiving a gift from a friend on a special day
B: Paying everything at once, in a single lump sum now
C: Paying for a purchase in several scheduled payments
D: Not paying at all for the goods that you took home
Why A: A gift is given freely and is not paid for, whereas an installment plan involves scheduled payments for a purchase.
Why B: Paying everything at once is a lump sum purchase, which is the opposite of an installment plan.
Why C: An installment plan splits the price of a purchase into several scheduled payments, often with interest or fees added.
Why D: Taking goods without paying is theft, whereas installment plans require full payment in scheduled amounts.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: If you save $50 a month at 3% interest compounded yearly for 3 years, which is closest to the total?
A: About $1,855
B: About $2,500
C: About $1,000
D: $1,800 exactly
Why A: Deposits total $50 x 36 = $1,800; adding about $55 of compound interest at 3% gives roughly $1,855 after 3 years.
Why B: $2,500 is far above what $1,800 in deposits plus a few dozen dollars of interest could reach at 3%.
Why C: $1,000 is below even the $1,800 she deposits, so it can't be the total after three years of saving.
Why D: Deposits alone total $1,800, and interest at 3% adds some more, so the total is slightly above $1,800 and not exactly equal.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the benefit of an automatic transfer to savings?
A: It removes the need for any bank accounts at all
B: It saves consistently without relying on willpower
C: It spends your savings before you can use them
D: It increases fees on your savings account every year
Why A: Automatic transfers still use bank accounts; they move money between your own accounts without manual effort.
Why B: Automatic transfers save consistently without needing willpower each month, so saving happens before you can spend the money.
Why C: Transfers move money into savings, which preserves it for later; they do not spend savings.
Why D: An automatic transfer does not raise account fees; many savings accounts have no fees to begin with.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does APY stand for?
A: Average payment year
B: Annual payment yield
C: Annual percentage yield
D: Applied profit per year
Why A: APY is not about average payments; it measures the interest earned on a deposit over a year.
Why B: APY does not stand for a payment yield; it is a savings measure that includes compounding.
Why C: APY stands for annual percentage yield, the real yearly return on savings after compounding is included, useful for comparing accounts.
Why D: APY is a standard banking term for annual percentage yield, not profit applied per year.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which account is best for $5,000 you may need within a few days?
A: A single volatile stock held in a brokerage
B: A 5-year CD with early withdrawal penalties
C: A long-term retirement fund of stocks and bonds
D: A savings or checking account with easy access
Why A: A volatile stock can lose value quickly, so it is a poor place for money you may need within days.
Why B: A 5-year CD charges a penalty for early withdrawal, so it is a poor fit for money needed soon.
Why C: Retirement funds are meant for long-term growth and carry market risk and withdrawal limits, which does not suit short-term needs.
Why D: A savings or checking account offers easy access, insured safety, and no market risk for money you may need within days.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does it mean to set a savings priority?
A: Save for everything equally with no plan or order
B: Decide which goals matter most and fund them first
C: Never save anything toward any goal in life at all
D: Spend first, save later with whatever is left over
Why A: Saving for everything equally with no plan ignores that some goals matter more and deserve funding first.
Why B: Setting a savings priority means deciding which goals matter most, such as an emergency fund, and funding them first.
Why C: Never saving toward any goal is the opposite of setting priorities, since priorities guide where saved money goes.
Why D: Spending first and saving what is left usually means little gets saved, whereas priorities direct savings before spending.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A saver has $3,000 and her monthly expenses are $1,500. How many months of expenses does she have saved?
A: 2 months
B: 0.5 months
C: 6 months
D: 1 month
Why A: Months of expenses saved = $3,000 / $1,500 = 2 months, which is below the 3 to 6 months often recommended.
Why B: 0.5 months comes from flipping the division ($1,500 / $3,000); the savings are larger than one month of expenses.
Why C: Six months would need $9,000 in savings ($1,500 x 6), but she has only $3,000.
Why D: One month would need only $1,500 in savings, but she has $3,000, which covers two months.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a savings bond?
A: A checking account that you use to pay bills from the bank
B: A credit card that lets you borrow money up to a limit at a bank today
C: A government debt security sold at a set value that earns interest
D: A share of a company that is owned by the stock holders of a firm
Why A: A checking account is a deposit account for paying bills, and a savings bond is a government security that earns interest.
Why B: A credit card lets you borrow up to a limit, whereas a savings bond is a loan you make to the government.
Why C: A savings bond is a government debt security bought at a set value that earns interest over time and is repaid at maturity.
Why D: A share of a company is stock, which represents ownership, while a savings bond is a government loan.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a good reason to keep savings separate from a checking account?
A: It reduces the temptation to spend it
B: It removes interest from your account
C: It prevents deposits from a paycheck
D: It increases fees on your own account
Why A: Keeping savings in a separate account reduces the temptation to spend it and makes it easier to reach your goals.
Why B: Savings accounts usually pay interest, so separate accounts don't remove interest; many checking accounts pay little or none.
Why C: A separate account does not stop paycheck deposits; you can direct part of your pay straight into it.
Why D: Separate accounts do not raise fees; many savings accounts have no fees if you meet minimum balance rules.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why does a longer time horizon usually allow for more risk in saving for goals?
A: Banks guarantee all returns on long-term stocks
B: There is more time to recover from market dips
C: Risk disappears over time for long-term savers
D: Investments cannot lose value over a long time
Why A: Banks do not guarantee stock returns; deposit insurance covers bank accounts, not market investments.
Why B: With a longer horizon, investments have more time to recover from market dips, so savers can accept more risk for goals far away.
Why C: Risk does not vanish over time; it only becomes easier to ride out because there is more time to recover.
Why D: Investments can lose value over any time period, even a long one, though long-term results have usually trended upward.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an emergency fund generally kept in?
A: Cash buried in a yard in a metal tin box
B: A speculative stock bought on a tip
C: A long-term locked CD with penalties
D: A liquid, safe account such as savings
Why A: Cash buried in a tin earns nothing and could be lost, stolen, or destroyed, so it is unsafe for an emergency fund.
Why B: A speculative stock can fall sharply just when you need money, so it is unsuitable for an emergency fund.
Why C: A locked CD charges penalties for early withdrawal, which defeats the purpose of quick access in an emergency.
Why D: An emergency fund belongs in a liquid, safe account such as savings so cash is available immediately and not at risk of loss.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the difference between saving and investing?
A: Investing is for spending only, while saving is for growth only in the long run
B: Saving prioritizes safety and access while investing seeks growth with risk
C: Saving has more risk than investing always, since money in a bank can be lost
D: They mean the same thing, as both put money in a bank account to grow
Why A: This reverses the idea: investing is meant for growth, while saving is for safety and short-term access.
Why B: Saving emphasizes safety and easy access, while investing aims for higher growth but carries the risk of loss.
Why C: Insured bank savings are generally lower risk than investing, so claiming saving always has more risk is incorrect.
Why D: Saving and investing differ in risk and return; investing buys assets like stocks that may lose value, unlike insured deposits.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A saver earns 2.5% on $4,000 for a year. How much interest does she earn?
Why A: $10 would come from a rate of only 0.25%, which is too low; 2.5% of $4,000 is more.
Why B: $25 would be about 0.625% of $4,000; the correct 2.5% rate yields four times that.
Why C: $1,000 is 25% of $4,000, ten times the stated rate of 2.5%.
Why D: Interest = principal x rate = $4,000 x 0.025 = $100 for one year.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A stock that pays a $2 annual dividend trades at $50. What is its dividend yield?
Why A: Dividend yield = annual dividend / price = $2 / $50 = 0.04, or 4%, the annual income return on the share price.
Why B: 25% is the price divided by the dividend inverted; yield must divide the dividend by the price.
Why C: 10% would need a $5 dividend on a $50 stock; a $2 dividend gives a much lower yield.
Why D: Two percent mistakes the $2 dividend for a percentage; dividing by the $50 price gives 4%.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does asset allocation mean?
A: Paying a broker fee for each trade that you make
B: Buying one stock only, which gives the best return
C: Dividing investments among stocks, bonds and cash
D: Selling everything you own and holding only cash
Why A: Paying broker fees is a cost of trading, not an allocation strategy for spreading money across asset types.
Why B: Buying one stock only is concentration, the opposite of allocating across different types of investments.
Why C: Asset allocation spreads your money among different asset classes such as stocks, bonds, and cash to balance risk and return.
Why D: Selling everything for cash abandons investing altogether rather than allocating across several asset classes.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which investment typically offers the highest long-term growth potential with higher risk?
A: Savings
B: Cash
C: T-bills
D: Stocks
Why A: Savings accounts are safe and liquid but offer low returns, so they lack high long-term growth potential.
Why B: Cash holds its value in the short term but loses purchasing power to inflation and offers little growth.
Why C: T-bills are very safe government securities with low returns, not high-growth, high-risk investments.
Why D: Stocks have historically delivered the highest long-term returns among common assets, but with more ups and downs and risk of loss.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A stock priced at $120 has a 3-for-1 split. What is the new price, all else equal?
Why A: A split does not change the stock price in the way this implies; with 3-for-1, the price falls to a third, not stays at $120.
Why B: A 3-for-1 split triples the shares and divides the price by 3, so $120 / 3 = $40 per share, with the total value unchanged.
Why C: $30 would result from dividing by four; a 3-for-1 split divides the price by 3, giving $40.
Why D: $360 multiplies the price by 3, but a stock split divides the price while increasing the number of shares.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why do many experts suggest investing in low-cost index funds for long-term goals?
A: They offer broad diversification and low fees
B: They guarantee profits for every single investor
C: They are exempt from market risk altogether
D: They never change in value over the long years
Why A: Index funds hold many stocks at once and charge low fees, which gives broad diversification and keeps more of the return for investors.
Why B: No investment guarantees profits for every investor, and index funds lose value when the market falls.
Why C: Index funds still carry market risk because they track the market; diversification reduces risk but does not erase market-wide declines.
Why D: Index fund values rise and fall with the market, so they change in value over time.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is liquidity in investing?
A: How much water a company uses to make its goods each year
B: How much profit a company makes from its sales each year
C: How easily an asset can be turned into cash without losing value
D: How many shareholders a firm has, found in its share register file
Why A: Water use by a company is an operations matter and has nothing to do with how easily an asset converts to cash.
Why B: Company profit measures earnings, while liquidity describes how easily an asset can be sold for cash.
Why C: Liquidity is how quickly and easily an asset can be turned into cash without a big loss in value; savings are very liquid, real estate is not.
Why D: The number of shareholders is a fact about ownership, whereas liquidity describes how easily an asset can be sold.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the risk of buying an investment only because it rose sharply last month?
A: It guarantees dividends for every stock you hold
B: Past gains always repeat, so a rising stock keeps rising
C: Past performance does not guarantee future results
D: It removes all risk from the investments you own
Why A: A recent price rise does not guarantee dividends; many stocks that rise pay none at all.
Why B: Past gains do not repeat on command, and assuming a rising stock keeps rising is a common cause of buying at the top.
Why C: Past performance does not guarantee future results, so buying only because of last month's gain may mean buying right before a drop.
Why D: No recent gain removes risk; any stock can fall, and chasing recent winners often adds risk.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a statement balance?
A: The minimum payment that you must make each month on the card
B: The total owed on a credit card at the end of a billing cycle
C: The rewards earned on the card over the whole billing cycle
D: The credit limit that is set on the card by the issuer
Why A: The minimum payment is the smallest amount due, while the statement balance is the full amount owed at the cycle end.
Why B: The statement balance is the total owed at the end of the billing cycle, and paying it in full by the due date avoids interest.
Why C: Rewards earned are tracked separately, while the statement balance is the amount owed on the account.
Why D: The credit limit is the maximum you can borrow, whereas the statement balance is what you actually owe.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A card has a $500 statement balance and 18% APR. If she pays $500 by the due date, how much interest does she owe on those purchases?
Why A: Paying the full $500 statement balance by the due date uses the grace period, so no interest is charged on those purchases.
Why B: $18 mistakes the 18% rate for dollars; with the full balance paid on time, no interest is owed.
Why C: $7.50 would be about one month of interest ($500 x 0.015), but none is charged when the balance is paid in full by the due date.
Why D: $90 is a full year of interest at 18% ($500 x 0.18), which applies only if the balance is carried for a year.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What happens if you only make the minimum payment each month?
A: Your limit rises each month
B: You pay no interest at all ever
C: The debt disappears in a year or so
D: You pay more interest over time
Why A: Paying only the minimum does not raise your limit; limits are changed by the issuer based on your credit profile.
Why B: Unpaid balances accrue interest, so paying only the minimum still costs interest every month.
Why C: Minimum payments are small, so debt lasts for years rather than disappearing in a year or so.
Why D: Minimum payments cover mostly interest, so the balance shrinks slowly and you pay much more interest over time.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person borrows $2,000 for 2 years at 8% simple interest. How much total interest will she pay?
Why A: $800 would be four years of interest at 8% ($2,000 x 0.08 x 5); the loan runs only 2 years.
Why B: Simple interest = principal x rate x time = $2,000 x 0.08 x 2 = $320 in total interest over two years.
Why C: $160 is one year of interest ($2,000 x 0.08); the loan lasts two years, so double it.
Why D: $3,200 is far too high; it equals 80% per year of the principal, not 8%.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a fixed-rate loan?
A: A loan with no interest to pay at all
B: A loan that has no payments to make at all
C: A loan whose rate changes with the market
D: A loan whose interest rate stays the same
Why A: A fixed-rate loan still charges interest; it simply keeps the rate constant over the life of the loan.
Why B: Every loan has payments, and a fixed-rate loan has regular, predictable payments through its term.
Why C: A loan whose rate changes with the market is a variable-rate loan, the opposite of fixed.
Why D: A fixed-rate loan keeps the same interest rate for the whole term, so payments are predictable.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a variable-rate loan?
A: A loan whose interest rate can change over time
B: A loan with the same rate for its whole life
C: A loan paid in one single payment on the due date
D: A loan that has no rate of interest at all, ever
Why A: A variable-rate loan's interest rate can rise or fall over time, usually following a benchmark rate, so payments can change.
Why B: A loan with the same rate for its whole life is a fixed-rate loan, not a variable-rate loan.
Why C: Loans paid in one payment are bullet or balloon loans; variable refers to the interest rate, not payment timing.
Why D: Variable-rate loans charge interest, though the rate changes; no loan of this type is interest-free.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Which is a risk of a variable-rate loan?
A: Payments never change in any month
B: The loan has no end date and no limit
C: Payments may increase if rates rise
D: Interest is waived for the borrower
Why A: Payments on a variable-rate loan can change from month to month, so they do not stay the same in every month.
Why B: Variable-rate loans still have a term and rate caps, so they do not run forever or without limits.
Why C: If the benchmark rate rises, the interest rate rises, so monthly payments on a variable-rate loan can increase.
Why D: The borrower still pays interest on variable-rate loans; only the rate changes, not whether it is owed.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is collateral?
A: The interest rate on the loan itself
B: A credit report on the borrower
C: Property pledged to secure a loan
D: A late fee a lender adds on top
Why A: The interest rate is the cost of borrowing, whereas collateral is property that backs the loan.
Why B: A credit report is a record of the borrower's credit history, while collateral is an asset the lender can claim.
Why C: Collateral is property, like a car or house, pledged to secure a loan that the lender can claim if the borrower defaults.
Why D: A late fee is a penalty for missed payments, whereas collateral is an asset used as security for repayment.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What does the annual fee on a credit card pay for?
A: The cost of having the card account
B: Taxes on purchases made with the card
C: The price of items bought with the card
D: Your interest charges on the card
Why A: The annual fee is a yearly charge for keeping the card account open, separate from interest, and issuers often justify it with rewards, travel perks or other benefits that come with the card.
Why B: Sales taxes are collected by the seller at checkout on purchases, not by the card issuer, so they are never what the annual fee pays for.
Why C: The price of purchases is what you owe the merchant through the card, billed separately, while the annual fee is a flat yearly charge for the account itself.
Why D: Interest charges are billed on balances carried past the due date and are separate from the annual fee, which you owe even if you never carry a balance.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A card has a $95 annual fee but offers 2% cash back. You spend $2,000 a year on the card. Do rewards beat the fee?
A: Yes: fees are free for the frequent users
B: No: 2% of $2,000 is $40, less than $95
C: It cannot be calculated from the data
D: Yes: $40 is more than the $95 fee
Why A: Fees are not waived for frequent users; an annual fee is charged to the account regardless of how much you spend, unless the issuer specifically offers a waiver.
Why B: Rewards are 2% x $2,000 = $40 a year, which is less than the $95 fee, so you lose $55 and the card does not pay for itself at that spending level.
Why C: The answer can be calculated: the spending, reward rate and fee are all given, and multiplying 2% by $2,000 and comparing to $95 settles it.
Why D: This is wrong because $40 is smaller than $95, not larger; the rewards earn $40 against a $95 fee, leaving a net loss of $55 per year.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person has three cards at 22%, 18% and 15% APR with equal balances. Which should she pay down first to save the most interest?
A: The 15% card
B: The 18% card
C: All equally
D: The 22% card
Why A: The 15% card costs the least in interest, so paying extra on it saves the least; extra payments should go to the highest rate instead.
Why B: The 18% card is in the middle, so extra payments there save more than on the 15% card but less than on the 22% card.
Why C: Cards with different APRs do not cost the same in interest, so paying them down equally wastes savings; with equal balances, the highest rate costs the most.
Why D: With equal balances, the 22% card accrues the most interest each month, so paying it down first (the avalanche method) saves the most money overall.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is credit repair?
A: Paying a company to guarantee a perfect score, whatever your history
B: Erasing true negative information on request by its owner or agent
C: Hiding your credit report from lenders and from all the banks
D: Fixing errors and building better habits to improve a credit score
Why A: No company can legally guarantee a perfect score, and credit repair firms that promise this regardless of your history are making a common deceptive claim.
Why B: True and accurate negative information, such as real late payments, generally stays on a report for years, and a firm cannot lawfully force its removal on request.
Why C: Credit reports cannot be hidden from lenders who have a permissible purpose, and trying to conceal them does not improve a score or history at all.
Why D: Credit repair means disputing real errors on your reports and building better habits, like on-time payments and low balances, which gradually improves your credit score over time.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a deductible in health insurance?
A: The most the plan pays, in a year, for all your care
B: The amount you pay before the plan starts paying
C: The monthly premium that you pay to the insurer
D: A tax on medical care that patients pay each year
Why A: That describes an out-of-pocket maximum, the most you pay in a year, after which the plan covers covered care; a deductible is only the first portion you pay.
Why B: A deductible is the set amount you pay yourself each plan year for covered care before the insurer begins sharing costs through coinsurance or paying benefits.
Why C: The monthly premium is the regular payment that keeps coverage active, and you owe it whether or not you use care; the deductible is separate.
Why D: A deductible is not a tax; it is a cost-sharing term in the insurance contract, and the money goes to the providers of your care, not to the government.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A health plan has a $1,500 deductible and 20% coinsurance. After meeting the deductible, a $1,000 bill leaves what patient share?
Why A: The $1,000 bill is below the $1,500 deductible only if the deductible is unmet; the question says it is already met, so coinsurance applies instead of the full bill.
Why B: The $1,500 deductible is already paid and does not apply again, and a $1,000 bill cannot cost the patient more than the bill itself.
Why C: After the deductible is met, the patient pays 20% coinsurance: 0.20 x $1,000 = $200, and the insurer pays the remaining $800 of the bill.
Why D: $800 is the insurer's 80% share of the bill; the patient owes the other 20%, so 0.20 x $1,000 = $200 is the patient's share, not $800.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A renter's policy has a $500 deductible and $12,000 in coverage. Thieves steal $3,000 of items. What does the insurer pay?
Why A: The insurer pays the loss minus the deductible: $3,000 - $500 = $2,500, which is within the $12,000 coverage limit, so the full remainder is covered.
Why B: $3,000 would be paid only with no deductible; the $500 deductible comes out first, so the insurer pays $2,500 and the renter bears $500.
Why C: $500 is the deductible, the amount the renter pays, not what the insurer pays; the insurer covers the remaining $2,500 of the loss.
Why D: $12,000 is the policy's coverage limit, the maximum payout, not the amount paid; the insurer pays only the actual loss less the deductible.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is an exclusion in an insurance policy?
A: A situation the policy does not cover
B: A discount on the cost of the policy
C: A bonus payment from the insurance firm
D: A refund of premium at the end of term
Why A: An exclusion lists causes of loss or property the policy does not cover, such as floods in many homeowners policies, so the insurer pays nothing for them.
Why B: A discount lowers the price of the policy, but an exclusion does the opposite kind of job: it narrows what is covered and does not reduce premiums.
Why C: A bonus payment from the insurer is not an exclusion; exclusions limit coverage and never add money, so they cannot be a payout of any kind.
Why D: A refund of premium at the end of a term is a different feature; an exclusion limits what the insurer will pay on a claim and refunds nothing.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: Why should you read your insurance policy?
A: To make claims easier without reading it
B: Because it is entertaining to read at home
C: To understand what is and is not covered
D: To avoid paying premiums for the policy
Why A: Claims are not easier if you skip reading the policy; not knowing the terms often causes denied claims and unpleasant surprises when you need coverage.
Why B: Policies are dense legal documents that few people enjoy, and entertainment is not the reason to read them; the real reason is protecting yourself.
Why C: Reading shows which events, limits, deductibles and exclusions apply, so you know what is covered before you file a claim or decide to buy more coverage.
Why D: You still owe premiums to keep coverage in force; reading the policy does not remove them, though it may help you spot discounts or unneeded coverage.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: A person refuses to buy health insurance to save $300 a month, then faces a $40,000 hospital bill. What was the main error?
A: Buying too much insurance in this case
B: Not managing a large financial risk
C: Having a low deductible on the plan
D: Saving too much money for the future
Why A: The person bought no insurance, so buying too much is not the error; the problem was too little protection against a large and unpredictable cost.
Why B: Skipping insurance to save $300 a month left the person exposed to a $40,000 bill; insurance exists to transfer large, unlikely losses and protect finances.
Why C: The person had no plan at all, so a low deductible was not the issue; a lower deductible would actually have reduced the out-of-pocket cost.
Why D: Saving money is generally good, and the person did not save too much; the error was ignoring a major risk that savings of $300 a month could not cover.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a claim?
A: A monthly bill that the insurer sends to the holder
B: A tax return that you file with the IRS each year
C: A refund of a deductible, paid by the insurer at year end
D: A request to the insurer for payment for a covered loss
Why A: A monthly bill sent to the policyholder is a premium notice; a claim goes the other way, from the policyholder to the insurer, asking for payment.
Why B: A tax return is filed with the IRS to report income and has nothing to do with insurance; a claim is made to an insurer after a loss.
Why C: A refund of a deductible is not what a claim is; a claim is the request itself, and the deductible is normally subtracted from any payout instead.
Why D: A claim is the formal request a policyholder files with the insurer asking for payment or services after a covered loss such as an accident, theft or illness.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is the best first step after a car accident?
A: Make sure everyone is safe and call for help if needed
B: Argue about fault with the other driver at the scene of it
C: Post about it online before you call anyone for help
D: Leave the scene of the accident before help arrives
Why A: Safety comes first: check yourself and others for injuries and call 911 if anyone is hurt or the road is blocked, then exchange information and document the scene.
Why B: Arguing about fault at the scene wastes time, can escalate, and is not the insurers' job; stay calm, trade information, and let the insurers decide fault.
Why C: Posting online first can hurt your claim, since statements may be used against you, and calling for help for anyone injured is more urgent than posting.
Why D: Leaving the scene before help arrives can be hit-and-run in many states, a crime that can bring fines or jail and also jeopardize your insurance coverage.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is fraud in the context of money?
A: A discount on the price of goods
B: A fair trade between two parties
C: Deception to gain money or property
D: A legal contract signed by both sides
Why A: A discount lowers a price and involves no deception, so it is not fraud; fraud is dishonesty intended to take money or property unfairly from someone.
Why B: A fair trade is an honest exchange where both parties understand and agree, which is the opposite of fraud, where one side is deliberately misled.
Why C: Fraud is intentional deception to gain money or property, such as identity theft, false insurance claims or fake investment schemes, and it is a crime.
Why D: A legal contract signed by both sides is a valid agreement, not fraud, though a contract obtained through lies or false statements can be fraudulent.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: What is a data breach?
A: A bank holiday when all the branches are shut
B: Unauthorized access to personal or financial data
C: A system update that fixes bugs in a computer app
D: A password change that you make on a website
Why A: A bank holiday is a day when branches are closed and has nothing to do with data security; a breach is a security failure, not a closure.
Why B: A data breach happens when unauthorized people gain access to personal or financial data, such as card numbers or Social Security numbers, often through hacking.
Why C: A system update that fixes bugs is routine maintenance and in fact helps prevent breaches; it is not an unauthorized intrusion into your data.
Why D: Changing your own password is a protective step you take, not an attack; a breach is when someone else gets in without permission.
Source: DECA career cluster instructional areas (deca.org/career-clusters), 2026-27

Question: After a data breach, which action best protects your credit?
A: Share your information widely with other people online
