Why C: The estimate is recorded by debiting Bad Debt Expense and crediting Allowance for Doubtful Accounts, which matches the expected loss to the period of the sales without removing a specific account.
Why D: Debiting Receivable and crediting Bad Debt Expense would raise receivables and cut expense, the opposite of what an estimate of uncollectible accounts does to the books.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A specific customer account of $350 is written off under the allowance method. What is the effect on net receivables?
A: Goes to zero
B: No change
C: Rises by $350
D: Falls by $350
Why A: Net receivables do not fall to zero; writing off one $350 account only removes that account from both receivables and the allowance, leaving the net figure on the others unchanged.
Why B: Writing off $350 debits the allowance and credits Accounts Receivable by the same amount, so net receivables (receivables minus allowance) stay the same, and no change occurs.
Why C: Net receivables do not rise, because both Accounts Receivable and the allowance decrease by $350, which cancels out in the net figure on the balance sheet.
Why D: Net receivables would only fall by $350 under the direct write-off method; under the allowance method the write-off reduces both receivables and the allowance, so the net is unchanged.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the effect of writing off an account under the allowance method on net income?
A: Net income increases in the same period
B: Net income decreases by the write-off
C: No effect in the period of the write-off
D: Revenue decreases in the same period
Why A: Net income does not increase because of a write-off; the expense was already recognized when the allowance was estimated, and the write-off only moves balances on the balance sheet.
Why B: Net income does not decrease at write-off, because the bad debt expense was already recorded when the allowance was set up; the write-off just debits the allowance.
Why C: A write-off debits the Allowance and credits Accounts Receivable, both balance sheet accounts, so it has no effect on net income in the period of the write-off.
Why D: Revenue is not reduced by a write-off under the allowance method; revenue was recorded at the time of the sale, and the loss is handled through the allowance account instead.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A customer whose account was written off pays in full. What must the business do?
A: Record the cash as a new liability
B: Record revenue for the amount received
C: Ignore the payment from the customer
D: Reinstate the account, then record cash
Why A: The payment is cash received, not a loan or borrowing, so recording a new liability would be wrong; the business is recovering a receivable it had given up on earlier.
Why B: Revenue was already recorded at the original sale, so recording revenue again would double count it; the recovery just reinstates the receivable and records the cash collected.
Why C: Ignoring the payment would leave cash and the records wrong; the business must record the recovery, even though the account was earlier written off as uncollectible.
Why D: The business first reverses the write-off (debit Accounts Receivable, credit Allowance) and then records the collection (debit Cash, credit Accounts Receivable), keeping a full record of the customer's history.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a note receivable?
A: A written promise by the business to pay a lender
B: A customer's written promise to pay by a date
C: A reminder to the accounting team each month
D: A list of unpaid customer invoices to date
Why A: A written promise by the business to pay a lender is a note payable, a liability; a note receivable is a promise made to the business by someone else.
Why B: A note receivable is a customer's written promise to pay a specific sum, usually with interest, by a stated date, and it is an asset for the business that holds it.
Why C: A reminder to the accounting team has nothing to do with notes receivable; a note is a formal written promise to pay money, carrying a maturity date and an interest rate.
Why D: A list of unpaid customer invoices is an accounts receivable listing; a note receivable is a more formal written promise to pay, often with interest, signed by the customer.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the interest on a $5,000 note at 6% for one year?
Why A: Interest equals principal times rate times time: $5,000 times 0.06 times 1 year equals $300, which is the cost of borrowing the money for the year.
Why B: $5,300 is the maturity value, which is principal plus interest; the question asks for the interest alone, which is the $300 added on top of the $5,000 principal.
Why C: $3,000 would be 60 percent of $5,000, a decimal error; 6 percent as 0.06 gives $5,000 times 0.06, or $300 of interest for one year.
Why D: $30 would be 0.6 percent of $5,000, a decimal slip the other way; 6 percent of $5,000 is $300, ten times larger than this figure.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the interest on a $4,000 note at 9% for 6 months?
Why A: Interest is $4,000 times 9 percent times 6/12 of a year, which is $360 times one half, or $180 for the six-month period of the note.
Why B: $360 is a full year of interest at 9 percent on $4,000, but the note runs for only six months, so the interest is half that, or $180.
Why C: $36 would be 0.9 percent of $4,000, a decimal slip; 9 percent of $4,000 for a half year is $4,000 times 0.09 times 0.5, which equals $180.
Why D: $720 would be 18 percent of $4,000 for a full year, or 9 percent for two years; for six months the interest is only $180.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the maturity value of a $2,000 note with $100 of interest?
Why A: $100 is just the interest earned on the note; maturity value is the principal plus that interest, which is the total amount due at the end of the note term.
Why B: $1,900 subtracts the interest from the principal, but maturity value is principal plus interest, so it must be larger than $2,000, not smaller than the principal.
Why C: Maturity value equals principal plus interest, so $2,000 plus $100 equals $2,100, the total the borrower must repay on the due date of the note.
Why D: $2,000 is only the principal; maturity value also includes the $100 of interest, so the borrower pays $2,100 when the note matures, not just the original amount.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the entry on the day a business borrows $8,000 on a note payable?
A: Debit Notes Payable, credit Cash
B: Debit Cash, credit Notes Payable
C: Debit Interest Expense, credit Cash
D: Debit Cash, credit Sales Revenue
Why A: Debiting Notes Payable and crediting Cash would record repaying a note, not borrowing; on the day of borrowing, cash increases and a liability is created.
Why B: Borrowing on a note increases the asset Cash with a debit of $8,000 and increases the liability Notes Payable with a credit of $8,000 owed to the lender.
Why C: Interest Expense is recorded as time passes and interest accrues; on the day of borrowing no interest has yet been incurred, and no cash leaves the business.
Why D: Borrowed money is not revenue, so crediting Sales Revenue would overstate income; the credit should go to Notes Payable because the business must repay the loan later.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business issues a note and recognizes accrued interest at year end before paying it. Which account is credited?
A: Interest Revenue
B: Notes Receivable
C: Cash received
D: Interest Payable
Why A: Interest Revenue is income earned by a lender, but the business issued the note and owes interest, so it records an expense, not revenue, on the borrowing.
Why B: Notes Receivable is an asset for a lender holding a note; the issuer of the note owes interest and a liability, so crediting Notes Receivable would not make sense.
Why C: No cash is received or paid when interest is only accrued at year end, so the credit cannot go to Cash; it goes to a liability account instead.
Why D: The adjusting entry debits Interest Expense and credits Interest Payable, a liability, because the interest has been incurred during the year but not yet paid in cash.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a vendor?
A: A customer who buys from the firm monthly
B: The owner of the business and its shares
C: A business's supplier of goods or services
D: An employee who sells products in a shop
Why A: A customer buys from the firm, whereas a vendor sells to the firm; confusing them reverses the direction of the transaction between the two parties in a purchase.
Why B: The owner of the business and its shares is a proprietor or shareholder, not a vendor; a vendor is an outside party that supplies the business with goods or services.
Why C: A vendor is a supplier from whom the business buys goods or services, often on credit, creating an account payable until the vendor is paid in cash.
Why D: An employee who sells products is a salesperson, who works for the business; a vendor is an outside company or person that sells to the business.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a receiving report?
A: A bill for goods sent to a buyer
B: A record of goods ordered by us
C: A list of payments received
D: A record of goods that arrived
Why A: A bill for goods sent to a buyer is an invoice from the seller; a receiving report is created by the buyer's own receiving department on delivery.
Why B: A record of goods ordered by the buyer is a purchase order, which comes before delivery; a receiving report instead documents the goods that actually showed up.
Why C: A list of payments received is a cash receipts record or deposit listing; a receiving report relates to goods delivered to the buyer from a supplier.
Why D: A receiving report records the goods that actually arrived, with quantities and condition, and is compared with the purchase order and invoice before the bill is paid.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a three-way match?
A: Matching debits, credits and all balances
B: Comparing order, receiving report and invoice
C: Having three managers sign each check issued
D: Matching three customers with three invoices
Why A: Matching debits, credits and balances describes checking a trial balance, not the three-way match, which compares three specific purchasing documents before paying a vendor.
Why B: A three-way match compares the purchase order, the receiving report and the vendor invoice, so the company pays only for goods actually ordered and received at the agreed price.
Why C: Three signatures on each check would be an approval control, but a three-way match refers to three documents compared, not three managers signing off on a payment.
Why D: A three-way match compares purchasing documents, not customers; three customers matched with three invoices would be a receivables task unrelated to verifying a vendor's bill.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why should the person who approves invoices not be the one who signs checks?
A: It separates duties to cut fraud risk
B: It speeds up payment to the vendor
C: It is required by every bank by law
D: It makes the checks cheaper to print
Why A: Separation of duties stops one person from both approving and paying a bill, so a fake invoice would need a second person's cooperation, reducing the chance of fraud.
Why B: Splitting the work between two people tends to slow the process slightly, not speed it up; the point is control and fraud prevention, not faster payment.
Why C: Banks do not require this by law for every account; it is an internal control practice companies adopt to reduce errors and fraud, not a universal legal requirement.
Why D: Printing cost has nothing to do with who approves invoices and who signs checks; the reason is internal control, specifically separation of duties to reduce the risk of fraud.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An invoice shows 100 units billed, but 90 units arrived. What should accounts payable do?
A: Ignore the invoice and pay it in full later
B: Pay for the units received after resolving it
C: Pay for 110 units to be safe and keep the peace
D: Pay the full invoice now and ask for a fix
Why A: Ignoring the invoice would damage the vendor relationship and leave a real payable unresolved; the discrepancy should be handled promptly instead of being paid later without any follow up.
Why B: Only 90 units arrived, so the company should resolve the discrepancy with the vendor and pay for what was received, rather than pay for 100 units that were not delivered.
Why C: Paying for 110 units makes no sense because only 90 were received and 100 were billed; overpaying wastes company money and does not resolve the discrepancy at all.
Why D: Paying in full first means paying for 10 units never delivered, and getting the money back later is harder; the discrepancy should be settled before payment is made.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a debit balance in Accounts Payable usually indicate?
A: A new loan from the bank for the firm
B: Revenue earned but not yet billed
C: An overpayment or unapplied return
D: A normal amount owed to suppliers
Why A: A new bank loan would create a credit balance in a liability such as Notes Payable; a debit balance in Accounts Payable is unusual and means the company overpaid.
Why B: Revenue earned but not billed would be an accrued receivable or unbilled revenue, an asset; it has no connection to a debit balance in the Accounts Payable account.
Why C: Accounts Payable normally has a credit balance, so a debit balance usually means the company overpaid a supplier or a return or credit memo has not yet been applied.
Why D: A normal amount owed to suppliers shows up as a credit balance in Accounts Payable; a debit balance is the opposite and signals something unusual, such as an overpayment.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A business returns $200 of damaged goods bought on account. Which entry is correct?
A: Debit Cash and credit Accounts Payable for $200
B: Debit Purchases and credit Accounts Payable
C: Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Inventory for $200
D: Debit Accounts Payable; credit Purchases Returns
Why A: Debiting Cash would mean receiving money, but returning goods on account only cancels part of what is owed; crediting Accounts Payable would instead raise the liability, the wrong direction.
Why B: Debiting Purchases and crediting Accounts Payable records a new purchase on account, which increases what is owed, whereas a return reduces the liability and the purchases.
Why C: Accounts Receivable is what customers owe the business, so it does not apply to returning goods to a supplier; the debit should reduce Accounts Payable, the amount owed.
Why D: Returning goods bought on account reduces the liability, so debit Accounts Payable $200, and credit Purchases Returns and Allowances to reduce the cost of purchases by the same amount.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A customer returns $150 of goods bought on account. Which entry is correct?
A: Debit Sales Returns and Allowances, credit Accounts Receivable
B: Debit Accounts Receivable, credit Sales Returns and Allowances
C: Debit Cash and credit Accounts Receivable for the $150 amount
D: Debit Sales Revenue and credit Cash for the whole $150 amount
Why A: A customer return reduces revenue through the contra account Sales Returns and Allowances (debit) and reduces what the customer owes by crediting Accounts Receivable by $150.
Why B: Debiting Accounts Receivable would increase what the customer owes, and crediting Sales Returns would reduce the contra account, which is the reverse of what a return does.
Why C: The goods were bought on account, so no cash is refunded; crediting Cash is wrong, and the debit to Cash would also increase cash rather than reduce the receivable.
Why D: Debiting Sales Revenue directly and crediting Cash assumes a cash refund; the purchase was on account, so no cash is paid, and the contra account tracks returns separately.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A company has $60,000 in credit sales and $8,000 in the allowance for doubtful accounts after adjustment. Which statement is accurate?
A: The allowance reduces receivables on the balance sheet
B: The allowance increases receivables on the balance sheet
C: The allowance is a revenue account on the income report
D: The allowance shows on the income statement as revenue
Why A: The Allowance for Doubtful Accounts is a contra-asset, so it is subtracted from Accounts Receivable on the balance sheet, reducing receivables to the amount expected to be collected.
Why B: The allowance reduces receivables because it is a contra account with a credit balance; it does not increase them, so this statement has the effect backward.
Why C: The allowance is a balance sheet contra-asset, not a revenue account; the related Bad Debt Expense appears on the income statement, but the allowance itself does not.
Why D: Revenue appears on the income statement, but the allowance is a balance sheet account that reduces receivables; it is never reported as revenue by the business at all.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The aging method estimates uncollectibles at $4,200 and the allowance already has a $700 credit balance. What is the bad debt expense?
Why A: $4,200 is the target ending balance of the allowance, not the expense; the existing $700 credit balance already covers part of it, so the expense is smaller.
Why B: $4,900 adds the existing credit balance to the target, but the existing $700 reduces the amount needed; the expense is $4,200 minus $700, not the sum.
Why C: The aging method sets the ending allowance at $4,200, and with a $700 credit balance already there, the adjustment is $4,200 minus $700, which equals $3,500 of expense.
Why D: $700 is only the existing allowance balance before adjustment; the expense is the amount needed to bring it up to $4,200, which is $3,500, not $700.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The aging method estimates uncollectibles at $4,200 and the allowance has a $300 debit balance. What is the bad debt expense?
Why A: $300 is only the existing debit balance in the allowance account; it ignores the $4,200 target, so the adjustment would be far too small to reach the needed ending balance.
Why B: Under the aging method the allowance must end with a $4,200 credit. Starting from a $300 debit, the adjustment is $4,200 + $300 = $4,500 of bad debt expense.
Why C: $4,200 is the desired ending credit balance of the allowance, not the expense; it forgets that the $300 debit balance must first be offset before the target is reached.
Why D: $3,900 subtracts the debit balance ($4,200 - $300) when it should be added; a debit balance means the adjustment must be larger than the target, not smaller.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a credit sale?
A: A sale made at a big discount
B: A sale paid for in cash at the till
C: A sale of a business's credit rating
D: A sale where payment is due later
Why A: A discount sale lowers the price but says nothing about when the buyer pays; a credit sale is defined by delayed payment, whether or not any discount is given.
Why B: A sale paid for in cash at the register is a cash sale, since the money is received immediately and no account receivable is created for the seller.
Why C: A business's credit rating is not something it sells; a credit sale is an ordinary sale of goods or services where the customer agrees to pay later.
Why D: In a credit sale the seller delivers goods now and the buyer pays later, so the seller records an account receivable until the customer pays, often within 30 days.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a statement of account?
A: An invoice for one purchase made by a buyer
B: A list of the business's debts to its suppliers
C: A summary of the business's profit for the year
D: A customer summary of invoices and balance due
Why A: An invoice bills a buyer for a single purchase. A statement of account is broader, summarizing several invoices, payments and the balance still owed over a period.
Why B: A list of what the business owes its suppliers is an accounts payable schedule; a statement of account is sent to customers and shows what they owe the business.
Why C: A summary of yearly profit is an income statement; a statement of account tracks one customer's invoices, payments and balance, not the firm's overall earnings.
Why D: A statement of account is sent to a customer, usually monthly, listing invoices, payments and credits and the balance due, which prompts timely payment and helps resolve disputes.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is factoring of receivables?
A: Lending money to customers on credit
B: Selling receivables for quick cash
C: Postponing payment to suppliers
D: Writing off receivables as expenses
Why A: Lending money to customers on credit is simply extending credit, which creates receivables; factoring is the opposite move, where the business sells those existing receivables to someone else.
Why B: In factoring, a business sells its accounts receivable to a factor at a discount and gets cash right away, trading some of the amount for faster liquidity.
Why C: Postponing payment to suppliers is stretching accounts payable, a way of managing payables; factoring deals with receivables owed by customers, not bills owed to vendors.
Why D: Writing off receivables treats uncollectible accounts as bad debt expense and removes them; factoring instead sells good receivables for cash, so no loss of the whole balance is recorded.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which ratio measures how many times receivables are collected during a year?
A: Debt ratio of a firm
B: The gross margin
C: Receivables turnover
D: The current ratio
Why A: The debt ratio compares total liabilities to total assets and shows how much of the firm is financed by borrowing; it says nothing about collecting receivables.
Why B: Gross margin is gross profit divided by net sales, a profitability measure showing what percent of each sales dollar remains after cost of goods sold, not a collection measure.
Why C: Receivables turnover equals net credit sales divided by average accounts receivable; a higher number means customers pay faster and the firm collects its credit sales more often each year.
Why D: The current ratio divides current assets by current liabilities to gauge short-term liquidity; it does not show how many times receivables are collected during the year.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Net credit sales are $480,000 and average receivables are $60,000. What is the receivables turnover?
A: 8 times
B: 80 times
C: 0.125 times
D: 420 times
Why A: Receivables turnover is net credit sales divided by average receivables: $480,000 / $60,000 = 8 times, meaning receivables are collected about eight times per year.
Why B: 80 times would result from a decimal slip, such as dividing $480,000 by $6,000; the correct division of $480,000 by $60,000 gives 8, not 80.
Why C: 0.125 times comes from inverting the formula ($60,000 / $480,000); turnover must divide sales by receivables, so the answer is 8 and not its reciprocal.
Why D: 420 times is not produced by any valid step; subtracting ($480,000 - $60,000 = $420,000) misuses the formula, which requires division to get 8 times.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If receivables turnover is 8, about how many days does it take to collect, using 360 days?
A: 90 days
B: 45 days
C: 2,880 days
D: 8 days
Why A: 90 days would be correct only if turnover were 4 (360 / 4); with turnover of 8 the collection period is half as long, so it cannot be 90.
Why B: Days to collect equals days in the year divided by turnover: 360 / 8 = 45 days, so customers take about a month and a half on average to pay.
Why C: 2,880 days comes from multiplying 360 by 8 instead of dividing; days to collect uses division, and a collection period longer than a year would make no sense here.
Why D: 8 days just repeats the turnover figure as if it were days; turnover counts times per year, and converting it to days requires dividing 360 by 8.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a remittance advice?
A: A note showing which invoices a payment covers
B: A bill for goods delivered to a buyer firm
C: A request to buy goods from a vendor firm
D: A report on slow-paying customers and bills overall
Why A: A remittance advice accompanies a payment and tells the seller which invoices are being paid, so the seller can apply the cash to the correct customer accounts.
Why B: A bill for delivered goods is an invoice; a remittance advice comes later from the buyer with a payment, identifying which invoices that payment settles.
Why C: A request to buy goods from a vendor is a purchase order; a remittance advice follows the purchase and delivery, accompanying the payment sent to the seller.
Why D: A report on slow-paying customers is an accounts receivable aging report used internally; a remittance advice is a payment document, not a collection analysis.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why do businesses offer early-payment discounts?
A: To raise the invoice total for the seller
B: To delay recording the sale of goods to buyers
C: To collect cash sooner and reduce bad debts
D: To avoid issuing invoices to the buyers
Why A: Early-payment discounts such as 2/10, n/30 reduce the amount the seller collects, so they lower rather than raise the invoice total; the benefit is faster cash.
Why B: Offering a discount has no effect on when a sale is recorded; revenue is recognized when goods are delivered, and the discount only influences when the customer pays.
Why C: Discounts motivate customers to pay within the discount period, which speeds cash collection, improves cash flow and lowers the risk that accounts become uncollectible bad debts.
Why D: Businesses still issue invoices for credit sales; the discount terms are printed on the invoice itself, so a discount cannot be a way to skip invoicing.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does an income statement show?
A: Assets, liabilities and equity on one date
B: Cash received and paid during a given period
C: Changes in the owner's capital only in a year
D: Revenue, expenses and net income for a period
Why A: Assets, liabilities and equity on a single date describe the balance sheet, a snapshot of financial position, not the income statement, which covers a period of time.
Why B: Cash received and paid during a period is the statement of cash flows; the income statement uses accrual accounting and reports earnings, not cash movements.
Why C: Changes in the owner's capital over a year appear on the statement of owner's equity; the income statement only supplies net income as one input to that statement.
Why D: The income statement lists revenues, subtracts expenses, and reports net income or net loss for a period, such as a month or year, showing how profitable the firm was.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a balance sheet show?
A: Assets, liabilities and equity on one date
B: Cash inflows and outflows for the period
C: Only the owner's withdrawals from the firm
D: Revenue and expenses over a period of one year
Why A: The balance sheet reports assets, liabilities and owner's equity at one point in time, following the equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity, showing financial position on that date.
Why B: Cash inflows and outflows for a period are shown on the statement of cash flows; a balance sheet only gives the cash balance at a single date.
Why C: Owner's withdrawals are reported on the statement of owner's equity, which reduces capital; the balance sheet shows much more than withdrawals, including all assets and liabilities.
Why D: Revenue and expenses over a year belong on the income statement; the balance sheet is a snapshot on one date rather than a summary of a whole period.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a statement of cash flows show?
A: Profit earned during the period
B: Cash received and paid in a period
C: Debts due to suppliers at year end
D: The value of all assets on one date
Why A: Profit earned during the period is reported on the income statement; the cash flow statement can differ from profit because it tracks actual cash instead of accrued revenue and expense.
Why B: The statement of cash flows reports cash received and paid during a period, grouped into operating, investing and financing activities, explaining the change in cash from start to end.
Why C: Debts due to suppliers at year end are accounts payable, a liability listed on the balance sheet, not an item the cash flow statement is designed to present.
Why D: The value of all assets on one date is shown on the balance sheet; the cash flow statement covers a period and focuses on cash movement only.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the statement of owner's equity show?
A: The total cash in the bank account
B: The company's sales by product line
C: The list of unpaid bills owed by us
D: Changes in owner's equity in a period
Why A: Total cash in the bank is a single asset listed on the balance sheet; the statement of owner's equity reports how the owner's total stake changed, not one account balance.
Why B: Sales by product line is a detail found in sales records or management reports; the statement of owner's equity tracks capital, net income and withdrawals instead.
Why C: Unpaid bills owed by the business are accounts payable, liabilities shown on the balance sheet; the statement of owner's equity concerns the owner's interest in the firm.
Why D: The statement of owner's equity starts with beginning capital, adds investments and net income, subtracts withdrawals, and ends with ending capital, showing how equity changed in the period.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which statement is dated 'for the year ended December 31'?
A: Trial balance
B: Chart of accounts
C: Income statement
D: Balance sheet
Why A: A trial balance lists account balances at a single date to check that debits equal credits; it is dated 'as of' that date, not for a year.
Why B: A chart of accounts is just a numbered list of the accounts a firm uses; it carries no dollar amounts or period, so it has no 'year ended' heading.
Why C: The income statement covers a span of time, so it is headed 'for the year ended December 31'; it reports revenue and expenses earned during that whole period.
Why D: The balance sheet is a snapshot at one moment, so it is dated 'as of December 31', not 'for the year ended'; a period heading belongs to flow statements.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which statement is dated 'as of December 31'?
A: Balance sheet
B: Equity report
C: Cash flow report
D: Income statement
Why A: The balance sheet shows financial position at one moment, so its heading reads 'as of December 31'; assets, liabilities and equity are balances on that single date.
Why B: An equity report such as the statement of owner's equity covers a period, so its heading says 'for the year ended', because it explains changes over time.
Why C: A cash flow report covers a period and explains how cash changed, so it is headed 'for the year ended December 31' rather than 'as of'.
Why D: The income statement summarizes revenue and expenses over a span of time, so its heading says 'for the year ended December 31', not 'as of'.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are current assets?
A: Assets that cannot be sold at any time as a rule
B: Assets used or turned to cash within a year
C: Assets the owner uses at home each day
D: Assets expected to last over ten years
Why A: Current assets are meant to be turned into cash soon, so they can usually be sold readily; assets that cannot be sold at all are not described as current.
Why B: Current assets such as cash, receivables and inventory are expected to be used up or converted into cash within one year or one operating cycle, whichever is longer.
Why C: Whether the owner uses an item at home has no bearing on classification; current assets are defined by how quickly they convert to cash in the business, not personal use.
Why D: Assets expected to last over ten years, like buildings or land, are long-term assets; current assets are expected to be converted or used within a year.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What are current liabilities?
A: Equity owed to the owner
B: Assets to be sold soon
C: Debts due within one year
D: Debts due after ten years
Why A: Equity owed to the owner is owner's equity, which is the owner's claim on assets and is not a liability; current liabilities are debts owed to outsiders.
Why B: Assets to be sold soon are current assets, which are resources the business owns; current liabilities are obligations the business owes to others.
Why C: Current liabilities are obligations due within one year or the operating cycle, such as accounts payable, wages payable and short-term notes, paid with current assets.
Why D: Debts due after ten years are long-term liabilities; current liabilities are those the business must pay within the next year, so the time frame here is far too long.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which of these is a long-term liability?
A: Taxes payable due next month
B: Wages payable next week
C: Accounts payable next month
D: A mortgage due in 20 years
Why A: Taxes payable due next month must be paid within a year, so they are current liabilities, not long-term; long-term liabilities are due more than a year away.
Why B: Wages payable next week are due almost immediately, making them a current liability; they will be paid long before the one-year cutoff for long-term debt.
Why C: Accounts payable due next month are short-term trade debts, classified as current liabilities because they are due well within one year.
Why D: A mortgage due in 20 years is repayable far beyond one year, so it is a long-term liability, though the portion due in the next year is current.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which of these is a plant (fixed) asset?
A: Cash on hand
B: Receivables
C: Stock on hand
D: Delivery truck
Why A: Cash on hand is the most liquid current asset, ready to spend at once; plant assets are long-lived items used to operate the business, not cash.
Why B: Receivables are amounts customers owe and are usually collected within a year, so they are current assets rather than long-lived plant assets.
Why C: Stock on hand is inventory held for sale, a current asset expected to be sold soon; plant assets are used in operations rather than resold.
Why D: A delivery truck is a tangible, long-lived asset used in operations over many years, not for resale, so it is a plant (fixed) asset that is depreciated.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Willow Florist has revenues of $84,000 and expenses of $61,500. What is its net income?
Why A: Net income equals revenues minus expenses: $84,000 - $61,500 = $22,500, so the florist earned a profit because revenues exceeded expenses.
Why B: $145,500 comes from adding revenue and expenses ($84,000 + $61,500); net income requires subtracting expenses from revenue, so adding gives a meaningless figure.
Why C: $84,000 is the revenue figure alone; net income is what remains after subtracting the $61,500 of expenses, which leaves $22,500.
Why D: $61,500 is the total of expenses, not income; subtracting it from the $84,000 of revenue gives the real net income of $22,500.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: The owner had beginning capital of $30,000, net income of $12,000 and withdrawals of $5,000. What is ending capital?
Why A: $42,000 adds net income but forgets to subtract withdrawals ($30,000 + $12,000); the $5,000 the owner took out must reduce ending capital.
Why B: Ending capital = beginning capital + net income - withdrawals: $30,000 + $12,000 - $5,000 = $37,000, because income raises equity and withdrawals lower it.
Why C: $47,000 adds the withdrawals instead of subtracting them ($30,000 + $12,000 + $5,000); withdrawals reduce the owner's capital, so they cannot be added.
Why D: $25,000 subtracts both income and withdrawals from capital, treating net income as a decrease; net income increases capital, so it must be added.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Total assets are $95,000 and total liabilities are $35,000. What is owner's equity?
Why A: $95,000 is total assets, which equals liabilities plus equity; to find equity you must subtract the $35,000 of liabilities from it.
Why B: $35,000 is the amount of liabilities, which are outsiders' claims on the assets; owner's equity is what remains after subtracting them from assets.
Why C: From the accounting equation, Equity = Assets - Liabilities: $95,000 - $35,000 = $60,000, which is the owner's residual claim on the business assets.
Why D: $130,000 adds assets and liabilities ($95,000 + $35,000); the equation requires subtraction, because liabilities are claims against assets, not additional assets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Where do owner's withdrawals appear?
A: On the statement of owner's equity
B: On the trial balance as revenue
C: On the income statement as an expense
D: On the balance sheet as an asset
Why A: Withdrawals are a reduction in the owner's capital, so they are listed on the statement of owner's equity alongside net income and investments.
Why B: Withdrawals are not revenue; revenue is income earned from selling goods or services, while withdrawals are the owner taking assets out of the business.
Why C: Withdrawals are not an expense because they are not a cost of earning revenue; they are a distribution to the owner and do not reduce net income.
Why D: Withdrawals reduce assets and equity, and are never an asset themselves; the balance sheet shows only the resulting lower capital balance.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In what order are assets listed on a classified balance sheet?
A: Alphabetically by account name
B: By size, largest account first
C: By the age of the asset's use
D: By liquidity, most liquid first
Why A: Alphabetical order would make cash, equipment and inventory appear randomly; the balance sheet follows a set order based on liquidity instead of account names.
Why B: Listing by size would shuffle assets differently every year; classified balance sheets follow a consistent order by liquidity, not by dollar amount.
Why C: The age of an asset's use is not a classification rule; assets are ordered by how quickly they can be converted to cash.
Why D: Assets are listed in order of liquidity, from cash and receivables to inventory, then plant assets, so readers can quickly see what is easiest to turn into cash.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a multi-step income statement show that a single-step one does not?
A: The trial balance totals for the full year
B: Gross profit and operating income subtotals
C: The owner's capital balance at period end
D: Cash flows from operations and investing
Why A: Trial balance totals are an internal check of debit and credit equality and are not part of either income statement format; they are not a subtotal on the statement.
Why B: A multi-step income statement shows subtotals such as gross profit (sales minus cost of goods sold) and operating income, while a single-step one lumps all expenses together.
Why C: The owner's capital balance at period end appears on the statement of owner's equity and balance sheet; neither income statement format reports it.
Why D: Cash flows from operations and investing appear on the statement of cash flows; both income statement formats show revenue and expense, not cash movements.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How is gross profit calculated?
A: Net sales minus all expenses paid
B: Net sales plus the cost of goods sold
C: Net sales minus cost of goods sold
D: Assets minus liabilities of the firm
Why A: Net sales minus all expenses paid gives net income, not gross profit; gross profit subtracts only the cost of goods sold before operating expenses.
Why B: Adding cost of goods sold to net sales would inflate the figure; gross profit is what remains after cost of goods sold is subtracted, not added.
Why C: Gross profit equals net sales minus cost of goods sold; it shows how much is left from sales to cover operating expenses and provide profit.
Why D: Assets minus liabilities is owner's equity, a balance sheet concept; gross profit is an income statement measure based on sales and cost of goods sold.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Net sales are $200,000 and cost of goods sold is $130,000. What is gross profit?
Why A: $200,000 is the net sales figure alone; gross profit must subtract the $130,000 cost of goods sold from it, leaving $70,000.
Why B: $330,000 adds sales and cost of goods sold ($200,000 + $130,000); gross profit requires subtraction, because the cost of goods sold reduces what sales leave over.
Why C: Gross profit = net sales - cost of goods sold: $200,000 - $130,000 = $70,000, which is available to cover operating expenses and produce net income.
Why D: $130,000 is the cost of goods sold, an expense; gross profit is the amount left after subtracting it from the $200,000 of net sales.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How is net sales calculated?
A: Gross sales minus the cost of all goods sold overall
B: Gross sales less returns, allowances, discounts
C: Gross sales plus sales returns and discounts
D: Cost of goods sold plus all expenses paid
Why A: Subtracting the cost of all goods sold gives gross profit, not net sales; net sales only adjusts gross sales for returns, allowances and discounts.
Why B: Net sales = gross sales - sales returns - sales allowances - sales discounts, which reduces total sales to what the company can actually keep from customers.
Why C: Adding returns and discounts would raise net sales above gross sales; those items are deductions from gross sales because they lower the revenue earned.
Why D: Cost of goods sold plus expenses paid is a total of costs, not a sales figure; net sales is calculated from sales, not from expenses.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Gross sales are $90,000, returns are $3,000 and discounts are $2,000. What are net sales?
Why A: Net sales = gross sales - returns - discounts: $90,000 - $3,000 - $2,000 = $85,000, since returns and discounts reduce the revenue the firm keeps.
Why B: $95,000 adds the returns and discounts to gross sales; they are contra-revenue deductions that reduce sales, so adding them overstates net sales.
Why C: $87,000 subtracts only the $3,000 of returns and forgets the $2,000 of discounts ($90,000 - $3,000); both must be deducted from gross sales.
Why D: $90,000 is the gross sales figure before any adjustment; net sales must reflect the $3,000 of returns and $2,000 of discounts, giving $85,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which financial statement would a lender most likely study to judge the ability to repay a loan?
A: Chart of accounts, a list of accounts
B: The year-end worksheet for adjustments
C: Source documents only, such as receipts
D: Balance sheet and cash flow statement
Why A: A chart of accounts is only a list of account names and numbers; it has no dollar amounts that would show whether a borrower can repay.
Why B: The worksheet is an internal tool for preparing adjustments and is not a formal statement for outsiders, so lenders look at final statements instead.
Why C: Source documents such as receipts support individual entries but do not summarize financial strength; lenders need statements that show the overall position and cash.
Why D: Lenders study the balance sheet for assets, debt and liquidity and the cash flow statement for cash generated, which together indicate whether loan payments can be met.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is working capital?
A: Total assets minus total liabilities
B: Current assets minus current liabilities
C: Cash plus fixed assets of the firm now
D: Revenue minus expenses for the whole year
Why A: Total assets minus total liabilities is owner's equity (net worth); working capital looks only at short-term items, not the entire balance sheet.
Why B: Working capital = current assets - current liabilities, which measures the funds available to meet day-to-day obligations; a positive amount indicates good short-term liquidity.
Why C: Cash plus fixed assets mixes a liquid and a long-term asset and ignores liabilities; working capital is calculated from current assets and current liabilities only.
Why D: Revenue minus expenses is net income, a profit measure for a period; working capital is a balance sheet measure of short-term financial strength.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Current assets are $48,000 and current liabilities are $30,000. What is the current ratio?
C: 18 to 1
D: 2 to 1
Why A: Current ratio = current assets / current liabilities: $48,000 / $30,000 = 1.6 to 1, meaning $1.60 of current assets for each $1 of short-term debt.
Why B: 0.63 to 1 inverts the ratio ($30,000 / $48,000); the current ratio puts current assets on top, so the correct answer is 1.6 to 1.
Why C: 18 to 1 comes from subtracting ($48,000 - $30,000 = $18,000) and mislabeling the difference as a ratio; the current ratio requires division.
Why D: 2 to 1 would need current assets of $60,000 against $30,000 of liabilities; with $48,000 the division gives 1.6, which is a little lower.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: A current ratio below 1 suggests what?
A: The business is highly profitable now
B: The business has far too much cash
C: It may struggle to pay short-term debts
D: The business has no debts at all to pay
Why A: High profitability is not shown by the current ratio; a ratio below 1 means current liabilities exceed current assets, a liquidity concern rather than a sign of profit.
Why B: Too much cash would push the current ratio well above 1, not below; a ratio under 1 indicates a shortage of liquid resources.
Why C: A current ratio below 1 means current liabilities exceed current assets, so the firm may have trouble paying bills due within the year without borrowing or selling assets.
Why D: A ratio below 1 requires current liabilities larger than current assets, so the business certainly has debts to pay; having none would make the ratio undefined.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Current assets of $20,000 include inventory of $8,000. Current liabilities are $10,000. What is the quick ratio?
Why A: 2.0 to 1 is the current ratio ($20,000 / $10,000), which counts inventory; the quick ratio excludes inventory and so is lower than this.
Why B: 0.8 to 1 would require quick assets of only $8,000, which is the inventory amount; the quick ratio uses current assets after removing inventory, not inventory itself.
Why C: 0.5 to 1 does not match any correct step; quick assets are $20,000 - $8,000 = $12,000, which divided by $10,000 gives more than 1.
Why D: Quick ratio = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities: ($20,000 - $8,000) / $10,000 = 1.2 to 1, a stricter test of liquidity than the current ratio.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does the debt ratio measure?
A: How quickly inventory is sold each year
B: The share of assets financed by debt
C: Cash available for emergencies only
D: The share of sales kept as profit
Why A: How quickly inventory is sold each year is measured by inventory turnover, an efficiency ratio; the debt ratio is a solvency measure based on liabilities and assets.
Why B: The debt ratio equals total liabilities divided by total assets, showing what share of the firm's assets is financed by creditors rather than by the owner.
Why C: Cash available for emergencies is a liquidity concern measured by cash or current ratios; the debt ratio deals with the financing structure of all assets.
Why D: The share of sales kept as profit is the profit margin (net income / net sales); the debt ratio relates debt to assets, not profit to sales.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Liabilities are $40,000 and assets are $100,000. What is the debt ratio?
Why A: 14% does not come from any correct calculation with these numbers; the debt ratio divides liabilities by assets, $40,000 / $100,000, which is 40%.
Why B: 60% is the equity share of assets ($60,000 / $100,000), the complement of the debt ratio; the question asks for the share financed by liabilities.
Why C: Debt ratio = total liabilities / total assets: $40,000 / $100,000 = 40%, meaning creditors have financed 40 cents of every dollar of assets.
Why D: 250% results from inverting the ratio ($100,000 / $40,000 = 2.5); the debt ratio puts liabilities on top and cannot exceed 100% unless equity is negative.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is profit margin?
A: Cost of goods sold over assets
B: Assets divided by liabilities
C: Gross sales divided by net income
D: Net income divided by net sales
Why A: Cost of goods sold over assets is not a standard profitability ratio; profit margin compares net income to net sales, showing profit per dollar of sales.
Why B: Assets divided by liabilities is a solvency comparison of what the firm owns against what it owes; it says nothing about profit relative to sales.
Why C: Gross sales divided by net income is inverted and uses the wrong sales figure; profit margin uses net income on top and net sales on the bottom.
Why D: Profit margin = net income / net sales, showing how many cents of profit the company keeps from each dollar of sales; higher margins signal better cost control.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Net income is $18,000 and net sales are $240,000. What is the profit margin?
Why A: Profit margin = net income / net sales: $18,000 / $240,000 = 0.075 = 7.5%, so the company keeps 7.5 cents of profit per dollar of sales.
Why B: 75% comes from a decimal error; $18,000 / $240,000 is 0.075, which is 7.5%, so moving the decimal one place too far gives a wildly high margin.
Why C: 0.75% shifts the decimal the other way; 0.075 as a percent is 7.5%, not 0.75%, so the margin is ten times larger than this.
Why D: 13.3% would be $18,000 / $135,000 or similar; it does not match $240,000 of net sales, which gives 7.5% when divided into $18,000.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Net income is $18,000 and average owner's equity is $90,000. What is return on equity?
Why A: Return on equity = net income / average owner's equity: $18,000 / $90,000 = 0.20 = 20%, so each dollar of equity earned 20 cents of profit.
Why B: 5% results from inverting the figures ($90,000 / $18,000 = 5 or 500%) and then misreading it; ROE divides income by equity, giving 20%.
Why C: 72% does not result from any correct step; dividing $18,000 by $90,000 gives 0.20, so a figure of 72% would require far larger net income.
Why D: 500% inverts the formula ($90,000 / $18,000 = 5); return on equity places net income on top, and the correct result is 20%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Cost of goods sold is $150,000 and average inventory is $25,000. What is inventory turnover?
A: 175 times
B: 0.17 times
C: 6 times
D: 125 times
Why A: 175 times comes from adding $150,000 and $25,000; inventory turnover divides cost of goods sold by average inventory, which gives 6 times.
Why B: 0.17 times is the inverse ($25,000 / $150,000); turnover puts cost of goods sold on top, so the correct result is much larger at 6.
Why C: Inventory turnover = cost of goods sold / average inventory: $150,000 / $25,000 = 6 times, meaning inventory is sold and replaced six times a year.
Why D: 125 times comes from subtracting ($150,000 - $25,000 = $125,000) and calling it a ratio; turnover requires dividing, which yields 6 times.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: If inventory turnover is 6, about how many days does inventory last, using 360 days?
A: 30 days
B: 6 days
C: 2,160 days
D: 60 days
Why A: 30 days would correspond to a turnover of 12 (360 / 12); with a turnover of 6, the days are doubled, so 30 is too low.
Why B: 6 days repeats the turnover figure as if it were days; turnover counts times per year, and days are found by dividing 360 by 6.
Why C: 2,160 days multiplies 360 by 6 instead of dividing; days in inventory uses 360 / turnover, and a period over 2,000 days makes no sense.
Why D: Days in inventory = 360 / turnover = 360 / 6 = 60 days, so on average goods sit about two months before being sold.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a high inventory turnover usually suggest?
A: The company has too much debt
B: Goods are selling quickly
C: Goods are not selling
D: The company is losing money
Why A: Heavy debt is shown by the debt ratio, not by inventory turnover; a high turnover tells about sales speed of goods, not how the firm is financed.
Why B: A high inventory turnover means stock sells and is replaced quickly, which usually signals strong demand, efficient purchasing and less money tied up in inventory.
Why C: Goods that are not selling would produce a low turnover, since inventory sits unsold; a high number indicates the reverse.
Why D: Losing money is measured by net income, not turnover; fast-selling goods can still be unprofitable, but a high turnover alone does not suggest it.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which section of the cash flow statement includes cash from selling goods and paying wages?
A: Operating activities
B: Investing activities
C: Equity activities
D: Financing activities
Why A: Operating activities cover the day-to-day cash effects of running the business, including cash from customers and payments for wages, rent and suppliers.
Why B: Investing activities involve buying or selling long-term assets such as equipment, land and investments, not routine sales and payroll.
Why C: 'Equity activities' is not a section of the cash flow statement; the three sections are operating, investing and financing.
Why D: Financing activities involve raising or repaying funds through loans, stock issues, dividends and owner withdrawals, not cash from sales or wage payments.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Buying a new delivery van for cash appears in which section of the cash flow statement?
A: Operating activities
B: Financing activities
C: No section at all
D: Investing activities
Why A: Operating activities cover routine sales and expenses; a delivery van is a long-term asset, so buying it is not an operating cash flow.
Why B: Financing activities involve borrowing, repaying debt and owner or stockholder transactions; paying cash to buy a van is a purchase of an asset instead.
Why C: Every cash transaction appears somewhere; a purchase of equipment is reported in a specific section of the statement, so it cannot be left out.
Why D: Purchases of long-term assets like vans, equipment and buildings are cash outflows classified under investing activities, as are the proceeds from selling such assets.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Borrowing money from a bank appears in which section of the cash flow statement?
A: Revenue activities
B: Financing activities
C: Operating activities
D: Investing activities
Why A: 'Revenue activities' is not a section of the cash flow statement; the sections are operating, investing and financing, and a bank loan is not revenue.
Why B: Borrowing from a bank is a way of raising funds, so the cash received is reported in financing activities, along with stock issues, loan repayments and dividends.
Why C: Operating activities cover cash from sales and payments for expenses; a loan is a source of funds, not a result of everyday business operations.
Why D: Investing activities involve buying or selling long-term assets, not obtaining loans; borrowing from a bank is a financing source of cash.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which of the following is a non-cash expense that is added back on the operating section under the indirect method?
A: Wages paid
B: Rent paid
C: Depreciation
D: Inventory buying
Why A: Wages paid are a cash expense, so no add-back is needed; the indirect method adds back only expenses that reduced net income without using cash.
Why B: Rent paid is paid in cash, so it has already reduced operating cash; it is not a non-cash item that must be added back.
Why C: Depreciation reduces net income but involves no cash outflow in the period, so the indirect method adds it back to net income to find cash from operations.
Why D: Buying inventory uses cash, and it is an actual cash payment affecting working capital, not a non-cash expense that gets added back.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Net income is $20,000, depreciation is $4,000 and accounts receivable increased by $3,000. What is cash from operations under the indirect method?
Why A: $13,000 subtracts depreciation and receivables ($20,000 - $4,000 - $3,000); depreciation is a non-cash expense that must be added back, not subtracted.
Why B: $27,000 adds the $3,000 receivable increase to net income plus depreciation; a rise in receivables means sales were not yet collected, so it should be subtracted.
Why C: $23,000 is net income of $20,000 plus the $3,000 receivables increase, which wrongly adds the increase and leaves out the $4,000 depreciation add-back; an increase in receivables must be subtracted because it ties up cash.
Why D: Net income $20,000 + depreciation $4,000 - increase in receivables $3,000 = $21,000, because depreciation uses no cash and uncollected sales are not yet cash.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is the purpose of the notes to the financial statements?
A: To record the daily transactions
B: To show the owner's private opinions
C: To explain methods and add detail
D: To replace the financial statements
Why A: Recording daily transactions is the job of journals and ledgers; notes are added to the finished statements to explain and expand on them.
Why B: Notes are factual disclosures required by accounting standards, not personal opinions of the owner, so they do not exist to share private views.
Why C: Notes to the financial statements explain accounting methods, such as depreciation and inventory policies, and give additional detail like debt terms and contingencies.
Why D: Notes supplement the statements and do not replace them; the balance sheet, income statement and other statements are still required.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Who are external users of financial statements?
A: The company's own managers only
B: Investors, lenders and agencies
C: Only the company's customers
D: The company's bookkeepers only
Why A: A company's managers are internal users who see detailed reports; external users are outside parties that rely on the published statements.
Why B: Investors, lenders and government agencies are outside the company and rely on its published statements to make decisions, which makes them external users.
Why C: Customers can be external users, but they are not the only ones; investors, lenders and regulators also use published statements.
Why D: Bookkeepers work for the company and use detailed records daily, making them internal users, not external ones.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which report would a manager use inside the company but not publish?
A: A budget variance report
B: A personal tax return
C: An audited balance sheet
D: A report to shareholders
Why A: A budget variance report compares planned and actual results and is used by managers for control, so it stays internal and is not published.
Why B: A personal tax return belongs to an individual and is not a company report; it is filed with the government, not used by managers internally.
Why C: An audited balance sheet is a formal statement meant for outside users such as investors and lenders, so it is published, not kept internal.
Why D: A report to shareholders is prepared for owners outside management and is typically published, so it is an external rather than an internal report.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is horizontal analysis?
A: Adding all accounts side by side in a row
B: Comparing two companies in the same year
C: Comparing financial data across periods
D: Comparing items to total sales in one year
Why A: Adding accounts side by side in a row describes simple totaling, not analysis; horizontal analysis compares the same item between different periods.
Why B: Comparing two companies in the same year is a comparison between firms (benchmarking); horizontal analysis follows one company across periods.
Why C: Horizontal analysis compares financial data across periods, showing dollar and percent changes from one year to the next, and reveals trends in sales, expenses and profit.
Why D: Comparing items to total sales within one year is vertical analysis (common-size), which expresses each item as a percent of a base figure.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is vertical analysis?
A: Adding up all the assets of the firm today
B: Comparing each item over several years' data overall
C: Listing items from top to bottom on a page
D: Showing each item as a percent of a base figure
Why A: Adding all assets gives a total, not an analysis; vertical analysis expresses each item as a percent of a base figure in a single period.
Why B: Comparing items over several years is horizontal analysis, which looks at changes across periods; vertical analysis stays within a single period.
Why C: Vertical analysis refers to percentages of a base figure, not how the items are arranged on the page from top to bottom.
Why D: Vertical analysis shows each item as a percent of a base, such as net sales on the income statement or total assets on the balance sheet.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Sales rose from $200,000 to $230,000. What is the percentage change?
A: 85% increase
B: 15% increase
C: 30% increase
D: 13% increase
Why A: 85% is not the change; the increase is $30,000 and must be divided by the starting figure of $200,000, which gives 15%.
Why B: Percentage change = (new - old) / old = ($230,000 - $200,000) / $200,000 = 0.15 = 15%, so sales grew by 15%.
Why C: 30% would result from treating the $30,000 change as thousands of percent or halving the base; dividing $30,000 by $200,000 gives 15%.
Why D: 13% divides the $30,000 change by the new figure ($230,000), but percentage change uses the starting amount as the base, which gives 15%.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: On a common-size income statement, cost of goods sold is $60,000 and net sales are $150,000. What percent is shown?
Why A: On a common-size statement each item is a percent of net sales: $60,000 / $150,000 = 0.40 = 40%, so cost of goods sold uses 40 cents of each sales dollar.
Why B: 60% confuses the dollar amount ($60,000) with a percent; the item must be divided by net sales of $150,000, which gives 40%.
Why C: 90% would result from subtracting or adding the wrong amounts; the correct step is simple division of $60,000 by $150,000, which is 40%.
Why D: 250% inverts the fraction ($150,000 / $60,000 = 2.5); common-size percentages put the item on top and net sales on the bottom.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does a statement of retained earnings show for a corporation?
A: The company's sales by month of the year
B: Changes in earnings kept in the business
C: The cash balance at the end of the year
D: Money owed to suppliers for goods bought
Why A: Sales by month are reported in sales records and income statement detail, not in the statement of retained earnings, which tracks profits kept by the corporation.
Why B: The statement of retained earnings shows beginning retained earnings, plus net income, minus dividends, equal to ending retained earnings, i.e. changes in earnings kept in the business.
Why C: The cash balance at year end is reported on the balance sheet and cash flow statement, not on the retained earnings statement.
Why D: Money owed to suppliers is accounts payable, a liability on the balance sheet; retained earnings is part of stockholders' equity.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: How do dividends affect retained earnings?
A: They are recorded as revenue
B: They increase retained earnings
C: They reduce retained earnings
D: They have no effect at all
Why A: Dividends are distributions of profit to owners, not income earned from customers, so they are never recorded as revenue.
Why B: Dividends take assets out of the corporation, so retained earnings go down rather than up; they are a distribution of profit already earned.
Why C: Dividends are declared out of profits, which reduces the earnings retained by the corporation, so they are subtracted on the statement of retained earnings.
Why D: Dividends clearly affect retained earnings, because they reduce the profits the corporation keeps in the business instead of paying them to stockholders.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: In a corporation, what are paid-in capital and retained earnings parts of?
A: Stockholders' equity
B: Operating expenses
C: Cost of goods sold
D: Short-term liabilities
Why A: Paid-in capital (money invested by shareholders) and retained earnings (profits kept) are the two main components of stockholders' equity on a corporate balance sheet.
Why B: Operating expenses are costs of running the business listed on the income statement; capital and earnings are balance sheet equity accounts.
Why C: Cost of goods sold is the cost of merchandise sold, an income statement item, whereas paid-in capital and retained earnings are owners' equity accounts.
Why D: Short-term liabilities are debts due within a year; paid-in capital and retained earnings are owners' claims, not debts owed to others.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is a footnote disclosure used for?
A: To advertise the company to new customers and buyers
B: To correct arithmetic errors found after printing
C: To hide unfavorable results from all the readers
D: To give readers details that prevent misleading them
Why A: Footnotes are factual disclosures, not marketing, so they are not used to attract customers; advertising has no place in financial statements.
Why B: Correcting arithmetic errors is done by revising the statements, not by footnotes; footnotes supply explanation and additional detail beyond the numbers.
Why C: Footnotes are meant to disclose information, not to conceal it; hiding unfavorable results would violate the full disclosure principle and could be fraud.
Why D: Footnotes provide details, such as accounting policies, debts and pending lawsuits, that are needed so readers are not misled by the numbers on the face of the statements.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An audit report that states the statements fairly present financial position is called:
A: An adverse opinion
B: A qualified opinion
C: A disclaimer of opinion
D: An unqualified opinion
Why A: An adverse opinion says the statements do not fairly present the company's position; it is the opposite of a clean report.
Why B: A qualified opinion says the statements are fair except for a specific issue or limit, so it is not a fully clean opinion.
Why C: A disclaimer of opinion means the auditor could not form an opinion, often because of limits on the work, so it gives no assurance either way.
Why D: An unqualified (clean) opinion states that the statements fairly present financial position in accordance with GAAP, the best result a company can receive from an auditor.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: An investor wants to compare the profitability of two companies of different sizes. Which tool is best?
A: Common-size statements and ratios
B: The number of employees hired
C: The raw dollar totals of net income
D: The length of the annual report
Why A: Common-size statements and ratios turn dollar amounts into percentages, so firms of different sizes can be compared fairly, such as profit margin or return on assets.
Why B: The number of employees hired says nothing about profitability and is not a financial analysis tool; it reflects size, not performance.
Why C: Raw net income totals favor larger firms; a big company usually earns more dollars, so they cannot fairly compare profitability across different sizes.
Why D: The length of an annual report has no relation to profitability and says nothing about how well a company uses its resources.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What does GAAP stand for?
A: General Auditing and Accounting Procedures
B: Guaranteed Annual Accounting Practices
C: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
D: Government Approved Accounting Policies
Why A: GAAP does not stand for auditing procedures; it covers accounting principles used to prepare statements, whereas auditing has its own standards (GAAS).
Why B: GAAP stands for accepted principles, not guaranteed practices; no accounting rule guarantees results, and the word 'Guaranteed' is not in the term.
Why C: GAAP stands for Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the common rules and conventions US companies follow so their financial statements are consistent and comparable.
Why D: GAAP is not set by government approval of policies; it comes from a private standard-setting body and is described as 'generally accepted'.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which organization sets GAAP for businesses in the United States?
A: The Federal Reserve Board system
B: Financial Accounting Standards Board
C: The Internal Revenue Service (IRS)
D: The Better Business Bureau (BBB)
Why A: The Federal Reserve is the central bank that conducts monetary policy and supervises banks; it does not write GAAP for businesses.
Why B: The Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) is the independent private body that writes GAAP for US businesses and issues accounting standards updates.
Why C: The IRS administers tax law and collects taxes; it does not set GAAP, and tax rules often differ from financial accounting rules.
Why D: The Better Business Bureau is a nonprofit that rates business practices and handles consumer complaints; it has no role in setting accounting standards.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which agency requires public companies to file financial reports with it?
A: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration
B: The Federal Trade Commission of the U.S.
C: The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC)
D: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
Why A: OSHA enforces workplace safety and health rules; it does not collect financial reports from public companies.
Why B: The FTC enforces consumer protection and antitrust laws; it does not require public companies to file financial reports.
Why C: The SEC requires public companies to file annual (10-K) and quarterly (10-Q) reports so investors get reliable information; it was created in 1934.
Why D: The EPA enforces environmental regulations and does not receive companies' financial reports; its focus is pollution and environmental protection.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an audit?
A: An independent check of financial records
B: A tax payment made each quarter by a business
C: A sales forecast for the next fiscal year
D: A daily entry of transactions in the books
Why A: An audit is an independent examination of a company's financial records and statements by a qualified outside party, giving users confidence that the statements are reliable.
Why B: A quarterly tax payment is an estimated tax payment, not an audit; an audit is an examination, not a payment to the government.
Why C: A sales forecast looks ahead to expected revenue, whereas an audit examines records of past transactions and statements already prepared.
Why D: Daily entry of transactions is bookkeeping, done by the company's own staff; an audit is an independent review carried out afterward.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is an internal control?
A: A tax deduction allowed by the IRS each year
B: A rule that sets the company's goods prices
C: A law passed by Congress for all firms and banks
D: A procedure that protects assets and records
Why A: A tax deduction lowers taxable income under IRS rules; internal controls are procedures a company uses to safeguard assets and ensure accurate records.
Why B: Setting prices is a marketing and management decision; internal controls are about safeguarding assets and records, not deciding what goods cost.
Why C: Congress passes laws such as Sarbanes-Oxley that require internal controls, but a control is a company procedure, not a law.
Why D: Internal controls are policies and procedures, like approvals and separation of duties, that protect assets, ensure accurate records and help prevent errors and fraud.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: What is fraud in a business setting?
A: An honest mistake in a calculation
B: A deliberate deception for gain
C: A late payment to a vendor firm
D: A legal tax deduction by a business
Why A: An honest mistake lacks intent; fraud requires a deliberate act, so an innocent calculation error is an error, not fraud.
Why B: Fraud is intentional deception to gain an unfair or illegal advantage, such as falsifying records or stealing cash; the intent to deceive is what separates it from error.
Why C: A late payment to a vendor is a breach of payment terms, perhaps poor management, but it involves no deliberate deception, so it is not fraud.
Why D: A legal tax deduction follows the tax law and is allowed; fraud involves deception, such as claiming false deductions.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Which is an example of separation of duties?
A: The owner signs checks alone with no review at all
B: One person opens mail, and records and deposits cash
C: Everyone shares the same password for the whole system
D: One person records sales and another handles the cash
Why A: Having the owner sign checks alone with no review removes oversight, so there is no check on misuse; separation of duties requires a second person.
Why B: One person opening mail, recording and depositing cash combines custody and record-keeping, which is the opposite of separation of duties and invites theft.
Why C: Sharing one password removes accountability, because actions cannot be traced to a person; it weakens control rather than separating duties.
Why D: Splitting recording and cash handling between two people means one cannot easily steal and hide it, which is the purpose of separation of duties.
Source: FBLA 2026-2027 Competitive Events Guidelines, Objective Tests, knowledge areas

Question: Why should checks be prenumbered?
A: To make checks harder to cash for outsiders
B: To save printing costs for the firm each year
C: So missing or unauthorized checks show up
D: To meet bank interest rules for savers
Why A: Prenumbering does not stop outsiders from cashing checks; security features and endorsements handle that, while the numbers help account for every check.
